caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 225 of 1972.
lawyer:
Md. Abdul Huq ------- For the appellant. 
Akbar Ali ------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Abbas Ali Pramanik ------- Appellant.
 Vs. 
Gafur Ali Pramanik ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
This application for compromise has been jointly filed by both the appellants and respondents. The appeal arises out of a suit for partition. The learned Munsif decried the suit and on appeal the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the findings and dismissed the appeal. Hence the present appeal at the instance of the defendant-appellant.

2. According to the terms of the present compromise-perdition the second appeal should be allowed and to title suit Out of which the present appeal arise should be dismissed. At the time of hearing of the compromise-petition in the presence of the learned Advocates of both the parties it transpired from the order book of the appeal that the respondent No.11 Chand Ali Pramanik, respondent No. 23 Abul Pramanik and respondent No. 27 Mofijan Nessa were all dead according to the report in the service return and by order dated 24-6-74 abatement was recorded in respect of the aforesaid respondents namely, respondent Nos. 11,  23 and 27. Further, by the same order the Deputy Registrar was appointed Guardian adlitem in respect of the respondent No. 14 (Kha), 14 (Ga) and 11 (Gha). In the vokalatnama tiled on behalf of the respondents before this Court respondent No. 11 Chand Pramanik and respondent No. 27 Mafijan Nessa had put  their thumb impression although according to the Order Book they were already dead.

3. Confronted with this situation the learned Advocates prayed for some time and accordingly two week's adjournment was granted. Mr. Md. Abdul Huq. the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants has now filed another application for setting aside abatement of the appeal with regard to the respondent No. 23 and 27 stating that peon’s report with regard to the respondents are incorrect and they are still alive. 1 propose to deal with the said application separately but it is admitted by the learned Advocate for the appellant that respondent No. 11 Chand Ali Pramanik is dead. Furthermore, respondent No. 13 (Ga) 14 (Ka) and IS have not signed the vokalatnama. It further appears that one Abdur Rahman and one Sreeman Bewa who are not parties in the appeal have also signed the vokatatnama as respondents in the appeal.

The compromise-petition has not been, signed by any of the appellants or any of the respondents. On behalf of the 7 appellants on record. Abu Bakar Sardar appellant No. 3 has sworn the affidavit. There are 38 respondents, including the 3 deceased respondents and on their behalf respondent No. 19 Md. Ator Ali Pramanik has sworn the affidavit.

This being a partition suit, all the  respondents who were-plaintiffs in the suit are necessary parties and particularly in a compromise-petition they all must be brought of record. From the Order Book it appears that the appeal is not yet ready for final heating. The appeal stands abated so far as the respondent No. 11, 23 and 27 arc concerned. The minor respondents 14 (Kha). 14(Ga) and 14 (Gha) are not represented. Moreover, respondent Nos. 13 (Ga), 14(ka) and 18 are not parties to the compromise petition.

4. As discussed earlier, two strangers who are neither appellants nor respondents in the appeal have signed the vokalatnama filed by the respondents. I have also examined the vokalatnanta filed on behalf of the appellants. It does not, contain any authorisation to compromise the appeal on behalf of the appellants. The authority to compromise it a vital authority which must be specifically given and cannot be implied or inferred. In my opinion the petition for compromise ought to have been signed by all the appellants an specific power to compromise must be given by the executants to the Advocate concerned. In the absence of all these essential prerequisites the learned Advocate for the appellants, in my opinion, had no authority to sign the compromise-petition on behalf of the appellants even if the terms of compromise are in layout of the appellants. Similarly the compromise-petition by which the respondents are relinquishing their claim upheld by the courts below ought to have been signed by all the respondents who were plaintiffs in the suit. The affidavit in support of petition may be sworn by any one of the appellants or any one of the respondents but the deponent must he specifically empowered by the parties concerned to affirm the affidavit on their behalf and the petition must also contain a statement to that effect. These requirements are in my opinion, essential and must he fulfilled to guard against any possible fraud. When confronted with this situation. Mr. Abdul Huq and Mr. Akbar Ali, the learned Advocates appearing for the appellants and respondents respectively  had no explanation to offer. They have however. expressed their regret and offered apology. I must however, record my strong sense of disapproval of the manner the learned Advocates discharged their duties. In a situation like this they should have been more careful.

<u>5. The appeal was filed on 30th October, 1970 i.e. more than 4 years back and with a large number of respondents on record. it was the duty of the learned Advocate for the appellant to check up the Order Book. Even before the Lawazima Court on 24-6-74 when the order of abatement was passed, the learned Advocate was not present. Had he been present he would not have faced this predicament today. I have noticed a regrettable tendency on the part of some of the learned Advocate not to be present before the Lawazima Court. This case is an example that they can do so at their own risk. Any one of the appellants or the respondents except the two deponents can now come up and disown or repudiate this compromise because there is nothing in this petition that can I bind them. They have neither signed it nor there is anything to show that they have authorised these two deponents to compromise the matter on their behalf.</u>

6. The learned Advocates certainly run risk of landing themselves into serious, difficulties if they are not careful. A situation like this called for almost care and diligence on the part of the learned Advocates in the discharge of their duties both to the clients as well as to the court. Had the court felled on the submissions made by the learned Advocate without checking up the Order Book and the records, it ixht have resulted in serious miscarriage of justice.

For the reason stated above I am constrmghtined to hold that this is not a genuine compromise between the parties and accordingly the application for compromise is rejected.

7. The compromise-petition however reveals certain unfortunate and serious matters which in the interest of justice cannot be ignored. In the compromise-petition the respondent No. 11 Chand Ali Pramanik and respondent No. 37 Mafijen Nessa have been brought on record as living persons although according to the service return they are already dead. Prima fade it appears that a heinous fraud was sought to be committed upon the court. It is therefore necessary that appropriate action should be taken against the persons responsible for the frxuo sought to be committed upon the court. I have therefore, decided to issue a suo motu rule separately against the persons concerned.

End.

caseno: Second Appeal No. 07 of 1973 with C. R. No. 692 (S) of 1972.
lawyer:
S. R. Paul, with Anil Chandra Sarker ------ For the Appellants. 
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Pathan Shafiqur Rahman ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Mst. Shamser Nessa Sakeba Banoo and ors ------ Appellants.
Vs.
A.H. Mohsenuddin Ahmed & others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the defendants is directed against a decree of affirmance.

2. The respondents have brought a suit for ejectment of the defendants from a premises in the city of Dhaka on the allegations that the defendants were monthly tenants in the disputed premises; that they are habitual defaulters and also the premises is bonafide required by the plaintiffs for their own use and occupation. According to the plaint, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 to 6 took lease of the premises in suit at a monthly rent of R. 37/- for a term of 5 years from 1940 on the basis of a Kabuliat and the rent was subsequently raised to Rs. 45/- per month. The said predecessor of the defendants began to change the nature of the premises by making constructions on the premises and by cutting down many valuable trees without any consent of the lessor. Consequently the House Rent Case No. 799 of 1956 was started for permission to sue the predecessor of the defendants for eviction and the necessary permission was granted by the House Rent Controller. But against this order of the House Rent Controller, the defendants who were in the meant the substituted in the House Rent Control case on the death of their predecessor filed an appeal which was also dismissed and a revision case which was filed in the High Court against the said order of dismissal of the appeal was also dismissed. The plaintiffs, thereafter, have brought this suit for eviction as well as for recovery of arrears of rent and for compensation after terminating the tenancy by serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

3. The defendants have contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that there was not valid and legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, that the defendants took the suit premises on lease for doing business by establishing printing and publishing machinery, that the defendants have constructed one ekchala pucca C. I. sheet for his type foundry business and another two storied building with C. I. sheet roof for his printing and publishing business and that they have spent about Rs. 35,000/- towards such construction. The Dhaka Municipality considering the dilapidated condition of the building sent a notice under section 364 of the Municipal Act whereupon The predecessor of the defendants instituted Title Suit No. 67 of 1956 in the 6th Court of Munsif at Dhaka for permanent injunction purporting to restrain the Municipality and its officers from demolishing the building in question and subsequently the predecessor of the defendants constructed some portion of the suit premises at a cost of Rs. 1619/8/- paisa with the consent of the plaintiff's predecessor. The defendants have also paid the Municipal Tax, Urban Property Tax and Wasa Taxes payable by the defendants and their predecessor amounting to Rs. 7046/50 paisa, that they are entitled to have the aforesaid amount paid by them adjusted against the rent of the premises, and as such the defendants are not defaulters, that they have been depositing rent in House Rent Case No. 1158 of 1964 and that as such they are not defaulters. The case of the plaintiffs that they require the suit premises for their own use and occupation has also been denied.

4. At the trial one for the points which was argued was that the tenancy was for manufacturing purpose and therefore it was not a monthly tenancy and as such the notice which was issued in the case purporting to terminate the tenancy by the end of the month treating the defendants as monthly tenants was not sufficient. The trial Court came to the finding on this question that the tenancy was a monthly one and as such the notice which was issued in this case was sufficient. The trial Court has also found that the defendants are habitual defaulters and that the plaintiffs require the house bonafide for their own use and occupation. On the basis of the said finding, the learned Munsif decreed the suit for ejectment as well as for arrear rents and for compensation as was claimed in the plaint.

5. On an appeal which was preferred against the said decree it was heard by the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca and the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed all the findings of the learned Munsif on the question of the nature of the tenancy and sufficiency of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act as well as on the question of the defendants being defaulters and the plaintiffs bonafide requirement of the premises in suit for their own use and occupation. The Court of appeal below, however, reduced the decreetal amount of Rs. 1620/- as arrear rent to Rs. 1422/50 paisa and affirmed the decree of the trial Court on all other matters.

6. In this Second appeal, Mr. S.R. Paul, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, has contended, firstly, that the Courts below committed an error of law in failing to note that the disputed tenancy was for manufacturing purpose and as such the purported notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act treating the defendants as monthly tenants was not valid and therefore there was no termination of the tenancy. Secondly, the Courts below erred in law in not holding that the money spent by the defendants or their predecessor for effecting reconstruction of the structure as well as the payment made on account of Municipal Tax, Urban Property duty and Wasa Tax are adjustable against the arrear rent under law and thirdly, the findings of the Courts below that the disputed premises was bonafide required by the plaintiffs for their own use and occupation was without any basis and as such not sustainable in law.

7. On the question of the nature of the tenancy and sufficiency of the notice, it has been argued in the Courts below that the tenancy in question was for manufacturing purpose and as such 6 months’ notice was required for termination of the said tenancy, on the basis that such a case has been pleaded in the written statement 'filed by the defendants but on a reference to the written statement I find that no such clear case has been made out in this written statement. The contention of the defendants in this regard has been stated in paragraph 6 of the written statement. In order to appreciate the defence case on this question, it will be useful to quote the following averments made in the written statement :

"6. That the defendants state their cases in brief as follows :—

(a) that the predecessor of the defendants took monthly lease of the demised premises with effect from 7-4-1940 for a contracted period of 5 years running from the said date with the option of renewal and registered therefor it Kabuliyat in favour of the plaintiff No. 7 and the predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 1-6.

(b) That on the expiry of the said contracted period of 5 years the predecessor of the defendants and after him the defendants are in possession of the demised premises in monthly tenancy right and that the said tenancy commences from the 7th day of every English Calendar month.

(c) That the initial monthly rent of Rs. 37/- was subsequently increased and raised to Rs. 45/-.

(d) that the predecessor of the defendant took the monthly lease of the demised premises for the purpose of running his printing and publishing business by setting up printing machineries and type foundry machineries in the demised premises. The predecessor of the defendants published a daily newspaper named 'Insan' from his said press and also published other books to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and their predecessors. The predecessor of the defendants ran his printing and publishing business under the name and style of 'Baliadi printing' and his Type-Foundry business under the name and style of M/s. Saiyed Type Foundry Corporation" and after him the defendants are carrying the said business in the demised premises as before to the knowledge and consent of the plaintiffs and their predecessor.

(e)

(f) that the lease was primarily for manufacturing business as stated above. In the demised premises there was, no doubt, one small building for residential purpose in which the defendants and their predecessor used to live.

(g)

(h) that the monthly tenancy was not according to English Calendar month but rent was payable according to English Calendar month. The tenancy was primarily for manufacturing purposes.

8. It will appear from the defense pleading as stated above that the defense case is that this is a monthly tenancy although in paragraph 6 sub-paragraphs (f) and (h) it has been stated that it was for manufacturing purposes but nowhere it has been averred that it was a yearly lease and the notice required for termination of such a lease was 6 months’ notice under section 106 of the Act. It has, of course, been asserted that although rent is payable according to the English Calendar month, the monthly tenancy is not according to English Calendar month but is to commence from the 7th day of every English Calendar month presumably because the Kabuliyat was executed on the 7th April, 1940.

9. The issues which were framed on the basis of the said pleadings also do not disclose that the defendants were claiming that it was a yearly lease. Issues Nos. 1 and 2 are to the following effect:—

"1. Is the notice u/s 106 of T.P. Act sufficient and proper ; if so, is it validly and properly served upon the defendant ?

2. Is the tenancy determined by due service of valid notice?

10. The issues, framed as they are, also do not throw any light for the purpose of showing that the defendants claimed that it was a yearly lease and six months’ notice was necessary for determination of such a lease.

11. However, both the courts below have approached the evidence on record as if the defendants tried to make out a case that the tenancy was for manufacturing purpose and as such it was a lease from year to year and the notice required for termination of this lease was a 6 months’ notice.

<u>12. It will appear from the averments made in the written statement that although it has been claimed that it was for manufacturing purposes but the dominant purpose is residential so far as the main building is concerned and the carrying out of the printing and publishing business in the rest of the premises. It has been clearly stated in the sub-para (d) of paragraph 6 of the written statement that the defendants took monthly lease of the demised premises for the purpose of running his printing and publishing business by setting up printing machineries and type foundry machineries in the demised premises. The setting up of type-foundry machineries as has been mentioned in the written statement appears to be ancillary and subsidiary to their main printing and publishing business. On a perusal of the written statement in does not appear that the defendants sought to make out a case that the main purpose was the type foundry business which may be contended to be kind or manufacturing business but the main purpose seems to be, according to the said written statement, the printing and publishing business.</u>

13. Mr. S. R. Paul, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants has submitted at the outset—I think rightly—that he is not going to contend that printing and publishing business is a kind of manufacturing business but that he will contend that both the Courts below have erred in law in misconstruing the Kabuliyat Ext. 1 and failing to hold that the purpose of the lease was also type foundry business, which was a manufacturing purpose. Mr. Paul has tried to show by reference to the terms of the contract as embodied in said Kabuliyat ,that the purpose deducible from the said terms of the contract is a manufacturing on e and the learned Advocate has laid much stress on the word ‘ইত্যাদি’ used in term No. 2 of the Kabuliyat. But, as it has been pointed out by the learned Subordinate Judge, if the language used in this term No. 2 of the Kabuliyat is scrutinized, it will appear that the word ‘ইত্যাদি’ has not been used at all in stating the kinds of things which the lessee would be permitted to do on the premises in question. In that term the defendants' predecessor actually said that he would not set up the printing machine etc. in the main building, but he would construct a C. I. sheet but on the vacant space at his own costs and set up a printing machine in the said hut, 'et'c (‘ইত্যাদি’) has been used in connection with the things which the lessee was not permitted to do but not in connection with the things which the lessee was allowed to do in the premises. Of course, I do not think that much difference could have been made by repeating the word ‘ইত্যাদি’ in the second sentence also, because by applying the 'ejusdem generis rule, the word ‘ইত্যাদি’ should connote things of the same kind or nature as the preceding word i.e. ‘ছাপার মেসিন’, and it requires too much stretching of imagination to think that the parties to the Kabuliyat Ext. 1 conceived at the time of execution of the said deed that the word ‘ইত্যাদি’ should cover type-foundry business as well.

14. Apart from this, it has been admitted by the defendants on a number of occasions in the past that the tenancy in question was a monthly one and the business which he was to carry on on the premises in question is a printing and publishing business. In the plaint of the suit being T. S. No. 67 of 1956 of the 6th Court of Munsif, Dhaka (Ext. E) the predecessor of the defendants Mi. A. H. Sayed who instituted the aforesaid suit for permanent injunction against the Municipal Commissioners and the Chairman of the Dhaka Municipality stated that he had been running extensive business in printing and publishing on the said premises. He did not state that he had any type foundry business or any manufacturing business there. In a petition, which was filed by the defendants predecessor to the Commissioner of the Municipality on 8. 4. 57 for certifying that the cost of Rs. 1619/13 paisa incurred by him was to be borne by the owners and a copy of which has been marked Ext. 1, the defendants' predecessor stated in paragraph I of the said petition that he was a monthly tenant of the premises in question. I do not, therefore, think that the construction which has been sought to be put upon the words used in Term No. 2 of the Kabuliat Ext. 1 for the purpose of showing that the tenancy was for manufacturing purpose is at all consistent with the words used in the said term or with the conduct of the parties and hence I do not find any reason to interfere with the findings of the Courts below on this question.

15. On the question of the defendants being defaulters, Mr. Paul, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has contended that the defendants are entitled to adjustment of the repairing costs amounting to Rs. 1619/80 paisa as well as the amount of Rs. 7040/4 5 paisa paid by the defendants on amount of the plaintiffs' dues by way of Municipal Tax, Urban Property Tax and Wasa charges against the arrear rent as a matter of right under law and if such adjustments arc allowed, the defendants could not be regarded as defaulters. In support of his above contention, Mr. Paul has referred to the provisions of section 108 Clause (f) and (g) of the T. P. Act which are to the following effect :—

"108. In the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, the lessor and the lessee of immovable property, as against one another, respectively possess the rights and are subject to the liabilities mentioned in the Rules next following, or such of them as are applicable to the property leased :—

(f) If the lessor neglects to make, within a reasonable time after notice, any repairs which he is bound to make to the property, the lessee may make the same himself, and deduct the expenses of such repairs with interest from the rent, or otherwise recover it from the lessor.

(g) if the lessor neglects to make any payment which he is bound to make, and which, if not made by him, is recoverable from the lessee or against the property, the lessee may make such payment himself, and deduct it with interest from the rent or otherwise, recover it from the lessor.

16. Mr. Paul has contended that sub-section (5) of section 18 of the East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 which requires a tenant to pay rent due by him in respect of the tenancy regularly if he wants to take benefit of the provisions of section 18(1) of the Ordinance is not in derogation of his right which he may have under the provisions of section 108 of the T. P. Act and as such, if the conditions as mentioned in the said provisions can be proved to have been in existence, then a tenant is, as a matter of right, entitled to the adjustment by paying himself off from the rent which he is required to pay to the lessor under the terms of the tenancy and recover the balance which has been spent by the tenant in excess of what is actually payable by the tenant by way of rent in respect of the said premises.

17. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents has submitted that with regard to the expenditure on account of repairs of the building, it is the finding of the Courts below that no consent of the lessor was taken in this case, as required under the terms of the Kabuliat Ext. 1 and secondly, this expenditure of Rs. 1691/80 paisa was made before 1956 and therefore irrespective of the question whether the consent was taken as required under Ext. 1 or notice was given as required under sub-section (f) of section 108, no adjustment of the rent fallen due prior to 1956 could have been made against this payment, and such payment was of no avail to the defendants predecessor who had already become a defaulter, as admittedly no payment of rent was being made since 1949.

18. Mr. Paul, the learned Advocate for the appellants has then submitted that in that case the payment of the Municipal Tax and other taxes as have been made by the defendants or their predecessor may be taken into consideration. The defendants have proved Municipal tax receipts, Exts. A series, covering the period from December, 1958 to December, 1968, Chalans Ext. B series showing deposit of rent in H. R. Case No. 1158 of 1964 since 9. 4. 65, Wasa bills with payment endorsements, Ext. C series for the period from 1965-1968 and a chalan dated 24. 3. 1965, Ext. D showing payment of Rs. 104-69 paisa as a Govt. Tax. They have also got the Collection Register of the Municipality proved as Ext. H series showing payment of Municipal taxes for a period prior to the period covered by the Municipal tax receipts Ext. A series. It does not appear that any evidence has been adduced in this case to show that the lessors neglected to make any payment which they were bound to make or that such payment was being make with the consent or on the basis of some agreement with the lessors. Apart from that, of the payments which has been sought to be proved by the Municipal Receipts Ext. A series and Collection Register of the Municipality, Ext. H. series, the earliest payment made by the tenant was pointed out by the learned Advocate for the appellants to be Ext. H which shows that the first payment of Rs. 68/8 annas was made on 17. 9. 53 and the second payment of Rs. 78/8 annas was made on 22. 3. 54. But I find on examination of the records that there are two other documents viz. Ext. H(I) and Ext. 1-1(14) showing earlier payment of Municipal taxes, Ext. H(14) shows payment of Municipal taxes amounting to Rs. 78/8 annas on 10. 7. 50 and another payment of the same amount on 12. 10. 50, while Ext. H(1) shows payments on 29. 7. 52 and 25. 10. 52. On an analysis of these payments it will be clear that he predecessor of the defendants had already become a defaulter before the payment of the Municipal Taxes by him on behalf of his lessors commenced on 10. 7. 50. Secondly it will appear from the records that such payments were not regular and had been made at intervals and such payment cannot be deemed to be due payment within the meaning of the East Bengal Premises Rent Control Ordinance. Thirdly event if it is assumed that the lessee had been making regular payment of Municipal Taxes on behalf of his lessors, such payment could not prevent him from becoming a defaulter because the total amount of Municipal taxes due in course of a year was less than the total amount of rent payable during that year.

19. The other question in this connection considered by the Court of Appeal below was that the defendants deposited rent by the Chalan Ext. B series on the 8th April, 1965 in respect of the period from January, 1964 to March, 1965 in the House Rent Control Case No. 1158/64 which was started in the latter part of 1964. Now this lump payment of rent for the period of 15 months is a clear evidence of the fact that the lessees became defaulters. This deposit prima facie shows that the defendants were not claiming adjustment with respect to the rent for this period and no evidence has been adduced to show that this payment was made under protest in spite of the previous adjustment. I do not, therefore, think that there is any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate that the finding of the Courts below on this question of default was in any way wrong.

<u>20. The question of bonafide requirement, as has been argued by the learned Advocate for the appellants is, in my opinion, in the present case essentially a question of fact. Evidence has been adduced by the plaintiffs to sow that excepting plaintiff No. 3 none of the plaintiffs have got their own house at Dhaka. Plaintiff No. 1 has been living in a rented house bearing a monthly rent of Tk. 300/- and plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 have 20 children. Mr. Paul has contended that the evidence on record shows that they have been well-accommodated in different houses. It is argued by the learned Advocate that plaintiff No. 1 is living in a rented house and since it has not been shown that his continuance as tenant in the said house is in jeopardy either by service of notice to quiet on them or otherwise, it cannot be held that the plaintiffs required the house bonafide for his own use and occupation. I do not think that the extreme test which has been sought to be applied by the learned Advocate in the present case is either warranted by the provision of the law or supported by any authority. The use of the term 'require' certainly indicates something more than a mere wish or fancy and it involves an element of need, that is to say, it does not connote a mere subjective phenomenon, but has also an objective import. The use of the qualifying word 'bonafide' along with the word 'require' tries to limit the scope of the subjective aspect of the landlords feeling of need for his house, although the word 'bonafide', the equivalent of which is 'honestly' is essentially a subjective concept. The Legislature seems to convey by using the words 'bonafide require' a kind of genuine feeling of need and not a colourable pretext. Chunder, J of Calcutta High Court, in interpreting a similar expression in an analogous West Bengal Act has observed in the case of Sri Naresh alias Narendra Chandra Sarkar Vs. Kanai Lal Roy Chowdhury, 56 C.W.N. 480 that there is an element of 'must have' in the need of the landlord and this want or need of the house must be genuinely felt by him. The priniciple laid down in the aforesaid case was followed in two single Judge decisions of the Dacca High Court. Viz. Jagadish Chandra Sarkar Vs. Abdul Aziz, 7 D.L.R. 314 (Akbar J) and MuIla Mahbub Ali and others. Vs. Janab Ali, 8 D.L.R. 448 (Rahman J). The learned Judges however made it clear in those two decisions that the expression 'bonafide require' implies a genuine present need but it does not go to the extent of saying that there must be absolute need or absolute necessity. The expression, therefore, connotes an honest feeling of need for the house and in ultimate analysis, it is a question of fact which is to be determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case.</u>

21. The plaintiffs have their house at Dhaka which is the disputed premises and it is fetching them a monthly rent of Rs. 45/- only. One of the plaintiffs has been constrained to hire a house at a monthly rent of Rs. 300/-. There seems to be sufficient space in the disputed premises on which new constructions can be made and it is the case of the plaintiffs in their plaint and in evidence that the plaintiffs require the premises for their own use and occupation and for making addition and alternation of the premises. Mr. Paul has drawn my attention to a certain statement made by P. W. 1 in cross-examination to the effect that they would build their respective buildings over the land of the disputed premises after partition among themselves as soon as the tenants were evicted. I do not see how this statement of P. W. 1 belies the plaintiffs' case of genuine need of the house nor does their statement appear to be in consistent with the case made out in the plaint. Nothing has been brought to my notice to show that the finding of the Courts below on this question have in any way been vitiated by any error which can be termed as an error of law. I do not think that there is any substance in any of the contentions of the learned Advocate of the appellants. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed with cots.

Leave under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent appeal as prayed for, is refused. The connected Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

Three months’ time is granted to the defendant—appellants for vacating the premises.

End.

lawyer:
Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury with Abul Kashem Sarker Advocates -------- For the Petitioners, 
Md Khalilur Rahman, Advocate -------- For the Opposite Parties,
parties:
Abdul Latif (Md) -------- Petitioners
Vs.
 Mohammad Ali  -------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 to 19 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 7-2-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Kurigram in Other Appeal No. 36 of 1993 affirming those dated 31-5-1993 passed by the Assistant Judge, Fulbari in Other Suit No. 23 of 1989 (Partition) should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiffs filed Other Suit No. 23 of 1989 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Fulbari, Kurigram for a decree of partition.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the properties as shown in Ka schedule of the plaint appertaining to CS Khatian No. 263 and 381 originally, was held by Jahar Uddin having 8 annas share, Ziaullah and Jamil Masud having 4 annas, each under the superior landlord and they were in ejmali possession of the suit jot and while possessing the same, Jaharuddin died leaving behind one son plaintiff  No. 1. Sona Bibi died leaving behind full sister, Sundari Bewa and thereafter Sundari Bewa died leaving behind two sons, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and one daughter defendant No. 1. The daughter of Sundari Bewa died before her mother, leaving behind one daughter and Galimuddin died leaving behind two daughters, Sakhina and Sakeron. One of the daughters died leaving behind one son plaintiff No.3, and, on the death of Amena, her share devolved upon her full sister, thereafter Sakhina died leaving her daughter, plaintiff No. 2 and there after Ziaullah died leaving one son Ilyasuddin and one daughter Menerunnessa. Elimuddin during his life time settled 66 decimals of land from plot Nos. 1 and 2 of Ka schedule and Kha schedule properties by a registered patta dated 9-2-1945 to plaintiff No. 1 and he has been possessing the land since then but the original patta was lost during the War of Liberation.

4. Defendant Nos. 6 and 35 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the case is barred by law of limitation and the plaintiff has got no possession and that the defendants were possessing the land adversely against the plaintiff and the genealogy given by the plaintiff in the plaint is not proper. The plaintiffs have intentionally suppressed facts and have not allotted any share which Ziaullah was entitled as residuary and thus the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit.

6. Being aggrieved thereby, the defendants preferred appeal before the District Judge, Kurigram which was transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Court No. 2, Kurigram for disposal. The Court of Appeal below affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved thereby, the defendants as petitioners filed an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the Court of appeal below passed the judgment and the decree without applying its judicial mind. He then submits that the judgment of the Court of Appeal below was passed in a slipshod manner and the Court did not discuss the evidence adduced by the parties. He further submits that the Courts below passed the judgments on mistaken views of law and facts and thus resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He next submits that the Courts below have failed to frame any issue on the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the present Partition Suit although possession in a suit for Partition is very much material, which ought to have been decided by framing and discussing issues. He also submits that all the persons having interest of title in the suit property were not brought on record for the proper adjudication of the matter and as the defect of parties is a very vital question in a Partition Suit, non- impleading of interested persons is a sufficient ground for dismissal of the suit.

9. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, files a counter-affidavit and submits that the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their case and have obtained relief from the Courts below. He next submits that considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence on record, the trial Court granted saham in the Partition Suit to the plaintiffs and the Lower Appellate Court affirmed the judgment passed by the trial Court on the basis of materials on record and there being no error in the decision and more so, no failure of justice being occasioned to the defendant-petitioners, the Rule is liable to be discharged. The learned Advocate submits that the trial Court decreed the suit rightly and the Court of Appeal below very cogently and legally dismissed the appeal. He submits that the scope of interference with the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is very limited and when the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below are supported by evidence on record and there being no error of law involving the case, there is no scope for interference in revision. In support to his contention, the learned Advocate has referred a decision as reported in 11 MLR 92. He points out that a mere denial by the defendant as to the title of the plaintiff in any portion of the property in a Partition Suit would not convert a Partition Suit into a declaratory suit for title and for possession and hence the contention that the Partition Suit is not maintainable without a declaratory suit for title, as it involves disputed question of title, as presented by the learned Advocate for the petitioner has no substance. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has referred to a decision as reported in 34 DLR 127.

<u>10. I have heard the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners and opposite parties and perused the revisional application, counter-affidavit along with other materials on record. It appears that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiff filed a Suit for partition in respect of 6.91-123/145 decimals of land as stated in the schedule of the plaint. The trial Court decreed the suit in preliminary form in respect of 6.91 decimals of land and the Court of Appeal below on hearing the parties dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. In a Partition Suit, disputed questions of title may be involved and such questions are to be decided by the Court trying the suit. A mere denial by a defendant as to the title of the plaintiff in any portion of the property in a Partition Suit would not convert a Partition Suit into a declaratory suit for title and a suit for possession, as the jurisdiction of a Civil Court in case of a Partition Suit could not be placed at the mercy of every profligate defendant to render the Court a mere ministerial agent only to carry into effect the wishes of the parties in case where there were no matters of controversy between them. It cannot be said that the present Partition Suit is not maintainable without a declaratory suit for title as it involved disputed question of title. The plaintiff is entitled to maintain a Suit for Partition if his possession in some part of the joint property is admitted or established. Partition signifies the transformation of joint possession into separate possession and the suit does not cease to be one for partition, merely because the defendants denies the title of the plaintiff to a share of the estate or to specific land of the estate and asserts a hostile title and adverse possession therein as in the present case. It is the claim of the plaintiff that Sajimuddin, being not a very intelligent person, deputed Elimuddin for recording the record of rights of the disputed jote and as the settlement officers made their camp in the house of Elimuddin during the survey, taking advantage to that situation, Elimuddin got the record of rights recorded in his name along with others. The Courts below found that there was no reason for getting the property recorded in the name of Elimuddin and others and believed that Elimuddin got the property recorded in his name along with others in a collusive manner. The plaintiff claimed that on 5-2-1980, defendants Nos. 5 and 6 and plaintiff No. 1 entered into an agreement of compromise and agreed that the record in the name of Elimuddin was wrong in which defendants Nos. 5 and 6 put their signatures and the said compromise agreement was produced before the Court by the plaintiff by way of Exhibit 3 and the trial Court compared the signature of defendant No.6 as in the compromise agreement and in the written statement and determined that the signature is of the same person Md Abdul Latif. On consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, the trial Court came to the finding that the plaintiff is the co-sharer of the disputed jote and is entitled to get the saham of 6.91-123/145 decimals of land by virtue of inheritance and pattan. The Court of Appeal below affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. The appellate Court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial Court must independently consider the evidence on record but in the case of affirming the findings of the trial Court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial Court are not essential. In such a case, expressions of general agreement with those of the trial Court are generally considered sufficient. It is not the duty of the appellate Court when it agrees with the view of the trial Court on the evidence either to restate the effect of the evidence or to reiterate the reasons given by the trial Court. Expression of general agreement with reasons given by the Court decision of which is under appeal would ordinarily suffice.</u>

11. It appears that the trial Court as well as the Lower Appellate Court considered all aspects thoroughly and concurrently found that the plaintiffs succeeded to prove their case. The decisions of both the Courts below, being based on facts, circumstances and evidence on record and there being concurrent findings over the points in issue and there being found no error of law or fact in passing the impugned judgment, I am of the opinion that the impugned judgment and decree do not warrant any interference by this Court.

12. Since both the Courts below on proper assessment of the evidence on record came to a concurrent finding, this finding is binding upon this Court unless it is shown that there is misreading or non-consideration of material evidence on record in arriving at such finding. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has failed to make out such a case.

13. The judgment of the Courts below are not tainted with legal infirmity and perversity justifying interference. After examining the record of the case and hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties, I am of the view that there are sufficient evidence and materials on record to come to the decisions which have been arrived at by the Courts below.

14. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgments of the Courts below stand maintained.

Send down the lower Court records and a copy of the judgment and order to the Court concerned.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated May 13, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision. No. 2335 of 1992).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: Appellants are the heirs of plaintiff Afsaruddin. The appeal has been filed against the judgment dated May 13, 1997 in Civil Revision No. 2335 of 1992 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree dated July 6, 1992 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 185 of 1968 affirming the judgment and decree dated March 30, 1968 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka in Title Suit No. 22 of 1967 decreeing the suit. The suit was tiled seeking declaration of title, recovery of khas possession and for separate saham upon partition of the land in suit.

2. It was the case of the plaintiff that the land of CS plot No. 366 of CS khatian No. 335 of Mouza Bara Maghbazar belonged to Abdul Gafur. He sold the same on October 31, 1932 to the defendant Nos.14, who are brothers. Defendant No.4 while in possession of his share to the extent of 4 annas, he transferred his said 4 annas share to his wife Safatunnessa by a Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated July 22rd 1942. Safatunnessa while in possession sold the land what she got by Heba-bil-Ewaz deed from her husband to the plaintiff Afsaruddin by the kahala datad January 22, 1953 and she delivered possession to the plaintiff.

3. The defendant No. 1's predecessor, Sheikh Imanuddin filed Miscellaneous Case (preemption) No. 62 of 1956 under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act seeking pre-emption of the transfer made by Safatunnessa Bibi to the plaintiff and at one stage of the Miscellaneous Case the defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiff from the land in suit and since then plaintiff is out of possession of the land in suit. The Miscellaneous Case was dismissed on August 2, 1958 being barred by limitation.

4. The defendant No.1 contested the suit. His case is that he purchased the entire land of CS plot No. 366 with his own money in his name and in the benami of his 3 minor brothers, that his brothers had never owned and possessed any part of the land of CS plot No. 366, that Heba-bil-Ewaz deed of defendant No. 4 in favour of his wife Safatunnessa is a forged document and, as such, plaintiff has not acquired any title by purchase from Safatunnessa. At one stage of the suit defendant No.1 filed an application on November 21, 1966 under section 4 of the Partition Act (Act No.4 of 1893) with the prayer for allowing him to buy back 4 annas share in the suit property (plot) on the ground that the suit plot i.e. CS plot No.366, is the undivided dwelling homestead of the defendant No.1 and the plaintiff being a stranger purchaser and outsider having no blood relationship with him should not be allowed to live with him in the suit homestead.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff by his purchase has acquired good title to 4 annas share of the suit plot, that defendant No.16 who is a stranger as well as other strangers are in possession of some portion of the suit plot since their purchase, that defendant No.1 and his wife have "accommodated a number of strangers in the suit plot long after the plaintiff's purchase", that entire suit plot is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No: 1, that defendant No.1 "is not legally entitled to buyout the plaintiff's share in the suit plot under section 4 of the Partition Act and that if it is presumed that plaintiff has right to buy back then, in that case he is to pay Taka 63,636 as the price of the plaintiff's share of the suit plot".

6. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, contesting defendant went on appeal. The appellant before the appellate Court primarily challenged the finding of the trial Court that the defendant was legally not competent to buyout the plaintiff's 4 annas share of the suit plot under section 4 of the Partition Act. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on the finding that plaintiff by his purchase from Safatunnessa, who was the rightful owner, acquired title to the extent of 4 annas in the land of CS plot No. 366 i.e. the plot in suit, that as the strangers are already in possession of the land of plot in suit, the claim of the appellant that the suit plot is an undivided homestead is not tenable in law that defendant dispossessed the plaintiff is a more or less admitted fact, that the suit plot as is not undivided "hut of the defendant No.1 he is not entitled to get the suit property as a part of his own undivided homestead" and in the background of the evidence on record the defendant No.1 is not entitled to buyout the suit property under section 4 of the Partition Act.

7. It appears that at one stage of the appeal defendant No.1, Shaikh Imanuddin died. After the disposal of the appeal defendant No. 1's heirs moved the High Court Division against the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing "Since the suit land is a part and parcel of land where other 3 brothers have got dwelling house, it is an adjacent land and part of the suit plot. It is admitted that the plaintiff-opposite party is a stranger purchaser In the instant case, it is found that the suit land is a contiguous parcel of an undivided homestead upon which house of the defendant No.1 and other members of his family is .situated. Though the suit land is stated in the kabala as chala land, it is a part of undivided homestead plot and that portion of the land is necessary for common use of the undivided family which has not been partitioned previously..... . adjacent buildings, garden, courtyard, orchard and all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of the house is a part of the dwelling house. So, the suit land though stated in the kabala as chala land, is a part of dwelling house. The petitioner, in his petition under section 4 of the Partition Act, stated that the suit land is a part of his own undivided homestead. So, the prayer made by the petitioner in the trial Court under section 4 of the Partition Act is considered legal", that Courts below overlooked the fact that the land claimed by the plaintiff is part of undivided homestead and thereupon arrived at the wrong finding, particularly the appellate Court, that the suit land is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No.1, that the other strangers' purchaser of the part of the some portion of the plot No. 366 "are compromising persons" and they have been accommodated by the defendant No.1 and the other cosharers and that those strangers having been accepted by the cosharers but plaintiff who is a stranger having not been accepted by the other co sharers, particularly defendant No.1. Plaintiff because of the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act cannot be allowed to come on the land forcibly purchased by him, that the appellate Court was in serious error in holding "the suit land is not the part of dwelling house of an undivided family".

8. It may be mentioned defendant No. 1 did not depose in support of the statement made in paragraph 3 of the petition filed under section 4 of the Partition Act. He has also not led any evidence to substantiate his claim that the land in suit i.e. 4 annas share of CS plot No.366, purchased by the plaintiff is the part of the dwelling house of an undivided family. From the defendants side 3 witnesses were examined and the said witnesses deposed about the prevalent price of the land in the locality. There is nothing in the evidence of the 3 DWs that the land in suit is part of the dwelling house of an undivided family i.e. dwelling house of the defendant No. 1.

9. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the Courts below having concurrently found that the suit properly is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No.1, the High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the concurrent finding of fact, that having regard to the facts that the preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1956 filed by the defendant No. 1, predecessor of the respondent Nos. 1-8, for preemption of the suit property was dismissed and the wife of defendant No. 1 transferred some portion of the suit property to strangers who are now in possession of the land of the suit plot, the High Court Division erred in law in finding that the suit land is part of the dwelling house of defendant No.1.

10. The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act does not contemplate that some stranger purchasers are to be accepted or accommodated by the members of the undivided family' in respect of their dwelling house and other strangers would not be accepted and that defendant No.1 having had accepted defendant No. 16 and some other strangers who made their purchase subsequent to plaintiff's purchase in his dwelling house, he is not, because of the said fact, entitled to buyout the 4 annas share of the plaintiff in CS plot No. 366 under the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act. The learned Counsel has also submitted that the High Court Division on wrong interpretation of the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act set aside the findings and decisions of the Courts below which are based on due consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, on the record that the defendant is not legally competent to discriminate between the plaintiff who, according to the defendant No.1, is a stranger and the other strangers who have purchased land of the suit plot from the defendant No.1’s wife and other cosharers of the land of the plot in suit and thereupon, taking recourse to the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act, made the prayer to buyout the share of the plaintiff, that the finding of the High Court Division that land in suit is part of dwelling house of undivided family of the defendant No.1 is based on no evidence, that finding of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court that the land in suit is not part of the dwelling house has not been reversed by the High Court Division.

11. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that when the finding of a Court as regard to a certain contention of a party in the suit, determination whereof has the bearing on the result of the suit, is not based on evidence, the same has always been considered by the Court as an error of law and, in support of the said contention, has referred to the case of Syed Yakoob vs KS Radhakrishnan reported in AIR 1964 SC 477.

12. Although it was the contention of the defendant that the plaintiff by his purchase from Safatunnessa did not acquire any title since the land of plot No. 366 was purchased by him in his name and in the benami of his 3 minor brothers, one of whom was Safatunnessa's husband but that was not established and that said contention of the defendant was contrary to his stand taking which defendant filed case seeking preemption of the transfer to plaintiff but same was dismissed. It is the case of the plaintiff that Safatunnessa by Heba-bil-Ewaz deed got the property in suit from her husband and she having been in possession of the land in suit transferred the sane to the plaintiff. The trial Court as well as' appellate Court on the basis of the evidence, both oral and documentary, concurrently held that the plaintiff has title in the land in suit. The said Courts also held that defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiff from the land in suit.

<u>13. The defendant No.1 filed Miscellaneous Case seeking preemption in respect of the transfer made by Safatunnessa to the plaintiff but the said preemption case was dismissed being time barred. During the pendency of the preemption case defendant No.1 having had dispossessed the plaintiff, he (the plaintiff) filed the suit seeking declaration of title, khas possession and separate saham of 4 annas share from the land of CS plot No. 366 on partition of the land of the said plot. As stated hereinbefore that the defendant contested the suit taking two grounds. One was that plaintiff did not acquire any title by his purchase from Safatunnessa and that he at one stage of the suit filed an application under section 4 of the Partition Act to buyout the property purchased by the plaintiff on the contention that the land in suit is part of dwelling house of an undivided family. Before the lower appellate Court mainly it was argued that the property in suit being part of the dwelling house of an undivided family, the trial Court was in error in not allowing the prayer of the defendant No.1 to buy out the property in suit under section 4 of the Partition Act. The said contention of the appellant was not accepted by the appellate Court upon assigning reason. The High Court Division set aside the concurrent finding of the Court of facts that the property in suit is not part of the dwelling house of the undivided family on the view that the land in suit is contiguous to the homestead of defendant No.1 and that the defendant for convenient occupation of his house requires the hind in suit. It has already been mentioned that the defendant No.1 has not deposed in the case nor he has led any evidence to establish that the land in suit is part of the dwelling house of the undivided family to establish the fact as considered by the High Court Division while setting aside the finding of the Court of facts that the land in suit is not part of the dwelling house of an undivided family. From the pleading of the defendant and the evidence led from his side we do not find any foundation was laid by the defendant No.1 for availing the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act to buyout the land which the plaintiff purchased from Safatunnessa or, in other words, defendant has not established any case for buying out the land in suit under section 4 of the Partition Act. Defendant in a suit for partition to avail the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act is required to establish that the person seeking partition is stranger purchaser from the cosharer(s) of dwelling house of an undivided family. In the instant case, the defendant No.1 although filled an application under section 4 of the Partition Act stating that the suit property is the internal part of the homestead of this defendant No.1 and the plaintiff being a foreigner and outsider and has got no blood relation with this defendant and, as such, he cannot be allowed to remain or to live in the said suit property, with the members of this defendant on taking possession of the same". So, it is seen that defendant No.1 intended to buy the property purchased by the plaintiff on the ground that the property so purchased by the plaintiff "is the internal part" of the homestead or the defendant No.1. The defendant did not lead any evidence to substantiate the contention that. the suit property is "internal part" of his homestead. In that state of the matter the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court concurrently held that property purchased by the plaintiff is not part of the dwelling house of an undivided family or, in other words, is not part of the homestead of the defendant No.1. Since the defendant No.1 did not establish any case to buy out the property in suit as per provision of section 4 of the Partition Act, the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that the land in suit is part of the dwelling house of the undivided family of the defendant No.1 and thereupon in setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment of the trial Court which decreed the suit.</u>

14. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the High Court Division was in serious error in setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment of the trial Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction when the judgments of the Courts below were based on due consideration of the evidence on record. The learned Counsel also submits that the High Court Division was quite unmindful of the extent of its revisional jurisdiction in interfering with the finding of the last Court of fact when the Same is based on due consideration of evidence or, in other words, there is no infirmity in the judgment of the last Court of fact because of misreading or non consideration of evidence. In that regard, he has referred to the case of Amanatullah and others vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan and another reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 199 and to the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another vs Niron alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 294 wherein it has been held-

"it cannot be gainsaid that a finding of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding on the High Court, as a revisional Court except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case"

15. From the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division while interfering with the judgment of the appellate Court did not arrive at any finding that the same was made upon misreading or non consideration of evidence or that upon misconstruction of any document. We have already mentioned that the defendant, for his entitlement to buyout the share of the plaintiff in the land of CS Plot No. 366, has not led any evidence to, establish the fact that the land in suit is part of the dwelling house of the undivided family or, in other words, part of the dwelling house of the defendant No.1. The High Court Division was unmindful of the fact that defendant No.1's prayer under. section 4 of the Partition Act could only be allowed, upon establishing of the fact that the land in suit is part of his dwelling house or that the land in suit is contiguous to the defendant's homestead or that defendant needs the land in suit for convenient use and occupation of his dwelling house. But the defendant did not establish anyone of the facts stated above. It may also be mentioned that defendant has not taken exception as regard the occupation of the land of CS plot No.366 by the other stranger purchasers who purchased the land of the plot in suit from the wife of the defendant No.1 subsequent to plaintiff's purchase. As seen from the judgment of the appellate Court, that it was contended from the side of the defendant No. 1 that the strangers, one of whom purchased the land from the 'wife of the defendant No. 1, are "compromising persons" and, as such, they have been accommodated by the defendant No.1 and others. Legally, the said contention is not sustainable since provision of section 4 of the Partition Act does not contemplate that a member of an undivided family will take exception in respect of a buyer who has purchased the part of the dwelling house of his undivided family but will not take exception in respect of the other stranger buyers who ate not his kith and kin, as in the instant case, who have purchased the land of the dwelling house of undivided family,

16. The learned Counsel for the defendant- respondent, from the materials on record, could not point out that the strangers, one of whom purchased the land from the wife of the defendant No.1, who have purchased the land of plot No. 366 are the kith and kin of the defendant No.1. The learned Counsel could also not point out that there is any evidence from the defendant's side to establish the claim that the property in suit is the internal part of the homestead of the defendant No.1 This being the position, we are of the view the High Court Division was in error in holding that the land in suit is part of dwelling house of the defendant No.1 and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereupon allowing the defendant's prayer to buy the share of the plaintiff under section 4 of the Partition Act.

17. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore, we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with costs at all stages.

End.
