case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 9th August, 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3175 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-8- 2000 of the High Court. Division passed in Civil Revision No. 3175 of 1993 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated 21-8-1993 of the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat passed in Title Appeal No. 207 of 1989 affirming those of dated 28-7-1987 of the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Bagerhat passed in Title Suit No. 94 of 1982 decreeing the suit.

2. Late Kawsar Ali Shaikh, the predecessor in interest of the appellants, filed the above Title Suit No. 94 of 1982 for specific performance of contract on the averments that late Noor Ali Akunji, the defendant No.1 in the above suit and the predecessors in interest of the respondent Nos. 5 to 12, was the owner in possession of the suit land measuring 3.93 acres and he on 29-11-1976 entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the suit land at a consideration of Taka 30,000 and on receipt of Taka 25,000 as advance he made over the possession of the suit land to the plaintiff and in the said agreement it was stipulated that the, defendant No.1 shall get back the possession of suit land in case of his refund of the advance amount of Taka 25,000 within the month of Chaitra 1386 BS and in default, the defendant No. 1 shall execute and register sale deed within the month of Baisakh 1387 BS in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of balance amount Taka 5,000; the defendant No. 1 having failed to refund Taka 25,000 within Chaitra 1386 BS, the plaintiff on tendering the balance consideration money requested the defendant No. 1 several times to execute and register the sale deed but the defendant No. 1 deferred the same on this or that plea and on 30-4-1982, corresponding to 16 Baisakh 1389 BS, he finally refused to execute and register the sale deed.

3. The added defendant Nos. 3 and 4, the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein, contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending that they purchased the suit land from the defendant No.1 by several sale deeds and the defendant No. 1 then handed over the possession of the suit land to them and thereafter they sold some land therefrom to the defendant Nos. 8, 11, 12, 15, 16 and 17 by sale deeds dated 18-8-1981 and delivered possession of the sold lands to them and that the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 and their transferees are bonafide purchasers for value without notice of alleged agreement for sale dated 29-11-76 and the above defendants are in actual and physical possession of the suit land since their purchase and the alleged agreement for sale is antedated, fabricated, collusive and fraudulent and the plaintiff did not also pay Taka 25,000 and/or tendered Taka 5,000 to the defendant No. 1 and the defendant No, 1 also did not make over possession of the suit land to the plaintiff.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), after hearing, decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff proved the agreement for sale dated 29-11-76, payment of advance Taka 25,000 and also handing over of possession of the suit land by the defendant No.1 to the plaintiff on the date of contract and also proved possession of the plaintiff to the suit land and the defendants failed to prove the purchase of the suit land by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 from the defendant No. 1 and also subsequent transfer thereof by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 to the defendant Nos. 8, 11, 12, 15, 16 and 17 and the witnesses of the defendants having materially contradicted each other as to the possession of the defendants in the suit land the possession of the defendants in the suit land was not proved. On appeal, the learned Additional District Judge Bagerhat, after hearing, dismissed the appeal on affirming all the findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court and with further findings that the witnesses Nos. 2, 3 and 4 for the defendant Nos. 3-4 did not assert that they had no knowledge of the earlier agreement for sale dated 29-11-76. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in CR No. 3175 of 1993 and after hearing the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that the defendants are bonafide purchasers for value without notice and this aspect of the matter has not been discussed by the courts below properly and in support of its decision the High Court Division referred to the case of Mukhtar Hossain Khan vs Suresh Chandra Dey, 42 DLR 86 and the case of In re Karamatullah, PLD 1972 (SC) 25.

5. Leave was granted on the submissions that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the contesting defendants are purchasers without knowledge of the earlier contract between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 for sale of the land in suit ignoring the concurrent finding of the Courts below that the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit, the High ,Court Division was in error in reversing the concurrent finding of facts without discussing and considering the evidence on record and without assigning any reason except holding that the defendants had no knowledge of the earlier contract for sale although the same is not a valid ground for refusing specific performance of contract and, as such, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law.

6. The learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff/appellants submitted that the High Court Division without adverting to the concurrent finding of the courts below erroneously held that the defendants are bonafide purchasers for value without notice of the agreement for sale dated 29-11-76 and also erroneously reversed the findings of the courts below as to the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and as to genuineness of the agreement of sale and the High Court Division also erroneously held that the onus lay on the plaintiff to prove that the defendants had knowledge of earlier agreement for sale of the suit.

7. The learned Counsel for the defendants submitted that the suit was filed on the basis of antedated and fabricated agreement of sale which was without any consideration and the defendant No. 1 never entered into any such agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the land in suit and possession of the land in suit was never made over to the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 sold some portion of the suit land along with his other lands to some of the contesting defendants in between the years 1977 and 1979 and also delivered possession of the lands sold to them and further the defendants are bonafide purchasers for value without any notice of the agreement for sale dated 29-11-1976 and that after their purchases the defendants mutated their names and paid rent to the government and the present suit has been filed by Hazratullah, the son of the defendant No.1, in the benami of the plaintiff upon creating forged and antedated agreement for sale.

8. As it appears the High Court Division just stating the submissions of the learned Advocate and referring to 42 DLR 86 and 1972 PLD (SC) 27 held that since DW 1 deposed that she did not know about the contract for sale and the defendants were bonafide purchasers for value without notice the onus shifted to the plaintiff to prove that the defendants had the knowledge of contract and the plaintiff having failed to discharge the onus is not entitled to obtain decree for specific performance of contract.

9. Before dealing with the points raised by the learned Counsel for the appellants, it will be useful to reproduce here section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act which is as under:

"27. Except as otherwise provided by this Chapter, specific performance of a contract may be enforced against (a)

(b) any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who had paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract.

(c)

(d)

(e)

10.It will thus be noticed that under the above provision of law, a contract can be specifically performed against any other person claiming title to the property arising subsequently to the original contract but an exception has been made in the case of transferee for value who has paid money to the transferor in good faith and without notice of the original contract. It is, therefore, for the transferee to prove that he was a transferee in good faith and without notice of the original contract for valuable consideration.

11. This provision of law has been the subject of interpretation in two decisions of the Privy Council, namely, Bhup Narain Singh vs Gokul Chand Mahton AIR 1934 PC 68 and Shankarlal Narayandas Mundade vs New Mofussil Co Ltd AIR 1946 PC 97.

12. In BhupNarain Singh 50 case the Privy Council observed as under:

"In their Lordships opinion, the section lays down a general rule that the original contract may be specifically enforced against a subsequent transferee, but allows an exception to that general rule, not to the transferor, but to the transferee, and, in their Lordships opinion, it is clearly for the transferee to establish the circumstances which, will allow him to retain the benefit of transfer which prima facie he had no right to get. Further, the subsequent transferee is the person within whose knowledge the facts as to whether he has paid and whether he had notice of the original contract lie, and the provisions of section 103 and 106, Evidence Act, 1872, have a bearing on the question."

13. In Shankarlal Narayandas Mundade’s case the Privy Council observed as under:

" Their Lordships have found it unnecessary to examine the evidence which was called on behalf of the plaintiff to show that these defendants in fact, had notice of the earlier contract, since a decision of this Board is clear authority for the proposition that the burden of proving good faith and lack of notice lay upon the defendants."

<u>14. It is thus quite clear that in a suit for specific performance of contract the onus lies heavily on the person whose title arises subsequent to the contract to sell and he must prove that he is a transferee for value and has paid the money in good faith and without notice of the original contract.</u>

15. In the present case, as already stated, the trial Court held that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and the defendants failed to prove the purchase of the suit land by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 from the defendant No. 1 and also subsequent transfers thereof by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 in favour of the defendant Nos. 8, 11, 12, 15, 16 and 17 and the witnesses of the defendants, having materially contradicted each other as to possession of the suit land, also failed to prove possession of the defendants in the suit land and the appellate Court not only affirmed the above findings but further found that the witnesses Nos. 2, 3 and 4 for the defendant Nos. 3-4 did not assert that they had no knowledge of the earlier agreement for sale dated 29-11-1976 and thus the defendant failed to discharge this onus.

16. In the case of Minhazuddin Talukdar vs Abdul Jalil Howlader 3 MLR (AD) 58 it has been held that in a suit for specific performance of contract the essential ingredients which the plaintiff is required to prove in order to succeed in a suit for specific performance of contract, are that the bainapatra is genuine, consideration money passed between the parties and delivery of possession was given in pursuance thereof. In the case of Hafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 47 DLR 583 it has been held that when in pursuance of a bainapatra/agreement to transfer property the intended transferee has taken possession, though the requisite legal document has not been executed, the position is the same as if document had been executed against all who want to threaten or disturb the possession of such possessor.

17. In the case of Haq Brothers vs Shamsul Haque 39 DLR 290 it has been held that the burden of proof lies on the person who asserts that a fact exists and so mere. denial by the defendants, subsequent transferees, to the effect that they had no notice or knowledge of the agreement for sale, will not discharge the onus that rests upon them in view of section 27 of the Specific Relief Act.

18. As has been stated earlier the plaintiff proved the agreement for sale dated 29-11-1976, payment of advance Taka 25,000 and also the handing over of possession of the suit land by the defendant No.1 to the plaintiff on the date of contract and also proved the possession of the plaintiff to the suit land and the defendants failed, to prove the purchase of the suit land by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 from the defendant No.1 and also subsequent transfer thereof by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 to the defendant Nos. 8, 11,12, IS, 16 and 17 and the witnesses of the defendants having materially contradicted each other as to the possession of the defendants in the suit land the possession of the defendants in the suit land has not been proved and the appellate Court, apart from affirming the above findings, further held that the witnesses Nos. 2, 3 and 4 for the defendant Nos. 3-4 did not assert that they had no knowledge of the earlier agreement of sale dated 29-11-1976.

19. In the case of Khurshid Ali vs Noorjahan Bewa 1 MLR (AD) 210 it has been held that the findings of fact arrived at on proper consideration of evidence by the trial Court cannot be interfered in revisional jurisdiction unless the same is found absolutely perverse. In the present case the High Court Division did not hold that the findings of the courts below are perverse. In the case of Rupa Jahan Begum vs Lutfe Ali Chowdhury, 1 MLR (AD) 374 = 49 DLR (AD) 73; it has also been held that the High Court Division generally in its revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court and appellate Court on proper appreciation of evidence, In the case of Md Fazlul Haque vs BM Rahman, 1 MLR (AD) 418 it was also held that the question as to whether a bainapatra is guanine or not is a finding of fact which can be decided by proper appreciation of evidence and such a finding of fact cannot be interfered with by the court in revisional jurisdiction. Further in the case of Shahana Alam vs Ms Farida Begum, 2 MLR (AD) 153 = 2 BLC (AD) 92 it was also held that the High Court Division, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, cannot interfere with the concurrent findings of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court except on the ground enumerated in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and cannot superimpose itself as a third court for fresh appreciation of evidence. Moreover, as held in the case of Mohammad Yeasin Khan vs Deputy Commissioner Brahmanbaria, 2 MLR (AD) 211, the trial Court and lower appellate Court are the final courts of fact and the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the trial as well as by the lower appellate Court on proper appreciation of evidence on record cannot be interfered with by the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction. Further, as held in the case of Nurul Islam vs Amirul Islam, 4 MLR (AD) 363 = 3 BLC (AD) 222, the court of appeal is the final Court of fact, when the question of fact is decided concurrently by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court on correct appreciation of evidence on record, no interference is called for.

20. In the present case the High Court Division by discussing the evidence on record did not hold the findings of the courts below are perverse for misreading, non reading and/or misconstruing the evidence on record and/or the courts below did not properly appreciate the particular parts of the evidence on record.

21. Accordingly, we are of the view that the judgment and order of the High Court Division being not sustainable is liable to be set aside.

Accordingly the appeal is allowed with cost.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated April 26, 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision. No. 2707 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J : The appeal by the defendant No.2 by leave, is against the judgment dated April 26, 1999 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2707 of 1995 discharging the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated June 24, 1995 of the 1st Commercial Court Chittagong in Other Appeal No.318 of 1991 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated January 29, 1991 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Raozan, Chittagong in Other Suit No.79 of 1979 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking a decree for pennant injunction against the defendant Nos. 1-4.

2. The case of the plaintiff is that the land in suit was owned by Abdul Hamid, predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-9. He sold the same to Abdur Razzaque by the kabala dated July 26, 1960 and said Abdur Razzaque sold the land so purchased from Abdul Hamid to the plaintiff on May 12, 1978 and since then plaintiff is in possession of the land in suit, that defendant Nos. 1-9 tried to purchase the land without paying the proper price but having failed to purchase the land in suit the defendant Nos. 1-4 out of vengeance threatened the plaintiff's bargadar on August 10, 1979 to dispossess him from the land in suit. Hence the suit for a decree of permanent injunction.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that their predecessor Abdul Hamid on July 26, 1960 sold 20 decimals of land to Abdur Razzaque with an agreement for reconveyance, that in the deed of reconveyance by mistake plot No.8275 was written instead of plot No. 8276, that pursuant to the agreement for reconveyance Abdul Hamid got the land sold on July 26, 1960 reconveyed by the kabala dated May 15, 1961 executed by Abdur Razzaque and since reconveyance Abdul Hamid possessed the land during his lifetime and after him his heirs defendant Nos. 1-9 are in possession of the land i.e. the suit land, that neither plaintiff nor the other defendants have any right, title and interest in the land in suit, that suit has been filed making untrue statements.

4. The suit was also contested by defendant No.10, brother of Abdul Hamid, by filing written statement. It was the case of the defendant No.10 that the land in suit belonged to the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-9 i.e. Abdul Hamid and he sold the land to Abdur Razzaque with an agreement for reconveyance, that Abdul Hamid because of his financial crisis was unable to get the land sold to Abdur Razzaque reconveyed and then the defendant got the land reconveyed in his name from Abdur Razzaque and since reconveyance he is in possession of the land i.e. the land in suit, that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 have no right, title, interest and possession in the land in suit.

5. The suit was also contested by defendant Nos. 11 and 12(ka) to 12(gha) and 16 by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that they are in possession of 23 decimals of land of the plot in suit i.e. plot No. 8276, on the basis of registered deed of gift and in the said land plaintiff or the other defendants have no right, title, interest and possession.

6. Plaintiff, defendant Nos.2 arid 3 and the defendant No. 10 examined witnesses. The defendant Nos. 11 and 12(ka) to 12(Gha) and 16 did not examine any witness but they cross-examined the witnesses examined by the plaintiff and the defendant Nos.2 and 3 as well as by the defendant No.10. Plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 10 also filed documents in support of their respective claims.

7. The trial Court on consideration of the oral and documentary evidence arrived at the finding that defendant Nos. 1-9's predecessor Abdul Hamid on the basis of the deed of reconveyance got the land sold on July 26, 1960 reconveyed in the year 1961. The trial Court noticed the fact that in the deed (Exhibit 1 dated July 26, 1960) whereby Abdul Hamid sold the land in suit to Abdur Razzaque, plot No.8276 was mentioned but in the agreement for reconveyance executed by Abdur Razzaque, in favour of Abdul Hamid on that very day i.e. July 26, 1960 (Exhibit Gha 2) and in the kabala (Exhibit Ga 9 dated May 15, 1961) whereby Abdur Razzaque, reconveyed the land which he purchased on July 26, 1960, from Abdul Hamid, plot number was mentioned as 8275, but in the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court arrived at the finding that the mistake in Exhibit Gha(2) and Ga(9) was an inadvertent mistake of the scribe although khatian number and the other description of the land as well as the quantity of land has been written correctly and, as such, held that as Abdur Razzaque reconveyed the land on May IS, 1961 to the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-9 and since then he having had no right, title and interest which he acquired by the kabala dated July 26, 1960, the plaintiff by purchase from Abdur Razzaque by the kabala dated May 11, 1978 (Exhibit 2) has not acquired any right, title, interest and possession in the land in suit. The trial Court on detailed discussion of the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 who deposed on behalf of the plaintiff held that plaintiff inisetably failed to prove her possession in the land in suit. It may be mentioned plaintiff or any of her sons or relatives did not depose in the suit. Plaintiff tried to establish her right, title and possession in the land in suit through the evidence of PW 1, the constituted attorney and PW 2, the servant of the plaintiff but their evidence being contradictory was not accepted by the trial Court and also did not consider them as reliable witnesses to prove the case of the plaintiff.

8. The trial Court, about the claim of the defendant No.10 held, that said defendant failed to prove his claim in the land in suit as well as possession. The trial Court disbelieved the case of the plaintiff as well as the case of the defendant No.10 since the plaintiff and the defendant No.10 as well as his sons figuring as plaintiffs have filed Partition Suit Nos. 90 of 1976 and 49 of 1981 impleading the defendant Nos.2and 3 and others as defendants but in the schedule of the said suits land 'in suit has not been incorporated and in the background of the said fact the trial Court observed that had the plaintiff and the defendant No.10 had title and possession in the land in suit they would have certainly included the land in suit in the partition suits. The trial Court also observed in the facts arid circumstances of the case and the materials on record that defendant No. 10 in collusion With his sister has filed the suit and defendant No.10 is instrumental in the institution of the suit and finally held that defendant No.10 has no right; title and possession of the land in suit. On the aforesaid findings and decisions, the trial Court dismissed the suit. The trial Court made the positive finding that plaintiff failed to establish her case i.e. the right, title, interest and possession in the land in suit.

9. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court plaintiff alone went on appeal. The "appellate, Court allowed the appeal on the finding that Abdur Razzaque while purchasing the land in suit on July 26, 1960 did not execute and register any deed of reconveyance i.e. Exhibit Gha(2), and that pursuant to the said Exhibit Gha(2) he did not reconvey on May 1st, 1961 by the kabala Exhibit Ga(9.), the land purchased by him (Abdur Razzaque) by Exhibit I dated July 26, 1960 since in the schedule of Exhibit 1 (kabala dated 26-7-1960) plot number has been mentioned as 8276 and in the schedule of Gha(2) plot number has been mentioned as 8275 although quantity of land of Exhibit 1 and Exhibit Gha (2) is 20 decimals, that as Abdur Razzaque did not execute any deed of reconveyance as regard the land of kabala Exhibit 1 dated July 26, 1960 and, as such, kabala dated July 26, 1960 was an out-and-out sale deed and that there was no contemporaneous agreement for reconveyance of the land of the kabala dated July 26, 1960, that defendants contention that there was an inadvertent mistake of the scribe as regard the mentioning of plot No. 8275 in the deed of reconveyance cannot be accepted because of the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act and that acceptance of the contention of the defendants negating the contents of the document Exhibit 1 and reading something in Exhibit Gha(2) would be the violation of the law as in section 91 of the Evidence Act, that the finding of the trial Court that because of the mistake of the scribe in Exhibit Gha(2) and in Exhibit Ga(9) plot No. 8275 was written instead of plot No.8276 was not legally sustainable since the same was contrary to the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act, that decision of the trial Court that Abdur Razzaque by the kabala dated May 15, 1961 reconveyed the land which he purchased on July 26, 1960 from Abdul Hamid is contrary to the materials on record, that finding of the trial Court that after reconveyance by Abdur Razzaque to Abdul Hamid, Abdur Razzaque had no right, title and possession in the land in suit and that by purchase from Abdur Razzaque by the kabala dated May 11, 1978 plaintiff did not acquire any right, title,interest and possession in the land in suit is not Legally sustainable, rather contrary to the materials on record, that there was no agreement for reconveyance between Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Hamid and that Abdur Razzaque did not reconvey the land in suit to Abdul Hamid and that Abdur Razzaque as owner and possessor of the land in suit transferred the same to plaintiff on May 11, 1978. In the background of the aforesaid findings and decisions the appellate Court held that the plaintiff has prima facie title and exclusive possession in the land in suit and that fact of possession of the plaintiff has been proved by the witnesses examined from the side of the plaintiff since plaintiff's witnesses in one voice have deposed both in-chief and cross-examination that plaintiff is in possession of the land in suit, that as plaintiff has prima facie title in the land in suit and that as the plaintiff has established his claim of possession in the land in suit and, as such, plaintiff is entitled to the relief sought in the suit.

10. As against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court the defendant No.2 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division discharged the Rule on the findings that in the kabala dated July 26, 1960 i.e. Exhibit 1, there is no recital as to re conveyance of the land sold by the said kabala, as such, the kabala dated July 26, 1960 was an out-and-out sale deed, that defendant's contention was that there was a mistake by the scribe in writing plot No. 8275 instead of 8276 in Exhibit Gha(2) and Exhibit Ga(9) is not tenable in law because of the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act. The High Court Division has observed: "The deed has been reduced to the form of a document and, as such, no evidence shall be given in proof of terms of such document, as such, the defendants attempt to explain away the mistake by other evidence is not acceptable in law", that the learned Assistant Judge was in error in holding that the scribe inadvertently committed mistake in writing plot No.8275 instead of 8276 in Exhibit Gha(2) and Exhibit Ga(9) since under the law the Assistant Judge was not competent to dislodge the fact in the document in question and, as such, the appellate Court was not in error in setting aside the Judgment and decree of the trial Court upon taking view as regard the matters i.e. the contents of the documents in question, contrary to the view taken as to the same by the trial Court. The High Court Division also held that the appellate Court was correct that there was no agreement for re-conveyance between Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Hamid and, as such, document dated July 26, 1960 was an out and out sale deed and thus, as Abdur Raizaque was the owner of the land in suit, the plaintiff by the kabala dated May 11, 1978 acquired right, title and possession in the hind in suit. The High Court Division has observed that the appellate Court has perused the evidence of the witnesses of both the sides and thereupon held that the plaintiff is in possession of the land in suit and the finding of fact so arrived at by the lower appellate Court being based on consideration of the evidence the revisional Court except in exceptional circumstance is not authorised by law to set aside a finding of fact arrived at by the final Court of fact. The High Court Division has also observed that defendants are claiming the land of some other plot which the plaintiff has not purchased and, in that background of the matter, the appellate Court. was correct in observing that plaintiff's claim of possession in the land in suit "is required under the law to be protected and he is entitled to get the decree for permanent injunction against the defendants so that the defendants may not give any threat for dispossession".

11. Leave was obtained for consideration of the submission that the High Court Division committed error in not considering that the finding of possession arrived at by the lower appellate Court is no based on assessment of the materials on record and that the High Court Division failed to consider that the finding of possession arrived at by the trial Court was not controverted by the appellate Court and thus the High Court Division was in error in concurring with the decision of the Court of appeal below.

12. The undenied position is that land in suit belonged to Abdul Hamid and he transferred the same to Abdur Razzaque on 26-7-1960. It is the case of the contesting defendants that on 26-7-1960 Abdur Razzaque executed and registered a deed of reconveyance in favour of Abdul Hamid regarding the transfer made by Abdul Hamid to Abdur Razzaque from whom plaintiff claimed to have purchased the land in suit on May 11, 1978. It is also the case of the defendants that pursuant to the deed of reconveyance Abdur Razzaque re-conveyed the land in suit to Abdul Hamid on May 15, 1961. The defendants have contended that although in the agreement for reconveyance plot number was incorrectly written 8275 instead of 8276, land whereof was sold by Abdul Hamid to Abdur Razzaque on 26-7-1960 followed by an agreement for reconveyance and thus when Abdur Razzaque reconveyed the land on May 15, 1961 mistake that occurred in the agreement for reconveyance crept into the deed executed by Abdur Razzaque in favour of Abdul Hamid in respect of the Iand in suit but on the basis of reconveyance the defendants are in possession of the land in suit which is of plot No. 8276. It has also been contended by the defendants that the other descriptions of the land i.e. khatian, mouza, quantity of land etc. were quite correct or, in other words, uniform to that of deed of sale dated 46-7-1960. This contention of the defendants though was considered correct by the trial Court but was not accepted by the appellate Court upon referring to the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act and the High Court Division concurred with the lower appellate Court. The Iearned Advocate of the appellant submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act was in no way relevant for consideration or, in other words, provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act had no manner of application in the background of the case put forward by the parties. The submissions so made merits consideration in the context of the frame of the suit.

13. The plaintiff has filed the suit seeking decree for permanent injunction restraining the defendant Nos.1-4 from causing disturbance to the possession and enjoyment of the land in suit described in the schedule attached to the plaint. In a suit for permanent injunction the primary question for determination is the possession of the party who is seeking the decree for permanent injunction and the matter of title of such party in the land in suit is incidentally gone into. The trial Court, on detailed discussions and consideration of the evidence led from the side of the plaintiff, arrived at the definite finding that plaintiff has failed to prove her possession in the land in suit and also title as regard the Iand in suit. The trial Court, ill the background of the materials brought on record by the parties, found title of the land in suit as well as possession thereof with the contesting defendants. The trial Court held that the suit filed seeking decree for permanent injunction was product of collusion between the plaintiff and defendant No.10 i.e. sister and brother respectively. It may be mentioned defendant No.10 is the brother of Abdul Hamid, father of the defendant Nos. 1-9 and said defendant No.10 came with the case that Abdul Hamid, pre-decessor of the defendant Nos. 1-9, because of financial difficulty as could not get the land reconveyed from Abdur Razzaque he then got the land reconveyed from Abdur Razzaque. The aforesaid fact gives credence to the case of the defendant Nos.2 and 3 while considered in the juxtaposition of the case of the said defendants, who asserted that Abdul Hamid sold the land in suit to Abdur Razzaque with an agreement for reconveyance and that in the light of the agreement for reconveyance Abdul Hamid got the land in suit reconveyed although there was inadvertent mistake in the agreement for reconveyance as to the number of plot which also crept in the kabala by which Abdur Razzaque reconveyed the land to Abdul Hamid and that, in fact, on the basis of reconveyance Abdul Hamid got the land of plot No. 8276 and possessed during his lifetime and thereafter defendant Nos. 1-9 are possessing the same. The admitted fact is that Abdul Hamid sold 29 decimals of land of plot No. 8276 to Abdur Razzaque by the kabala dated July 26, 1960. There is no material on record to show that Abdul Hamid transferred any other land of any other particular plot including plot No. 8275 to Abdur Razzaque on July 26, 1960. There is no case from the side of the plaintiff that Abdur Razzaque purchased common quantity of' land, i.e. 20 decimals from each of the plot Nos. 8276 and 8275 and that Abdur Razzaque executed and registered the agreement for re-conveyance in favour of Abdul Hamid only in respect of the land measuring 20 decimals of plot No.8275 and he reconveyed the same by the kabala dated May 15, 1961. Since Abdur Razzaque purchased land measuring 20 decimals of plot No.8276 and no other land of any other plot, in that state of the matter, the case put forward by the contesting defendant Nos. 2 and 3 that there had been inadvertent mistake by the scribe in writing plot No.8275 in the agreement for reconveyance as well as in the deed by which Abdur Razzaque reconveyed the land which he purchased from Abdul Hamid on July 26, 1960 appalls to be credible and rational. Consideration of this aspect of the matter by the trial Court had in no way offended the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act, nor can it be considered that defendants in establishing the aforesaid fact offended the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act. Furthermore, the trial Court was not in error in dismissing the suit since plaintiff or her sons did not figure as witness in the suit with- out explanation and did not examine disinterested and nonpartisan witnesses to prove her claim of possession in the land in suit. In our view, the appellate Court was in error ill reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court upon referring to the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act without considering the facts that were brought on record from the side of the defendants which had in no way offended the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act. In that state of the matter, the High Court Division; in our view, was in error in concurring with the judgment of the appellate Court by which appellate Court decreed the suit.

<u>14. Now coming to the question of possession on the establishment whereof the suit could only be decreed, even though title of the land in suit may be of the plaintiff, which though in the instant case was not. The trial Court, on detailed discussions of the evidence brought on record from the side of the plaintiff and upon assigning reason for non- accepting the evidence of the witnesses examined by the plaintiff on the question of possession, made the finding that plaintiff failed to prove her possession in the land in suit. The trial Court noticed the contradiction and discrepancies in the evidence of PWs.1 and 2 as to the location of the land and the quantity of the land in suit as well as boundary of the land. The trial Court noticed that PW 1 is not certain about the possession of the plaintiff since the witness has stated that plaintiff is in possession of the hind in two or three plots although, in fact there is only one plot. The trial Court also noticed in the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 that the said witnesses do not know the land in suit. In the said state of the matter and because of the aforesaid nature of the evidence of the PWs; the trial Court made the afore stated finding as to the possession of the plaintiff. It may be mentioned plaintiff nor her sons deposed in the case in support of the plaintiff's case. The appellate Court without discussing and considering the evidence of the plaintiff or the defendants made the sweeping finding that plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit. The lower appellate Court did not at all advert to the reasoning of the trial Court for not accepting the evidence of the PWs, particularly on the point of possession. The lower appellate Court, being the last and final Court of fact under the law, was required to discuss the evidence and thereupon on assigning reason was required to reverse or set aside the finding of the trial Court on the question of possession and that as having had not done so the finding of the appellate Court that plaintiffs are in possession is not legally sustainable. The High Court Division, having had not considered the evidence and having had not noticed the manner in which the appellate Court made the finding on the vital and important question of possession of the land in suit and that only concurred with the judgment of the appellate Court which was not made upon discussions and consideration of the evidence, was in error in affirming the judgment of the appellate Court. Since the finding of possession made by the trial Court is based on due consideration of the evidence and the said finding and decision of the trial Court on the question of possession having had not been reversed or set aside by the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court, the judgments of the said Courts are not sustainable in law. Plaintiff, in a suit for perm anent injunction, can have the relief only upon establishment of his exclusive possession in the land in suit. In the instant case plaintiff having had not established her exclusive possession in the land in suit, rather out of possession, she was not entitled to the relief sought for and, as such, the trial Court was quite correct in dismissing the suit.. As has already been stated that the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court have not discussed the evidence of the plaintiff led on the point of possession and that upon discussion and consideration of the evidence, finding of the trial Court on possession was not set aside by the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court.</u>

15. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant Shaherunnessa and Mohiuddin obtained the above Rules upon making separate revision application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgments and decrees of affirmance dated 11-8-03 passed by Additional District Judge, Court No.3 at Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 543 of 2002 and No. 535 of 2002 respectively, which confirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court for khas possession of the suit premises after eviction of the defendants.

2. Opposite party as plaintiff on 10-8-2000 instituted a suit being OS Suit No. 138 of 2000 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Chittagong for eviction of defendant Shaherunnessa, arrears and compensation. The suit was then on transfer re-numbered as OS Suit No. 10 of 2002.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that Mujibor Rahman and Solaiman on 29-1-62 purchased the suit premises, which was described to be a one-storied semipucca house in plot No. 705(part) and 706(part) and fully described in the schedule to the plaint. By a sale deed dated 14-11-73 Solaiman transferred his share to Mujibor Rahman. Mujibor Rahman then transferred the suit premises to Md Lutfor Rahman and his wife Nur Jahan Begum by two sale deeds-dated 12-2-15 and 13-2-75. They got their names mutated in both revenue record and Chittagong Municipal Corporation and got electric connection, etc. They paid rents and taxes, etc.

4. Thus being owner. Lutfor Rahman let out the suit premises to said defendant Shaherunnessa on the basis of an oral agreement. Then, Lutfor Rahman transferred the suit premises along with other properties to his daughter, the plaintiff, by way of a registered gift dated 17-6-98 and delivered possession. The plaintiff then got her name mutated in BS Kbatian.

5. The plaintiff authorised her "Debor" SGM Feroj Alam Gazi, a practicing Advocate of the Chittagong Bar, to look after her properties and collect rents from the tenants. Being requested said defendant agreed to pay rent to the plaintiff through said Feroz Alam acknowledging the plaintiff as her landlord; and rent of the premises on consultation was fixed at Taka 3,000 per month from June, 1998.

6. But in spite of repeated demands the defendant did not pay any rent either to her or to said Feroz Alam. Then, the plaintiff sent a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the tenancy with the end of June, 2000 and asking the tenant to vacate the premises by 30th day of June, 2000 but without any result.

7. The plaintiff also on 9-10-2000 instituted Other Suit No. 175 of 2000 in the same Court against defendant Mohiuddin exactly on similar averments regarding title, ownership, attornment and monthly tenancy for similar relief of eviction of the defendant, arrears and compensation. Suit was then renumbered as OS Suit No.7 of 2002 in the same Court.

8. In this suit, the plaintiff averred that the defendant agreed to pay rent at the rate of Taka 3,500.00 per month with effect from June, 1998.

9. Both defendants contested the suits by filing separate written statements. Their Common defence was that the plaintiff had no cause of action and the suit as framed was not maintainable.

10. Defendant Shaherunnessa contended that Md Soleman Khalifa and Mujibor Rahman became owners in possession of the suit premises by registered deed No. 518 dated 29-9-62. By amicable partition, Mujibor Rahman got the suit land with the structures thereon. Mujibor Rahman then on 10-10-72 transferred the suit premises to his very close friend and her husband Sheik Noor Hossain and delivered possession and divested of all his interest in the suit premises. Thus got possession, her husband lived in the suit premises with his family and after his death, she was living in the suit premises with her family.

11. She denied that the plaintiff or her father Lutfor Rahmari was ever her landlord. She never accepted the plaintiff or her father as her landlord nor did she agree to pay rent to the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not entitled to any relief in the suit since there never existed any relationship of landlord and tenant between her and the plaintiff.

12. Gazi, husband of the plaintiff and said Feroz Alam having threatened him to dispossess from the suit premises, he was constrained to institute Other Suit No. 33 of ;f000 for perpetual injunction against them.

13. In his written statement, Mohiuddin also contended, in brief, that Mohammed Solaiman, who was lawful owner in possession of the suit premises, was his distant relation. Solaiman on 5-1-69 transferred the suit premises to him and delivered possession by demarcation and divested of all interest therein.

14. Thus getting the suit premises, he possessed the suit premises by living with his family for more than the statutory period in assertion of his own right and title. Shahjahan Gazi, husband of the plaintiff and said Feroz Alam having threatened him to dispossess from the suit premises, he was constrained to institute Other Suit No. 32 of 2000 for perpetual injunction against them.

15. He was never tenant under Lutfor Rahman. He never accepted the plaintiff as landlord and agreed to pay rent to her. The plaintiff was not entitled to any relief since there was never existence of any relationship of the landlord and tenant between him and the plaintiff.

16. On the party pleadings, number of issues was settled, in both the suits, including the ones as to whether the defendant was a tenant in the suit premises and whether the suit as framed was maintainable.

17. In support of her case, the plaintiff examined two witnesses including her brother-in-law (husband's brother) said Feroz Alam in both suits. Defendant Shaherunness examined her son while defendant Mohiuddin examined him only. Documents produced by the plaintiff were marked Exhibits 1 to 18 and 19 series in the suit against Shaherunnessa and the papers and documents adduced by the plaintiff in the suit against Mohiuddin was marked Exhibits 1 to 10. Documents produced by Mohiuddin were marked as Exhibits 'Ka'to 'Ga'. Shaherunnessa also produced voter ID card and certificate issued by the local ward commissioner.

18. Upon the evidence, oral and documentary, on record, the trial Court decreed both the suits directing the defendants to hand over possession of the suit premises, money decree for arrears at the rate of Taka 3,000 per month from June, 1998 to 2000 and compensation at the rate of Taka 150 for each day of unauthorised occupation of the suit premises until handing over possession against Shaherunnessa and at the rate of Taka 3,500 per month from June, 1998 and compensation at the rate of Taka 150 for each day of unauthorised occupation of the suit premises from 1-10-2000 against Mohiuddin as prayed for.

19. On appeals presented therefrom by said defendants Shaherunnessa and Mohiuddin, the appellate Court affirmed both the decrees of the trial Court by impugned judgments and decrees.

20. In both the Rules, Mr Subrata Chowdhury for the petitioners, submitted that the Courts below erred in law in finding the defendants tenants under the plaintiff and the defendants defaulted in the payment of rents in the absence of any evidence on record and upon such erroneous views, most illegally decreed the suits, which resulted in serious failure of justice.

21. On the other hand, Mr JaliI on behalf of the plaintiff, submitted that the Courts below having concurrently found that the defendants were tenants under the plaintiff and that they defaulted in the payment of rents, the impugned decrees were now binding in revision.

22. He also submitted that the defendants made an application before the appellate Court tor additional evidence in order to show that the suit premises were abandoned property but ultimately failed to prove that.

23. As both the Rules arise out of the decrees of eviction of monthly tenants from the suit premises on similar pleadings and evidence and in view of same submissions adopted by the learned Advocates in the Rules, we heard both the Rules together and now, dispose of them by this judgment.

24. We have perused the record.

25.	The suits as framed were ones for eviction/ejection of monthly tenants from the suit premises, and also for arrears and compensation for unauthorised use and occupation. The plaintiff did not seek any declaration of her title in the suit premises. Of course, she was not required to seek such declaration for eviction of a monthly tenant, which she is always entitled on any ground of breach of the tenancy.

26. In such suits, it must, however be remembered that it is not only sufficient for the plaintiff to prove her ownership in the suit premises but she must also prove that there was existence of a relationship of landlord and tenant between her (him) and the tenants, the defendants were tenants under her and they defaulted in the payment of rents or breached any term of the contract of tenancy. For instance, one may become owner of a premises by purchase or otherwise in the occupation of persons who never acknowledge him (her) landlord and could resist her from evicting them for want of existence of such a tenancy and in such cases, the owner would not succeed to get a decree for eviction of such persons in a simple suit for eviction only.

27. The plaintiff based her suit on oral agreement. She did not claim the monthly tenancy on any written agreement or contract. In both suits, on the entry of the defendants into the suit premises, the plaintiff claimed that her father Lutfor Rahman purchased the suit premises and let out them to the defendants "on oral agreement on temporary monthly bharatia basis".

28. Then, after getting gift of the suit premises from her father, the plaintiff averred, in the plaint against Shaherunnessa, that "the defendant agreed to pay monthly rent regularly to the plaintiff through aforesaid Mr SGM Feroz Alam Gazi Advocate acknowledging the plaintiff as her landlord and on consultation the rent of scheduled premises was fixed at Taka 3,000 per month to be paid from June, 1998". In the suit against Mohiuddin, the plaintiff claimed that the defendant agreed to pay Taka 3,500 per month on similar averments.

29. In both suits, the plaintiff averred that the defendants never paid any rent to the plaintiff in spite of demands. The plaintiff never claimed that any of the defendants did ever pay any rent to her or her father Lutfor Rahman.

30. From the above positive averments what is clear is that the plaintiff could not say when the defendants did enter into the suit premises. She could not even give any particulars of the oral tenancy on which she asserted in the plaint that her father let out the suit premises to the defendants, rate of rents, date of commencement of the tenancy, date of entry of the defendants into the suit premises, etc.

<u>31. It is needless to say that rate of rents, date of commencement of tenancy, date of entry of the tenant, etc. are no doubt essential ingredients in the proof of a monthly tenancy. No monthly tenancy based on oral agreement if denied and contested could be proved without proof of such terms, namely, rate of rent, date of commencement, date of entry into the premises, etc. And no Court is permitted in law to decree such a suit for eviction, arrears and compensation for unauthorised use and occupation of the premises in the absence of proof of the tenancy.</u>

32. The trial Court found to the effect that the plaintiff proved her ownership in the suit premises but the defendants failed to prove their case of gift. The trial Court also found that the defendants were tenants under the plaintiff. It appears that the .trial Court reasoned that whenever the tenant entered into the suit premises as a tenant they entered acknowledging someone as landlord since the premises never could remain without being owned by someone.

33. Hearing both the appeals which were presented by the defendants together, the appellate Court affirmed said findings of the trial Court on the ownership of the premises. On the statement of DW 1 Sohrab Hossain, son of defendant Shaherunnessa during cross-examination that his mother paid rent to Lutfor Rahman, father of the plaintiff accepting him as landlord on receipt and on Exhibit 19 a counterfoil adduced in Other Suit No. 138 of 2000 it was also found that both the defendants were tenants under the plaintiff.

34. I find no basis for such concurrent finding that the defendants were tenants under the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not examine her in support of her case in the suits. Aforesaid Feroz Alam Advocate examined himself as PW 1 on her behalf on the basis of a power of attorney. From 23-9-01 to 13-10-02 he was examined. On the first day of his examination, he claimed to be aged about 35 years old.

35. It is the case of the plaintiff that her father purchased the suit premises in 1975. And case of defendant Shaherunnessa is that she started living in the suit premises on the basis of an oral gift dated 10-10-72 and that of defendant Mohiuddin that he started living on oral gift dated 5-1-69. So, said PW 1 Feroz Alam was mere a boy of 8/9 years old in 1975 and is not competent to prove the fact that the defendants entered into the suit premises as tenant. He cannot be relied upon on the terms of an oral agreement for the tenancy.

36. Similarly, other witness Md. Abdul Huq appears to be examined in both suits as PW 2 to prove mainly gift and attornment. He claimed to be a tenant under Lutfor Rahman. He said defendant Shaherunnessa was occupying a room as a tenant. He however, did not say that defendant Mohiuddin was also occupying any room as a tenant. He however did not say that he saw the defendants entered into the suit premises as tenant.

37. Reasoning of the trial Court that the defendants having admitted entering into the suit premises as tenant they must have someone as their landlord has got equally no basis. We have found that none of the defendants ever claimed and admitted in their written statements to have entered into the suit premises as tenant. Had it been their case that they entered into the suit premises as tenant, then, the reasoning might have some force and/or logic on the maxim that once a tenant is always a tenant.

38. Appellate Court similarly, fell in serious error on acting on the solitary statement of DW 1, a son of defendant Shaherunnessa, that in 1969 they entered under Solaiman as tenant as an admission of both the defendants to be tenants. DW 1 Sk. Sohrab Hossain was about 34 years old at the time of examination on 13-10-02. So, he was born some time in 1968 and he was merely one year old in 1969. Such statement was also beyond the pleading as made in the written statement of defendant Shaherunness.

39. Similarly, the appellate Court most illegally relied upon Exhibit 19 adduced in Other Suit No. 138 of 2000, which is a counterfoil showing payment of rent of Taka 500 for the month of April, 1996 and bearing signature of defendant Shaherunnessa. Signature of defendant Shaherunnessa was not proved and was not even drawn to the attention of DW 1. Trial Court by comparison found the signature was of defendant Shaherunnessa. Such finding falls through when we turned to the plaints. In the plaint, it was the definite case of the plaintiff that the defendants never paid any rent. It was never claimed that said defendant Shaherunnessa paid Taka 500 as rent per month to Lutfor Rahman. In the circumstances, said receipt ought to have been found to be created for the purpose of the suit.

<u>40. We understand the worry of the trial Court as to what would be the basis of possession of the defendants when they failed to prove their story of oral gift. First, it must be remembered that failure of the defendants to prove oral gift did not ipso facto prove the case of the plaintiff that they were tenants. Law is now settled that when the defendants fail to prove their case of gift, their possession must be held to be one that is based on invalid title and becomes adverse against the whole world.</u>

<u>41. In Sadak Ali vs Suruj Ali and others 7 DLR 94 Mr Ibrahim J held- "Possession under a mistaken or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser, and, if sufficient in length of time and continuity, gives the holder a title."</u>

<u>42. His Lordship followed number of authorities including the one reported in AIR 1942 PC 64 in coming to such finding. We have already' found that it was never the case of the defendants that they entered the suit premises as tenant.</u>

<u>43. Similarly, both the Courts below erred in law on attornment. The word "attornment" is not found in any British or American English dictionary. Sam sad English Bengali Dictionary however defines "attornment" as "to acknowledge a new landlord". We find acceptance by our Courts of such general meaning of "attornment". "Attornment" does not mean mere information of transfer of the ownership. In order to establish "attornment" there must be some sort of acknowledgment on behalf of the tenant by any action. Even payment of rent does not constitute "attornment".</u>

44. In Amar Chandra Saha vs Ajit Kumar Das, 33 DLR (AD) 37 our Appellate Division defined "attornment" in such way, "Attornment means the act of the tenant putting one person in place of another as his landlord. It is well settled that mere payment of rent, or agreement to pay rent in favour of a particular person, without any other evidence, does not always constitute an attornment."

45. Case of the plaintiff as made out in the plaints is that after gift, her father and said Feroz Alam informed the defendants of the transfer of the suit premises. In the same plaints, it is stated that the defendants did not pay any rent which they orally agreed. PW 2 also in his deposition just said that he was present when they informed the transfer of the premises on the basis of gift. They however, did not mention any date of information. Such information does not constitute attornment.

46. Both the Courts therefore erred in law in finding that the defendants attorned the plaintiff as landlord in the absence of any evidence whatsoever.

47. For foregoing reasons, concurrent findings of the Courts below that the defendants were teriants under the plaintiff have got no basis in the record and must be held to be perverse. Such findings are therefore, not binding in revision. Both the Courts below fell in serious error in decreeing the suit for eviction, arrears and compensation in the absence of any proof of existence of a relationship of landlord and tenant between the defendants find the plaintiff, which, no doubt, resulted in serious miscarriage of justice.

48. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute with cost. Cost is assessed at Taka 5,000 in each of the Rules. Impugned judgment and decree affirming the decree of the trial Court decreeing the suits are hereby set aside and both the suits are dismissed.

Send down the records at once.

End.
