full_judgment:
SM Ziaul Karim J: This appeal is directed against the order dated 23-2-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 10 of 2005, vacating the order of ad-interim injunction granted earlier on the suit property and granting temporary injunction on a portion of land measuring 2.50 kathas.

2. Short facts leading to this appeal are that in 9-1-2005, the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 10 of 2005 in the Third Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka impleading respondents as defendants for partition of her saham measuring an area 3.60 kathas more or less out of total suit property measuring 20 kathas.

3. The plaintiffs case, put in a nutshell, is that her father Basharat Ali was the owner of 20 kathas of land described in the schedule of the plaint who died leaving behind four sons namely, Anisul Haq, Rabiul Haq, Iqbal Karim and Reazul Karim and two daughters namely Rowshan Ara Begum (herein plaintiff) and Hoshne Ara Begum and two wives namely, Rashida Begum and Razia Begum; that Reazul Haq died unmarried and Razia Begum (second wife) voluntarily surrendered her share to her sons and daughters by taking formal permission from the concerned Ministry; that the property measuring 20 kathas will be distributed and allotted amongst three sons, two daughters and one wife Rashida Begum i.e. the mother of the plaintiff that according to Muslim law of succession, the plaintiff got 3.60 kathas more or less including her mother's share measuring 1.25 kathas; that the matter was compromised between the parties, accordingly the plaintiff was alloted 2.5 kathas of land in southwestern comer shown in schedule B in sketch map, while defendants' portion was shown as schedule "A", however her remaining portion was lying within the garage; that the suit premises comprises a building constructed by her father, wherein she lived but her step-brothers were trying to dispossess her, without any formal settlement, and they entered into an agreement with Navana Real Estate Company Limited and the developer started demolishing the building, Hence the suit.

4. After filing of the suit, the plaintiff filed an application under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining the defendants from demolishing the three-storied building and not to change the nature and character of the same till disposal of the suit. After preliminary hearing the learned Joint District Judge by the order dated 15-1-2005 asked the defendants to show cause as to why an order of temporary injunction should not be granted as prayed for. In the meantime passed an order of ad-interim injunction to the above effect.

5. The application for injunction was contested by defendant-respondent Nos. 1-4, 7-8 by filing written objection stating, inter alia, that Sheik Basharat Ali, the original lessee of the suit plot, died leaving behind one wife Razia Begum, four sons, the defendant Nos. 1-3 and Rezaul Haque, two daughters the plaintiff and defendant No.4 as his legal heirs; that Rezaul Haq died leaving behind three full brothers and two sisters including the plaintiff; that Razia Begum transferred her share by way of oral gift to her sons and daughters, accordingly each daughter got 2.5 kathas and each son got 5 kathas in the suit plot; that the defendant Nos. 1-3, being sons, used to live in the building with their respective family and the plaintiff being married was at her father-in-law's house and at one stage she constructed a tin shed building in the back side of the plot and had been living therein with her family; that the plaintiff earlier filed Title Suit No. 218 of 2001 and the defendant Nos. 1-3 also filed Title Suit No. 169 of 2002, both for partition, that, as the plaintiffs share of land being of 2.50 kathas was not permissible to separate from the entire plot and, as such, both the suits were withdrawn and the matter of partition was handed over to the lessor i.e. the Ministry of Works as per partition deed, who on 31-3-2004 and 10-11-2004 partitioned the suit plot as per the possession of the parties giving the plaintiff and another sister 5 kathas land and exclusive pathway totaling 6.47 kathas which is more land than they are legally entitled to, that the plaintiff has filed the suit only to harass the defendants with some ulterior purpose, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

6. Eventually, after hearing the learned Joint District Judge by order dated 23-2-2005 vacated the order of ad-interim injunction over the suit property but granted temporary injunction over 2.50 kathas of land. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order the plaintiff as appellant filed this appeal.

7. After filing of this appeal, the appellant filed an application for stay operation of the impugned order dated 23-2-2005, upon which this Court by the order dated 30-8-2005, issued Rule, calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-6 to show cause as to why the operation of the impugned order dated 23-2-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 10 of 2005, should not be stayed the Rule was registered as Civil Rule No. 757 (FM) of 2005. Both the appeal and Rule, having arisen out of a common order, these have been heard together and are being disposed of by the judgment.

8. Mr AK Azad, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, supports the appeal and submits that the learned Judge of the Court below has committed illegality without considering actual allegations brought by the plaintiff, thus committed an error of law by deciding the entire merit of the case by passing the impugned order and the appellant had been highly prejudiced by the said order and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel has drawn our attention to the certified copies of the plaint (Annexure-A), order dated 15-1-2005 granting ad-interim injunction (Annexure-B), Sketch Map for mutual partition duly signed by the parties (Annexure-C), proposed saham of the plaintiff (Annexure-D), original copy of the tress map showing actual position after passing the impugned order by which the plaintiff has been put into trouble (Annexure-E) and GDE No. 1673 dated 27-7-2005(Annexure-F), furnished with the application for stay. Referring to those annexure, the learned Counsel submits that during pendency of ad-interim injunction the respondent Nos. 1-4 and 7-8 demolished the building against which violation Case is pending; that the defendants are continuously disturbing the plaintiff’s peaceful possession over the property measuring 2.5 kathas on the north-western comer as shown in Schedule-B of Annexure-C. He adds that learned joint District Judge came to an erroneous conclusion that the plaintiff got 2.50 kathas of land at southwest corner. He adds that the said partition of land having no entrance of gas, electricity and sewerage lines which was alleged to have been done by the Ministry of Works at the instance of respondents and, as such, the plaintiffs fundamental rights have been infringed. At the time of hearing, the learned Counsel filed a supplementary affidavit dated 22-5-2006 furnishing deed of amicable partition dated 14-11-2001 (Annexure-G), written objection dated 13-4- 2004 against so-called partition as shown by defendant Nos. 1-4 without signature of plaintiff (Annexure-H), GD Entries dated 8-9-2004 (Annexures I and I-1), written objection dated 9-11-2004 against the conspiracy of the brothers (Annexure-J), permission by Ministry for partition dated 10-11-2004 (Annexure-K), written objection dated 25-11-2004 against such permission (Annexure-L). Refer- ring to the above annexure, the learned Counsel submits that after the death of Basarat Ali, plaintiff was staying in the building; that after some time her step-brothers started problems with her, which gave rise to a criminal case; that during pendency of the Criminal Case, the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka settled the matter between the parties by amicable partition of their respective share. Accordingly, her share was given to the north-western comer facing front road. Sketch map was also prepared in which her share has been shown as Schedule-B of Annexure-C. Meanwhile, her step-brothers entered into agreement with Navana Real Estate for constructing multi storied building and accordingly, they demolished the building. So; according to the learned Counsel if the possession of the plaintiff be restored to the north-western comer of the plot (Annexure-C) which was partitioned by the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka then she has no objection. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the learned Judge of Court below failed to weigh and sift the materials on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

9. Mr Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 and 7-8, opposes the appeal and submits that the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction by suppressing facts stating some false and concocted story which contradicts with the plaint itself. He adds that the defendants already completed three-storied building in their 13.53 kathas land being sub-plot No. 43/A, out of proposed six-storied building as per approved plan of RAMK leaving sub-plot No. 43/B consisting of 5 kathas land for the plaintiff and defendant No.4 and also sub-plot No. C and exclusive pathway of 12' x 88' = 1056 sft. equivalent to 1.47 kathas and total being 6.47 kathas land. So, the balance of convenience and inconvenience are in favour of defendants. Moreover, the plaintiff and her another sister; have jointly in possession in 5 kathas land appertaining to sub-plot No. 43/B; that the partition is being effected keeping present possession of the parties, so, if the injunction as sought for is granted equitable principle of partition would be violated. The learned Counsel adds that in an urban area co-sharer in possession should not be restrained by an order of injunction from constructing buildings in their respective share of land in possession. The learned Counsel further submits that the suit land being not ordinary plot of land as inherited from predecessor, but the leasehold land from the Ministry of Works, the partition, transfer, etc is subject to the terms and conditions laid down in the lease deed No. 6912 dated 29-12-1955; that clause 19 of the lease agreement provided that no partition can be made or acted upon without prior approval of the lessor i.e. the Ministry of Works; that the plaintiff on accepting the said strict condition as binding had tried her best to partition 2.50 kathas land showing the same in the front side, but the lessor refused it on 13-1-2004 as minimum size of a plot must be of 5 kathas; that the plaintiff by suppressing such facts filed this appeal. He adds that the plaintiff and defendant No.4 are jointly in ownership and possession of sub-plot No. 197(b) (12) consisting of 5 kathas land along with pathway of 1.47 kathas running from that sub-plot to the main road No. 9/A of Dhanmondi Residential Area. The plaintiff has nothing to be suffered any irreparable loss if injunction be not granted. He adds that the original lessee late Basharat Ali had no wife named Rashida Begum. At the time of hearing the learned Counsel filed supplementary affidavit showing a good number of documents i.e. lease deed of agreement dated 29-12-1955 (Annexure-2), many correspondences between lessor and lessee, sketch map showing partition duly approved by the Ministry of Works. The learned Counsel has drawn our attention to paragraph No.3 of Supplementary Affidavit dated 16-7-2006 and submits that the defendants by this time already constructed incomplete four-storied building out of six-storied building in sub-plot No. 43/A as per plan approved by RAJUK with the knowledge of the appellant and, as such, the petition for injunction is barred by the principle of acquiescence, estoppel and waiver. He adds that for the sake of equity and justice the contesting respondents undertake that after final adjudication of the suit if the plaintiff at all gets any portion of property in sub-plot No. 43/A in her saham then they will pay the actual price at the market rate to her or any other way to satisfy her as the Court deems fit and proper. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel referred the case of Mofazzal Hossain (Md) vs Moinuddin being dead his legal heirs Shams Begum, reported in 3 BLC (AD) 78 wherein it is held:

"Code of Civil Procedure

Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2

The plaintiffs have neither a prima facie nor arguable case and defendants cannot be restrained from making construction on the suit land taking the risk that a portion of it will be liable to be demolished if the plaintiffs get a decree in future as has been rightly found by the High Court Division, the refusal of injunction was not either illegal, improper or inequitable.

10. The learned Counsel further refers the case of Fahim-al Haque vs Md Abdul Aziz reported in 43 DLR 226 wherein it is held:

Code of Civil Procedure

Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2

There is no specific area or demarcation of the land allegedly encroached by the defendants-opposite parties; in such a case, no order of temporary injunction can be granted.

In a partition suit concerning land in the urban area, a co-sharer should not be granted injunction if the proposed construction by other co-sharers does not diminish the value of the suit land.

In these days of scarcity of accommodation in urban areas a co-sharer should not be deprived of using the land in his possession, which is a subject matter in this suit for partition, by making construction at his own risk and peril. If any portion of the constructed area falls in the saham of another co-sharer, the possession thereof shall be given to the allottee by demolishing the construction."

11. So, according to him, the impugned order dated 23-2-2005 is just and proper which calls for no interference by this Court.

12. In reply to the above submissions, the learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the facts leading to those cases are distinguishable to that of the instant case, so the principles enunciated therein are not applicable in the present case.

13. We have gone through the application for temporary injunction, written objection, grounds taken in revisional application, annexure furnished with counter-affidavit, supplementary affidavits, other materials on record and given our anxious considerations to the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides.

14. Admittedly, the plaintiff is a co-sharer by inheritance. The suit property comprising 20 kathas belonged to Sheikh Basarat Ali who died on 20-5-1983. His property, now inherited by his three sons, defendant Nos. 1-3 who jointly got 15 kathas of land and two daughters, plaintiff and defendant No. 4 who got 5 kathas of land. They are possessing in their respective share. Defendant Nos. 1-3 entered into an agreement with defendant Nos. 7 and 8 for reconstructing multistoried building in their 15 kathas of land. In the meantime, they constructed incomplete four-storied building out of six-storied building.

15. Now the question that calls for our consideration is, whether the plaintiff is entitled to get an order of temporary injunction in the entire suit property or only her portion of land and whether the learned Joint District Judge was justified in passing the impugned order.

16. We find from the record that appellant as well as contesting respondents filed a good number of annexure furnished with the revisional applications, counter-affidavit and supplementary affidavits. After critical analysis of those annexure, it appears to us that those documents touch the merit of the suit, therefore, we shall refrain to make any comment upon the same; however, we shall consider the principle of granting temporary injunction in this case. In the case of Ainunessa vs Md Obaidul Haq reported in 35 DLR 25 wherein it is held:

"Civil Procedure Code

Order XXXIX

Temporary injunction-Principles under which such injunction granted

Three well established principles of law governing the grant of temporary injunction are the following:

First, the plaintiff has to establish a prima facie case. Secondly, it was to be shown that the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss if the in unction prayed for is not granted and thirdly, the balance of convenience lies in favour of the plaintiff and in favour of granting the temporary injunction prayed for."

17. In the plaint, the plaintiff herein appellant categorically stated at paragraph 3, that defendant Nos. 7 and 8 were demolishing the building of her father, on the contrary in the application for temporary injunction she prayed in the fol1owing manner:

অতএব সবিনয় বিনীত নিবেদন এই যে, দয়া করিয়া বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে অত্র মামলা নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত বিবাদীগন যাতে নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে অবস্থিত তিন তলা বিল্ডিং কোন প্রকার ভাংচুর করিতে না পারে বা বিল্ডিং এর কোন প্রকার বর্তমান আকার/প্রকার পরিবর্তন করিতে না পারে এবং অন্যান্য বিষয়ে তৎসমর্মে এক অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দানে মর্জি হয়।”

18. So the prayer of temporary injunction appears to us as contradictory with that of the statement made in the plaint.

19. Moreover, the contesting respondents categorically stated at paragraph No. 3 of their supplementary affidavit in support of Counter-Affidavit dated 16-7-2006 to the effect that in the meantime they already constructed incomplete four-storied building out of six-storied building in sub-plot No. 43/A as per plan approved by RAJUK with the knowledge of the appellant. They also undertook that after final adjudication of the suit if the plaintiff-appellant at all gets any portion of property in sub-plot No. 43/A in her saham in addition to her present existing absolute possession of 5 kathas land in sub-plot No. 43/B, then they will pay the actual price at the market rate to the plaintiff-appellant or in any other way satisfy her as the Court decides in her favour.

20. In view of such facts, balance of convenience and inconvenience lies against the plaintiff. The learned Joint District Judge rightly granted temporary injunction in respect of the share of plaintiff-appellant and vacated the order of ad interim injunction in respect of share of defendant Nos. 1-3. The impugned order is well reasoned which cannot be interfered.

21. In our jurisdiction, it appears that the question of injunction against construction in urban areas for the first time was considered in the case of Ali Ahmed vs Rezia Begum reported in 1986 BLD 326 and a Division Bench of this Division rejected the prayer for injunction on the following view: "In our view, the nature and character of a suit land in urban areas may be allowed to be changed pending decision in partition suit by improvements but no change in the nature and character of the suit land which would diminish the value of the land or cause prejudice to the other co-sharers should be allowed.........in the present-day scarcity of accommodation in the urban areas a co-sharer should not be deprived of using the land in his possession by making constructions at his risk. If a co-sharer makes a construction in his possession on a land which is a subject matter in the suit for partition, he may do so at his risk and peril; if co-sharer chooses to make a construction at his own risk he should not be restrained from making constructions. If any portion of the constructed area falls in the saham of another co-sharer, the possession thereof shall be given to the allottee by demolition of the construction."

22. In the case of Fahim Al Haque vs Md Abdul Aziz, reported in 43 DLR 226 another Division has followed the decision in upholding an order of affirmance rejecting the prayer for injunction. In Mofazzal Hossain vs Moinuddin being dead his legal heirs, Shams Begum reported in 3 BLC (AD) 78 the Appellate Division affirming the decision of this Division rejecting the prayer for injunction against construction in urban areas noticed the aforesaid decision in Ali Ahmed case. In the case of Serajuddin vs Mizanur Rahman, reported in 29 DLR (SC) 82, the then Supreme Court was of the view:

"A party in order to get interlocutory injunction must claim, inter alia, a legal right, and allege an injury which is not ordinarily reparable by monetary compensation."

23. In the case of Uttara Bank vs Macneill Kilburn, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 the Appellate Division rejected the prayer for temporary injunction against enactment of a letter of guarantee as the balance of convenience was against the plaintiff.

24. In the case of American Cyanamid Co vs Ethicon Ltd. reported in 1975 AC 396 wherein it is held:

"The object of the interlocutory injunction is to protect the plaintiff against injury by the violation of his right for which he could not be adequately compensated in damages recoverable in the action if the uncertainty were resolved in his favour at the trial; but the plaintiffs need for such protection must be weighed against the corresponding need of the defendant to be protected against injury resulting from his having been prevented from exercising his own legal right for which he could not be adequately compensated under the plaintiffs undertaking in damages if the uncertainty were resolved in the defendant's favour at the trial. The Court must weigh one need against another and determine where the balance of convenience lies."

<u>25. After scrutiny of the above decisions, we are of the view that scarcity of the land and pressure for accommodation either for residential and commercial purposes in urban area was growing hand in hand every day while the time for resolution of the dispute is so uncertain that nobody can say certainly when it will finally come to an end. In such situation right to develop the land in his specific possession cannot be denied by an interlocutory order of injunction which would be inequitable.</u>

26. Having regard to the facts, we are unable to accept the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the appellant, on the contrary, the legal plea taken by the learned Counsel for the contesting respondents prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

<u>27. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the principles enunciated in the aforesaid cases and foregoing narrative, we are led to the conclusion that the plaintiff-appellant had no prima facie and arguable case to get an order of temporary injunction in respect of entire suit property, rather balance of convenience and inconvenience is against her. The impugned order suffers from no illegality and impropriety and calls for no interference by this Court. Thus, the appeal, having no merit, fails.</u>

28. In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 23-2-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Title. Suit No.10 of 2005 is hereby affirmed with the observation made above.

Civil Rule No. 757 (FM) of 2005 is discharged. Communicate the order to the Third Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka at once with a copy of judgment for information.

End.
