full_judgment:
The plaintiff has brought the suit claiming Taka 25,22,897.91 for damages and late delivery of cargo. Initially, the plaintiff laid the claim for Taka 45,00,962.00 on account of damages for non delivery and or late delivery of cargo. The amended claim is for the aforesaid amount for damages and compensation under different heads as detailed in paragraph 6(c) of the plaint.

2. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that the plaintiff is the importer of rice and other goods. The defendants Nos. 1-3 are the carriers of various goods including rice. Their local agent is defendant No.4, Karnaphuli Shipping Corporation. By the bill of lading No. 47 dated 30-3-95, issued by 'MV Sargodha' the defendant Nos. 1-3 contracted to carry 296.910 tons of rice from Karachi to Chittagong and loaded the goods on 'MV Sargodha'. It is averred 7 that the plaintiff forward sold the entire quantity of 8 rice to Messers Lokman and Hafiz Enterprise at a price of Taka 14.00 per Kg and a total price of Taka 41,56.740.00. The ship 'MV Sargodha' arrived at Chittagong Port on 21-4-95 but did not have the cargo on board to deliver them to the plaintiff. The plaintiff believed that the containers were unloaded somewhere between Karachi and Chittagong and that the plaintiff apprehended that with the coming of Bora season when the price of rice will come down the ship owner may offer to deliver the rice depriving the plaintiff of the profit. It is revealed from the report of the clearing agent and surveyor that the consignment against the bill of lading had not arrived at Chittagong by 'MV Sargodha'. The plaintiff claimed C&F price of Taka 33,41,707.00 plus loss of profit of Taka 11,59,255.00 and in total Taka 45,00,962.00. That after filing of the suit the defendants have delivered damaged cargo by another ship and the plaintiff received damaged and inferior cargo to the extent of 1002 bags out of 3,299 bags and that there was short delivery and torn bags in total 18.90 and the plaintiff has lost 1020.90 bags of rice worth of Taka 11,86,182.91 including duty, tax, port and clearing charges. The survey was conducted on 6th and 8th June, 1995 and the defendants refused to nominate their surveyor on flimsy pretext. The defendants loaded and unloaded cargo several times from one ship to another ship causing damage. The entire claim of the plaintiff on account of damage and compensation according to the amended pleadings is as follows:

"1. Damaged" 1002 bags x 90 Kgs = 90,180 Kgs x 12.91 (cost price) Taka  11,64,223.00

2.	Torn 338 bags: 5% Lost i.e. 16.9 bags. x 90= 1521Kgs x 1291. 19,636.11

3.	Short received 2 bags (180) Kgs= 2,323.00

4.	Loss due to fall in price of rice

5.	with the inflow of New Crop on 2,96,910 Kgs Taka 2.50 = 7,42,275.00

5.	Additional Bank Interest due to delayed shipment 1,440.00

6.	Post Landing Survey charges  18,000.00 due to delay.

7. Compensation to the party. 1,50,000.00 Loss of Business Continuity.

8. Loss of Business Continuity 3,75,000.00

Total Taka 	   25,22,897.00

3. The defendant Nos. 1-4 to resist the claim of the plaintiff have filed written statement and denying the material allegations the defendants contended that the suit is not maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction and that the plaintiff has no cause of action against the vessel 'MV Sargodha' and the vessel Sargodha was not liable to be arrested. The further claim of the defendants is that the suit having been filed against the vessel 'MV Sargodha', which did not carry the cargo, the security obtained from the vessel is not legal as the alleged damaged cargo was carried by another vessel 'MV Lanka Mohapola'. The defendants further pleaded that the plaintiff instituted the suit for non delivery of the cargo of 296.910 metric tons of rice which the defendants contracted to carry by vessel 'MV Sargodha' from Karachi to Chittagong but due to vessel's instability the cargo could not be carried by 'MV Sargodha' and thereafter the cargo was carried by 'MV Lanka Mohapola' in the FCL containers and the C&F agent of the plaintiff Messers Trade Point International received the cargo of the plaintiff on 7-6-95. The bill of ladinz be clearly stipulated that the containers have been carried under FCT/FCL basis which means the shippers packed the cargo into the containers and sealed it at their risk, responsibility and cost at their yard and similarly, the consignee unsealed the containers and unpacked the goods from the containers at their own risk, cost and expenses. The containers were discharged from the vessel with seal intact and the said seal was broken in presence of the representative of the Customs, Port Authority and the consignee's C&F agent and thus the defendants are not responsible for the alleged damage as claimed by the plaintiff. It is the case of the defendants that the containers in question were discharged by the carrier at the port of Chittagong with the seal intact. The defendant No.1 discharged their contractual obligations by delivering goods to the plaintiff at Chittagong Port against the original bill of lading. The plaintiff took the containers without serving any notice to the carrier for the survey of the ship within the stipulated period from its discharge which proves that the suit consignment has been delivered to the plaintiff in sound condition and no shortage and damage took place while it was in the custody of the carrier. It is contended that the ship owners under the compelling circumstances had to furnish Bank Guarantee for immediate release of the vessel, the suit is liable to be dismissed and the Bank Guarantee dated 6-5-1995 furnished by the defendants for the claim amount issued by the Banque Indosuez is to be returned to the defendants. In the written statement the defendants have also made counter-claim for the loss suffered by the defendants due to illegal detention of the vessel on account of the charter hire for 14 days and financial expenses and bunker cost upto the time of departure of the vessel from Chittagong Port and loss of earning for US $ 60,000 @ US 4355 per day for illegal detention of the vessel for 14 days, US $ 22,400 @ US $ 1600 per day on account of financial losses and US $ 7,070 for consuming additional bunkers. The defendants claim that for the loss they suffered the defendants are entitled to a decree for US $ 90,440 equivalent to Taka 36,17,600.00.

4. Upon the pleading of the parties the following issues were framed to adjudicate upon the dispute:

i) Is the suit maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction?

ii) Has the plaintiff any cause of action against the vessel MV Sargodha?

iii)Is the suit bad for misjoinder and non joinder of parties ?

iv) Was the cargo of the plaintiff carried into the containers under FCT/FCL basis?

If so, will it affect the liability of the defendants?

v) Are the defendants responsible for the claim of the plaintiff. If so, to what extent ?

vi) Is the counter-claim maintainable in the admiralty jurisdiction? If so, to what extent the defendants are entitled to a decree/relief, if any."

5. The plaintiff has examined 2 witnesses and also adduced documentary evidence to prove the claim. The defendants examined Md Hadis as the only witness and also adduced documentary evidence.

6. Mr Ohiullah, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendants, has contended that the vessel 'MV Sargodha' did not carry the goods and the goods were carried by the vessel 'MV Lanka Mohapola' and, consequently, the plaintiff has no cause of action against the vessel 'MV Sargodha' and the vessel is liable to be released. He has further contended that the plaintiff originally made their claim on account of non delivery of the goods, as the cargo was delivered by 'MV Lanka Mohapola' the cause of action against the vessel 'MV Sargodha' for the alleged damages ceased to exist. He has argued that the cargo having been delivered according to the bill of lading at the port of discharge the defendants have no further liability. He has pointed out that the plaintiff has based his claim on the joint survey report Exhibit A which is not binding upon the defendants as no notice was given in writing to the defendants or their agent at the port of discharge within 72 hours from the date of discharge of the consignment as contemplated under Article III rule 6 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 and the goods having been removed from the port area without the knowledge of the carrier no liability could be fixed upon the carrier for the alleged damage. His contention as regards claim on account of loss due to fall in price of rice, additional bank interest due to delay in shipment, post landing survey charges, compensation to the party, loss of business continuity as made in item Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 of paragraph 6c of the plaint is that those claims have not been proved by any evidence and, as such, those claims are liable to be dismissed. It is also contended that PW 1 Md Shahidul Huq who is an associate of the plaintiff Resource International is not competent to depose before the Court as he had no power of attorney from the plaintiff while deposing and his deposition is unauthorised and should not be used as evidence.

7. The issue relating to the maintainability of the suit in Admiralty Jurisdiction and that whether the plaintiff has any cause of action against the vessel 'MV Sargodha' having been raised and has been decided by this Court indirectly in an interlocutory application made by the defendants for vacating the order of arrest of the vessel by judgment and order dated 7th May 1995. The question whether the plaintiff has cause of action against the vessel 'MV Sagodha' is dependent on the Bill of Lading which is the prima facie evidence of contract to carry the goods. The suit is maintainable under section 6 of the Admiralty Courts Act, 1861 as the Bill of Lading was issued by 'MV Sargodha'. So, the issue is decided in favour of the plaintiff.

8. As regards the liability of the carrier which is related to issue Nos. 4 and 5, Mr Ohiullah has contended that the cargo was delivered at the port of discharge in sealed containers and the goods were stuffe1in containers by the shipper in their yard and the sealed containers were delivered to the plaintiff in presence of their agent and the Port Authority and the Customs, the defendants discharged their liability having discharged the same containers which they took on board the vessel. Reliance has been placed upon a decision in the case of FFUI Co Ltd vs American President Lines reported in PLD 1992 (SC) 291 where it has been stated that the law has given choice to the carrier to enter the particulars declared by the shipper or not to enter them and further protects the carrier by making shipper liable for compensation for misrepresentation taking into consideration the commercial nature of the bill of lading which is a negotiable document it is necessary that where COGSA or Hague Rules as enacted, apply, they must be followed. Therefore, if the number of packages and the nature of goods are mentioned in the bill of lading then the words "said to contain" or "particulars furnished by the shipper" Cy/Cy and similar notation will not permit the carrier to dispute the prima facie character of the bill of lading issued in the prescribed manner. It has further been held that a bill of lading with notation like Cy/Cy CFS or SLC is a prima facie evidence as provided by law but its rebuttal by the carrier becomes easier and the burden becomes much lighter than in other cases. Such or similar notations on the bill of lading have gained currency and their meaning is well understood in shipping, commercial and banking circles to mean that the carrier was not associated with the stuffing of the container which was exclusively done by the shipper. In the face of such bill of lading the carrier need not prove these facts unless rebutted. It has only to establish that such sealed container was properly and carefully loaded, handled, stowed, carried, kept-cared for and discharged. The burden will then shift to the shipper to prove that the number of packages or goods as shown in the bill of lading were stuffed in it. Without such proof the claim for loss or damage cannot succeed. Whether the bill of lading is in respect of container without describing the goods contained in it, the words "apparent order and condition" will refer to the apparent condition of the container.

9. Mr Ohiullah pointing out the notation Cy/Cy on the bill of lading exhibit. B contends that the notation indicates and it prima facie proved that the containers were stuffed exclusively by the shipper in their container yard and the containers were fully discharged with the seal in tact and therefore the defendants have incurred no liability as alleged by the plaintiff.

10. Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel representing the plaintiff, has contended that the suit is in rem against 'MV Sargodha' under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act 1861 which provides a remedy for consignee of bill of lading. The bill of lading in the instant case was admittedly issued by 'MV Sargodha'. The owners of the ship Sargodha offered to deliver the goods by 'MV Lanka Mohapol' and the plaintiff received the goods to mitigate the loss it was suing to recover. He has contended that the defendants had failed to deliver the goods by the vessel 'MV Sargodha' which admittedly arrived at Chittagong Port on 21-4-95. The plaintiff instituted the suit claiming Taka 45,00,962.00 for non delivery of cargo and on the prayer of the plaintiff the vessel 'MV Sargodha' was arrested. When the goods were delivered by another ship of the owner the plaintiff made the amended claim for Taka 25,22,897.00 and the plaintiff made the claim for damage for damaged cargo, short delivery and compensation after the cargo was discharged by 'MV Lanka Mohapola'. The survey was conducted between 6th and 8th July, 1995 and notice had been given to the defendants but they failed and or refused to nominate their surveyor for making joint survey. The survey report exhibit A revealed that in the discharged cargo there were damaged rice and there were also torn bags for which damage was calculated at the rate of 5% and there was shortage of 2 bags. The survey report having been accepted in evidence without any objection the same is a valid evidence in support of the claim of the plaintiff. The defendants having failed to carry the goods as per contract they cannot avail of the protection of law. He has further argued that Lanka Mahapola did not issue any bill of lading, so no suit lies against 'MV Lanka Mohapola' and the liability arose from the bill of lading issued by 'MV Sargodha', the defendants are liable to give an account of the goods which was taken on board 'MV Sargodha' but failed to carry by the said vessel to the port of discharge. He has chiefly argued that the defendants are liable for fundamental breach of the contract of carriage as the defendants contracted to carry the goods by 'MV Sargodha' which they failed to do, and he referred to "Four corners" rule as recited in rule 299 of Carver Carriage by Sea Vol-I (part one) which is to the following effect "if you undertake to do a thing in a certain way, or to keep a thing in a certain place, with certain conditions protecting it, and have broken the contract by not doing the thing contracted for in the way contracted for, or not keeping the article in the place in which you have contracted to keep it, you cannot rely on the conditions which were only intended to protect you if you carried out the contract in the way in which you had contracted to do it."

<u>11. Dr Zahir has further argued that the defendants contracted to carry the cargo by 'MV Sargodha' but had not done so and the goods were delivered late and the defendants thus committed fundamental breach for which the defendants cannot rely on the conditions incorporated in the bill of lading which were intended to protect them. For fundamental breach of the contract the defendants are liable to deliver the consignment in the order and conditions in which the goods were stuffed in the containers and were received by them on board the vessel. Admittedly defendants failed to carry the goods by vessel 'MV Sargodha' for its instability and thereby breached the contract and so the defendants cannot escape the liability of discharging the goods in the order and condition in which the goods were stuffed in the containers. Since the defendants are guilty of fundamental breach the burden is upon them to prove that at the point of discharge the goods were in the same order and condition in which they took on the vessel 'MV Sargodha'. The defendants failed to establish that they carefully loaded, handled, stowed, carried, cared for and discharged the goods. There is no evidence adduced by the defendants that in their presence the goods were delivered to the consignee in the order and condition in which the goods were received. The survey report Exhibit A although is not the result of joint survey but its veracity cannot be questioned, for, the defendants took no step to see the condition of the goods which the defendants could have done even after the goods were received by the plaintiff. In the written statement it is admitted that the goods were received by the plaintiff on 7th June, and the plaintiff's case is that the survey was made between 6th and 8th June, 1995 and that the plaintiff requested the defendants to appoint joint surveyor by the fax message as it is evident from Exhibit C. The defendants were not careful to make any survey nor did they care to see whether the goods carried by 'MV Lanka Mohapola was in the same order and condition in which it was received on the ship 'MV Sargodha'. The contention raised by the learned Counsel of the defendants that the deposition of PW cannot be accepted, but it is seen that the PW 2 Zarre Omar, the proprietor of the plaintiff firm, himself deposed before the Court and stated in cross-examination that the cargo was discharged from the vessel 'MV Lanka Mohapola' and there was no bill of lading issued by 'MV Lanka Mohapola'. There was one bill of lading for the cargo imported and there was no bill of lading issued by the second carrier and the cargo was surveyed within the port premises of the Chittagong Port. DW 1 Md Hadis deposed that the cargo was booked for the vessel Sargodha but it was not carried by the vessel due to technical reasons. Therefore, considering the evidence both oral and documentary and also the principle as enunciated in the aforesaid 'four corners' rule it can be said that the defendants cannot escape the liability at least in respect of the damaged cargo to the extent of 1002 bags the price of which is Taka 11,64,223.80 and then damage for torn bags at the rate of 5% which comes to Taka 19,630.11 and for short delivery of 2 bags the price of which is Taka 2,323.00 and thus the defendants' liability is assessed at Taka 11,86,176.91. It appears from the bill of lading that 2% discolored rice was there in the consignment which is not disputed and accordingly, the price of the said damaged rice which comes to Taka 23,723.54 should be excluded from the amount to be awarded to the plaintiff. The claim on account of loss due to fall in price of rice with the inflow of new crop could not be proved by any cogent evidence either oral or documentary. The price index of Consumers Association of Bangladesh Exhibit 'Y' which appears to be a photostat copy cannot be accepted as valid evidence, for, that has not been proved by any officer of the Consumers Association. The claim in item Nos. 5, 6, 7 and 8 calculated under various heads are too remote and those are not supported by any evidence, as such, those are dismissed. Thus the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for Taka 11,62,453.40. The suit is accordingly, partly decreed with cost. The plaintiff shall realise the decretal amount by encashing the bank guarantee furnished by the defendants and the remainder will be returned to 'the contesting defendants.</u>

The vessel 'MV Sargodha' was arrested by this Court due to the default of the defendants and consequently, the counter-claim is not entertainable and the same is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mushfiquddin Bakhtiar with Jabunnessa Mushfique, Advocates-For the Petitioner. 
Md Manirul Islam Khan, Advocate-For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Salina Begum ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Mojibur Rahman and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-10 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 13-11-2001 passed by the learned District Judge, 2nd Court, Narsingdi, in Title Appeal No. 43 of 2000 affirming the judgment and decree dated 21-11-99 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Monohardi, District-Narsingdi, in Title Suit No. 46 of 1996 and partly decreed the suit for preliminary partition.

2. The short fact of the case is that the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner as plaintiff instituted the suit for Partition being numbered as Title Suit No. 46 of 1996 before the Senior Assistant Judge, Monohardi, Narsingdi for partition of the suit land at Mouza Nischantapur, District-Narsingdi. The suit land originally belonged to Bhabani Kishore and Kailash Chandra Chakraborty respectively in CS Khatian No. 140, Whose name was also recorded properly in R,SKhatian No. 146. But during the SA operation for preparing the SA record wrongly recorded the name of one Deen Bandhu who has got no right and title in the suit land. Bhabani Kishore died leaving behind only one son Manik Kishore who became the absolute owner of the plot Nos. 70, 71 and 567. Thereafter, he sold .32 decimals of land out of 96 decimals to Abdul Hashem, the husband of the plaintiff, by a Deed No. 8235 dated 3-12-88 and registered in Monohardi Sub-Registry Office but in that deed the caste of the vendor and District were wrongly written. The caste was written Muslim instead of Hindu and the District was written Mohongonj instead of Munshigonj. The suit property pertaining to CS Khatian No. 141 originally belonged to Syed Obaidullah, Syed Azizullah, Syed Ahmed Ullah, Syed Rafiqullah, Syed Atikullah, Syed Sarafat Akhter, Syed Sara Akhter Khatoon, Syed Md Hafizullah whose name was also recorded in SA Khatian No. 146 correctly. Thereafter, Syed Rafiqullah was enjoying the suit property by amicable partition with his brothers and out of which Rafiqullah sold .35 decimals of land to Abul Hashem, the husband of the plaintiff, by a Registered Deed No. 8234 dated 3-12-88. The original registered deed was lost, as such, the certified copy of the same was submitted.

3. The suit property pertaining to 51 khatian originally belonged to and owned by Gour Kishore who died leaving behind 2(two) sons namely, Krishon Kishore and Harendra Kishore Das who orally gifted 32 decimals of land of Rafizuddin, the father of the plaintiff, on 10 Chaitra, 1365 BS. But due to restriction on registration of Hindu property the same property was gifted to Abul Hashem, the husband of the plaintiff who gifted the same to plaintiff including other suit property in CS Khatian Nos. 140 and 141 through Registered Deed No. 5900/3889 dated 30-9-93 and 9-5-90. Thus the plaintiff became owner and possessor of 132 decimals of the suit property which she could not develop due to non-partition. Plaintiff asked defendant to make partition of the suit property because the defendants occupied more than their entitlement. But the defendants refused to make partition of the suit property. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed a suit for permanent injunction and a title suit for recovery of possession being Title Suit No. 19 of 1990 and 42 of 1992 which were dismissed against which the plaintiff preferred an appeal but the appeal was also dismissed. Hence, the plaintiff filed the instant partition suit.

4. The defendants contested the suit by filing the written statements and admitted the plaintiff's title over 8 decimals of the suit land. The defendant further denied the material allegation made by the plaintiff in the plaint and stated that defendant was the owner and possessor of the suit property accepting 8 decimal of the suit land b virtue of Patta dated 5-6-47 issued by Nayeb of Zaminder in favour of Khodeja Akhter and Deel Bahar whose name was recorded in SA Khatian and who subsequently on 29-3-74 sold 16 decimal of 1 and to defendant No.5, 11 decimals of land to defendant No.6, 15 decimals ofland to defendant No.9, 17 decimals ofland to defendant No. 21 and 44 decimals of land to one Shamsuddin, Naimuddin Tejimuddin and Md Hanif who on 15-3-84 sold the property to defendant Nos. 1-4 and thus the defendants became owner and possessor of the suit land and the plaintiff had no right and title over the suit property excepting 8 decimal of land. The defendant further stated in his written statement that the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 19 of 1990 and 42 of 1992 which were dismissed and the appeals were also dismissed.

5. During the trial the learned trial Court framed issues on 4 points namely,

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

2. Whether the plaintiff has got any right title and possession over the suit land?

3. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties?

4. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get preliminary decree in partition suit.

6. The plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and exhibited 1 and 2 series. Defendants examined 5 witnesses and exhibited Ka-Cha series. It was stated that although the plaintiff was able to prove this case by producing registered documentary evidences against the defendant but the learned trial Court illegally decreed the suit for 8 decimal to the  plaintiff.

7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 21-11-99 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Monohardi, Narsingdi in Title Suit No. 46 of 1996, the plaintiff preferred an appeal before the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narsingdi being Title Appeal No. 43 of 2000 stating, inter alia, that the  learned Senior Assistant Judge, Narsingdi did not apply his judicial mind and failed to consider and discuss the evidence on record properly. The learned Joint District Judge also without going through the merit of the suit and discussing the evidence on record and without considering the registered deed erroneously supported the decision and finding of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Narsingdi and illegally dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 13-11-2001.

8. Being aggrieved by the judgment of affirmance the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner filed the instant revisional application before the High Court Division.

9. The learned Advocate Mr Mushfiquddin Bakhtiar, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the plaintiff successfully proved the case by adducing 4 witnesses and produced the registered deed executed by Manik Kishore on 3-12-88 in support of his right and title at least with regard to 32 decimals of the suit land. He further submits that the learned trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court without considering the registered deed and also the oral evidence of the witnesses partly decreed the suit. He further submits that the defendant on the basis of the Patta claimed his right and title over the suit land. But the Patta procured by the defendant appeared to be forged.

10. The learned Advocate Mr Md Manirul Islam Khan appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite parties submits that the plaintiff prior to filing the partition suit filed a title suit being Title Suit No. 42 of 1991 which was dismissed then an appeal was preferred by the plaintiff being Title Appeal No. 17 of 1992 which was dismissed. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed another suit for permanent injunction being No. 19 of 1993 which was also dismissed. Thereafter, the instant partition suit been filed, as such, the partition suit is barred by res judicata. Next she submits that the defendant inherited the property from Khodeja Akhter and Deel Bahar who received the Patta from the Nayeb of Zaminder Suresh Chandra Singh on 5-6-1947 and since then they had been in peaceful possession of the suit land. He further submits that the defendant examined as many as 5 witnesses who categorically stated in their deposition about the right, title and possession of the suit land by the defendant. DW 1 Mojibur Rahman stated in his deposition that as a matter of fact the plaintiff has got no right, title and possession in the suit land and the original Patta was produced and exhibited by him as Exhibit-Gha. In this connection, the learned Advocate cited the decision in the case of Raja Sreenath Roy and others vs Moharaja Pratap Udai Nath Sahai Deo reported in Indian Cases Volume No. 82 Privy Council at page 879 wherein it was held-

"A Kabuliyat predicates a Patta. A Patta is granted by the Zaminder as a title deed to the tenant. The Kabuliyat, as its name implies, is a mere acknowledgment, an engagement by the tenant, to carry out the terms Of the Patta."

11. Next, he submits that the schedule of the suit land is vague and indefinite, as such, the plaintiff is not entitled to get any decree. He further submits that both the Courts below observed that the registered deed produced by the plaintiff is a faulty one. The caste of the vendor was written Muslim instead of Hindu and the district also wrongly written as Mohanganj instead of Mymensingh. Finally, he submits that the deed produced by the plaintiff is not genuine and he could not produce the original deed and on the basis of this sort of faulty deed the plaintiff cannot claim of the suit land for partition. Moreover, the plaintiff could not prove his right and title on the basis of this faulty document in the Title Suit No. 42 of 1991 and in the injunction suit No. 19 of 1993. The plaintiff miserably failed to prove the partition suit and, as such, the revisional application should be dismissed.

12. On a meticulous examination of evidence on record, registered deed, the judgments of both the Courts and other connected papers it appears that the learned trial Court by his judgment discussed the evidence and also the registered deed produced by plaintiff and observed that the plaintiff could not produce the original deed and the certified copy which was produced by the plaintiff appeared to be not genuine. The learned trial Court further observed that the partition suit is barred by res judicata but since defendant admitted that the 8 decimal of land is under the possession of the plaintiff and plaintiff has got title over the 8 decimal of land where his homestead is situated. The lower Appellate Court by his judgment and finding stated that the plaintiff could not prove his title and possession for 1.32 decimals of land in the title suit and also in the appeal arising out of the title suit. Thereafter, the lower appellate Court stated in his judgment that the plaintiff filed a suit for permanent injunction which Was also dismissed as because the plaintiff could not prove his possession by adducing any evidence. The learned lower appellate Court further observed that the registered documents which were produced by the plaintiff did not appear to prove right and title of the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court also observed that the Partition suit is barred by res judicata since the defendant admitted that the plaintiffs claim over 8 decimal of suit land arid right and title of plaintiff over the 8 decimal of land, the plaintiff is entitled to get 8 decimal of larid as his saham. The Court's below further observed that the suit land is vague and indefinite, as such, the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed.

<u>13. By now the settled principle of law in exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure has been laid down in several judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division that the concurrent findings of fact should not be disturbed unless it is manifestly perverse. The principle which has been laid down by our Appellate Division is that when the Appellate Court as the final Court of finding of facts' affirms or reverse the judgment of the trial Court on a proper assessment of the evidence on record and the findings do not suffer from any error of law and the case is concluded by finding of facts no interference is called for in the revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection, I rely on the case of Khurshed and others vs Noorjahan Rewa and others reported in 1995 BID (AD) 82 wherein it was held that the finding of facts and when can be disturbed? When the appellate Court as the final Court off acts decides questions of fact and records its finding on consideration of the evidence, the High Court Division cannot interfere with the finding of facts in revision unless the said findings are found to be perverse. When the material findings of the appellate Court are upheld by the High Court Division to be correct, no interference is called for by the Appellate Division unless a substantial error of law is proved.</u>

14. Another decision can be cited in this connection in the case of Hazari Bala Chana and others vs Nira alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 1997 BID (AD) 294 wherein it was stated that it is a settled principle that the finding of facts whether concurrent or not arrived at by the appellate Court is binding on the High Court Division as revisional Court except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case.

15. The judgment of the lower Appellate Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record both oral and documentary including the registered deeds. The learned Advocate for the petitioner could not point out any error, illegality or infirmity of law in the judgment passed by the lower appellate Court.

16. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, I do not find that the lower appellate Court in affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court committed any error of law or acted illegally.

17. The discussion made above, the facts and circumstance of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 13-11-2001 and 22-11-2001 affirming the judgment and decree dated 21-11-99 and 29-11-99 respectively and the case having been concluded on finding of facts, as such, no interference is called for in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to the costs.

Lower Court's record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment

End.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam with Probir Neogi, Advocates------ For the Appellants. 
Fazlul Karim with Khandakar Aminul Islam, Advocates------For Respondent No.1.
parties:
Ali Akbar (Md) and others ------ Appellants
vs
Sakina Begum and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J : This appeal was presented by defendant Nos. 1 to 4 against an order dated 15-1-2002 of Joint District Judge (in-Charge) and Artha Rin Adalat No.2 in Dhaka in Title Suit No. 95 of 1997, appointing a receiver of the suit property.

2. Short facts for disposal of the appeal is that respondent Nos. 1 to 4 as plaintiffs instituted the suit against the appellants and another for declaration that deed of partition being No. 8692 executed on 10-8-1991 and registered on 14-8-1991 by defendant No.5 as described fully in schedule F to the plaint and number of affidavits dated 18-11-1984 are all fraudulent, illegal, void, and not acted upon and binding upon them and also for partition for 2/5th share of the suit property. All the defendants jointly denied the plaint case by filing a written statement.

3. Then, on or about 3-7-2001 the plaintiffs made an application under Order XL rule 1(a) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of a receiver for maintenance, preservation, protection and management of the suit property as described in schedules A to E and also for collection of rents and profits. On 9-9-2001 the defendants opposed the claim by filing a joint written objection. The application was however heard on 15-1-2002 and allowed by the learned Joint District Judge by the impugned order and Mr AKM Enamul Huq Advocate was appointed receiver at a remuneration of Taka 5,000 per month.

<u>4. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, assailed the order on various grounds both on law as well as facts. He submitted that the plaintiffs and defendants are full brothers and sisters, and their father left the suit property. In 1991 all of them amicably partitioned the suit property by a registered deed of partition and since, they were possessing and enjoying their specific shares. He submitted that there was no basis for making an application for appointment of a receiver and plaintiff Nos. 2 to 3 therefore, dissociated themselves from such application.. Lastly, he submitted that the learned Joint District Judge most illegally appointed a receiver of the suit property and such order was against the established principles of law governing appointment of a receiver in a partition suit. In support, he cited the cases of Faiz Ahmed vs Baktear Ahmed, 36 DLR (AD) 97 and Md Musa and others vs Tajul Islam. 38 DLR 134.</u>

<u>5. On the other hand, Mr Fazlul Karim, learned Senior Counsel, submitted that as the plaintiffs were being deprived of their share in the ancestral property, so they were constrained to institute the suit and ultimately, was further constrained to make the application for appointment of a receiver. He submitted that the plaintiffs also impugned the deed of partition as forged since they never subscribed to the deed and they claimed that the deed was brought into existence by false personification. Mr Karim submitted that learned Joint District Judge did not commit any error in appointing a receiver, which would prejudice none. He also cited a case of Ramji Ram and others vs Saligram, 14 CWN 248.</u>

6. The issue facing us is, whether the order appointing a receiver in a partition suit is well founded on the facts of the case and the law.

7. Admitted case is that Maulavi Alimullah was owner in possession of the entire suit property. He died leaving a wife, Hasina Begum two sons and six daughters. Then, Hasina Begum, died. Of the sisters, four instituted the suit against the brothers and two sisters. In the application for appointment of a receiver, it is alleged, inter alia, that defendant No. 1 was collecting rents and profits of the suit property and misappropriating without giving them any account or share. As daughters, they were entitled to the 2/5th share of the property and there was every chance of success in the suit. At the end of the suit, they would get nothing out of the income of the suit property unless a receiver was appointed for collection of rents and profits of the suit property and for keeping the accounts. It was therefore prayed that for the ends of justice and management and protection of their share, the appointment of a receiver was necessary.

8. Opposing the application, the defendants contended that after the death of Alimullah on 18-10-1976, his sons and daughters appointed their mother Hasina Begum as their duly constituted attorney by a registered power of attorney dated 5-12-1977. So empowered she transferred number of properties with the concurrence of all her sons and daughters. After such transfers, the rest of the properties were amicably partitioned amongst the plaintiffs and defendants by the aforesaid registered deed of partition, which was duly acted upon. After the partition, the plaintiffs had got no right, title or interest in the suit property. The institution of the suit and making of the application for appointment of a receiver was ill advised and mala fide. It was also claimed that appointment of a receiver would result in mismanagement and destruction of the property.

9. It also appears when the suit reached the stage of peremptory hearing and recording of deposition of plaintiff No. 2 by an Advocate Commissioner was pending, the application for appointment of a receiver was made. It further appears, at the hearing of the application learned Advocate of plaintiff Nos. 2 to 4 did not press the application on their behalf. On consideration of the application and the objection, the learned Joint District Judge was of the view that the suit was for partition and the decision in which might take time; that the question of title could be decided in the suit and that the property was admittedly ancestral property. Upon such view of the matter, he allowed the application and appointed a receiver for collection of rents, and for accounts of income and expenditure and management of the suit property, pending decision in the suit.

10. Order XL rule 1(a) of the Code empowers a Court to appoint a receiver of any property, whether before or after a decree whenever it appears to it to be just and convenient. The object and purpose of the appointment are to preserve the subject matter of the suit pending decision of the rights of the parties. It however rests with the discretion of the Court.

11. What is just and/or convenient has not been described in the Code; nor there is no hard and fast rule for exercise of the discretion. A consensus in the decisions of superior Courts has however developed into some general principles for guidance for appointment of a receiver. One of the principles is the power should be sparingly used. Secondly, it should be exercised for the safeguard of the interest of the parties as well as the suit property. Thirdly, the possession of persons bona fide in occupation of the property should not be disturbed unless there is clear case of wastage or dissipation of property or apprehension of irreparable loss or injury.

<u>12. In a suit for partition, of course there is no bar for appointment of a receiver. But the above principles require the exercise of caution about putting a third party in possession of the joint property. Special circumstances for appointment must be proved before the Court. It should be exercised in extreme cases. In a case where one Co- sharer occupies the entire property and excludes other co-sharers from the rents and profits of the property, a receiver should be appointed even when no waste or malversation by such co-sharer in occupation is clearly proved. Or where the peril or danger to the property appears to be great and imminent; Cf Faiz Ahmed vs Baktear Ahmed, 36 DLR (AD) 97. Another aspect should also be remembered, the plaintiff prima facie should have an excellent chance of success in the suit. But where members of a family are in separate possession of the property for a long time, there should be no appointment of a receiver without the consent of the parties.</u>

13. In the case before us, the parties are in separate possession of the suit property left by their father on the basis of a registered partition amongst them since 1991. Out of six sisters and two brothers, plaintiff No. 1 only wants appointment of a receiver. And her success in the suit mainly depends on the proof that the registered deed of partition was forged and void, and/or not acted upon. In the circumstances, introduction of a third party as a receiver of the valuable property cannot be surely said would not result in mismanagement of or harm to the property.

14. In view of the above facts of the case and the law, the learned Joint District Judge clearly fell in serious error in the exercise of the discretion in appointing a receiver of the suit property, and such appointment cannot be sustained in law. This appeal has therefore got merit.

15. Result being the appeal is allowed with costs. Impugned, order dated 15-1-2002 appointing a receiver of the suit property is hereby set aside. The application for appointment of a receiver is rejected. Connected Rule is also discharged and order of stay is recalled.

16. Learned Joint District Judge is directed to proceed with the suit, expeditiously.

Communicate at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Tobarrak Hossain, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner 
Mahbubey Alam with Mr Safar Ali, Advocate ----- For the respondents.
parties:
Dr Manzoor Rasheed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Principal, DMC Dhaka & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the action of the respondents refusing admission of the petitioner in the MS (Urology) course under Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University conducted by the Dhaka Medical College, Dhaka on false plea of the petitioner being over age on the basis of the notification dated 7-10-99 as contained in Annexure-G should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and or such other of further order or orders passed as may be deemed fit and proper.

2. The petitioners case as stated in the application that he passed the MBBS Examination in May 1983 from the Sylhet Medical College and served in different places in different capacities. While he was serving as the Assistant Registrar (Urology), Dhaka Medical College, the petitioner got himself admitted in Pakistan Institute of Medical Science to obtain MS Degree in Urology and was granted two years study leave from 1-2-1991. The petitioner had to come back from Pakistan without completing the course due to his family problems and after return he submitted his joining report in the Ministry of Health but he was not given any posting then and there. After a long period his joining report was accepted and he was again posted as Indoor Medical Officer in the Department of Urology Dhaka Medical College Hospital where he has been working at present. The petitioner's further case is that Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University, hereinafter referred to as University, was established under Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University Act 1998 (Act 1 of 1998), hereinafter referred to as the Act, and the said Act has been made applicable notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, and as such, the Act has a superseding effect. According to section 45 of the said Act the policy of admission in the Post Graduate Class shall be regulated by the academic council of the University and the University has the power to affiliate the Medical Colleges and Institutes under it by section 6 of the said Act. The Dhaka Medical College is affiliated with the said University vide annexure-A along with other Medical Colleges and Medical Institutes of the country.

3. The course of MS Urology of Dhaka Medical College is affiliated to the said University by order dated 28-7-99 giving an effect from July 1999 session (Annexure-B). The University issued a notification under Memo No. BSMMU/CS Jan/2000/3705 dated 28-9-99 published in the daily newspaper, Janakantha, on 30-9-1999 inviting applications from the candidates including the candidates who are in government service. The age limit for the government candidates for the admission in the post graduate course was fixed at 40 years as on 31-12-99 (Annexure-C and C-1). Subsequently, the University published another amended notification dated 4-11-99 published in the said newspaper on 5-11-99 which increased the age limit of the Government candidate from 40 to 45 years for this year only (Annexure-D and D-1). The Medical Education Division, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Government of Bangladesh, in its recent deputation policy circulated by memo dated 3-2-98 (Annexure-E) for Post Graduate Education of the BCS (Health) cadres has also fixed age limit up to 45 years. The other affiliated colleges and institutes including Non-Government Institutions vide Annexure-F series also issued notice inviting application for admission in the post graduate course fixing the age limit for the government candidate up to 45 years complying with the aforesaid government policy. The Dhaka Medical College published notice Annexure-G dated 7-10-99 inviting application for admission in various courses including MS Urology by fixing 40 years age limit for the government candidate following the previous notification of the University 28-9-1999 (Annexure-C). After publication of the notification dated 5-11-99 (Annexure-D) by the University the petitioner, in order to avail the last chance for obtaining decree of MS (Urology) from Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University under the Dhaka Medical College, obtained the admission form on payment of requisite fees and submitted it after up filling with required documents on the same day on 14-11-99, and the petitioner was expecting to get admit card for appearing at the, admission test. The petitioner, without getting admit card on 21-11-99, the date of admission test, made an inquiry in the office of the Principal and his department in the Dhaka Medical College and came to know that Professor Dr SAM Golam Kibria, Head of the Department of Urology (respondent No. 2) made an endorsement in the petitioner's admission form "over age not eligible" (Annexure- H) and as such, his form was not processed, The age of the petitioner will be 42 years 4 months 25 days on 31-12-1999 and this is the date to be counted and he is quite eligible for admission according to the amended notification of the University and government policy as per Annexure-D and E as mentioned above. But the respondent No.2 illegally did not process the petitioner's admission form with malafide intention although the opportunity for post graduate course to the government candidate over 40 years was given by the University for this year only. The petitioner having learnt that the respondent No. 2 illegally made the remarks as "over age not eligible" in his application form contacted the respondent No. 1, the Administrative Head of the Dhaka Medical College, and brought to his notice the illegality committed by the respondent No. 2 and requested him to take appropriate steps to allow the petitioner to study (MS Urology) Course at Dhaka Medical College considering that this is the last chance for him, but without any result. Being constrained, the petitioner filed application on 29-11-99 to the Vice-Chancellor, Bangabandhu Medical University, respondent No. 3, and prayed for making an arrangement for his admission into the post graduate course namely, MS (Urology) of Dhaka Medical College, but no result. The petitioner, therefore, served a legal notice demanding justice and to which the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 jointly replied to the said demand notice stating to the effect that in relaxation of age from 40 to 45 years as made is a decision of the University being an' autonomous body and they have taken their own decision, Dhaka Medical College being a purely Government institution cannot do anything without government directing by a notification.

4. The petitioner being thus aggrieved moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

5. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 have opposed the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying all the material allegations contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 has neither illegally nor malafide intention made remarks as "over age not eligible". The respondent No. 2 has followed the decision of the Academic Council of Dhaka Medical College as the Post Graduate Cell of Academic Council in its meeting took decision fixing the age limit for the government candidate up to 40 years of age and accordingly notification was issued. Bangabandhu Medical University being the autonomous body published the notice of admission and Dhaka Medical College did not to follow the same.

6. Regarding issuance of admit card in favour of Syed Amjad Ali it has been stated that Dr Syed Amjad Ali appeared in the list and qualified for the admission but when it was detected that he crossed the age limit more than 40 years, his admission was cancelled. The said Dr Syed Amjad Ali made a representation to the University and in view of the said representation Dhaka Medical College wrote University authority and wanted direction and the Registrar of the university replied that the University has not yet framed any rules for admission and, as such, no illegality has been committed by the Dhaka Medical College in fixing 40 years of age limit for the Government candidate. it has been further stated that the circular dated 3-2-98 (Annexure-E) issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the deputation policy for BSC Cadre doctors and it is not the admission policy and, as such, the Annexure-E is not applicable for admission of the petitioner. In that circular the age limit which has been mentioned is not for admission in any course, rather it relates to granting of deputation for higher studies. It has been further stated that Dhaka Medical College did not publish notice inviting application following the notification dated 28-9-1999 issued by Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University, rather aforesaid two institutions published their notice independently. Under the above circumstances the Rule is liable to be discharged.

7. The petitioner replied to the affidavit-in-opposition and it has been reiterated as to what has been stated in the writ petition and also denied certain statements regarding deputation policy and education policy with reference to the circular dated 3-2-1998 (Annexure-E-1) issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The petitioner has reiterated that Dr Syed Amjad Ali, who was aged over 40, was allowed to sit for the written test for admission whereas the petitioner was not allowed and thereby he has been discriminated.

8. Mr Md Tobarak Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, having taken us through the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and the petitioner's affidavit-in-reply thereto as well as the different annexures therein, and thereafter submitted that the respondent No. 1 and 2 denied the petitioner an opportunity to undergo the Post Graduate course, that is, MS (Urology) course, in violation of the circular and notification issued by the University in contravention of the Act of 1998 (Act I of 1998) and it is therefore the action of the respondent in not allowing sit petitioner to sit for the admission test to undergo the post graduate course by issuing admit card without lawful authority being an act of discrimination between the petitioner and Dr Syed Amjad Ali.

9. Mr Tobarrak Hossain, in elaborating the above contention pointed out that one Syed Amjad Ali, candidate of Serial No. 66 in the Department of Neuro Surgery, and Dr Gabinda Chandra Saha, candidate of Serial No. 87 in the department of Paediatrics, were aged more then 40 years and they were given the chance to sit over the admission test by issuing admit card in their favour but the petitioner having been denied the admit card to be issued has deprived the petitioner to appear in the admission test by the Head of the Department of the same College, which is an illegal act being tainted with malafide intention. The petitioner has been discriminately treated thereby. It is, therefore, argued that to pursue higher education which is the fundamental right as guaranteed under the Constitution has been infringed. It has been further argued that since the University by notification allowed the Government candidate to be eligible for admission up to the age limit of 45 years to undergo. the course for particular one year, the endorsement on the petitioner's admission form being made as "over age not eligible" by the Head of the Department of Urology is an illegal and arbitrary act done with malafide intention and the same is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority. It has been further contended that the Dhaka Medical College is admittedly an affiliated College under the Bangabandhu Medical University and the course of MS (Urology) is also affiliated to the said University and that being the position the age limit of 45 years as recognised by the University by amended notification dated 5-11-99 was binding upon the Dhaka Medical College to be followed and as such the action of the responded Nos. 1 and 2 is a gross violation of articles 27, 28, 31 of the Constitution in not issuing the admit card in favour of the petitioner, It is further submitted that the Academic Council of the Dhaka Medical College has no legal entity and as such, was not authorised to decide and fix the age limit up to 40 years in view of the fact that the University directed the respondents to follow the admission policy of the government on the ground that the college being government institution in the absence of any admission rules framed by the University (Annexure-3A to the affidavit-in-opposition), and furthermore, the respondents ought to have followed the policy as spelt out in the Circular vide Annexure-E, but the respondents having not followed the same acted illegally and without lawful authority in depriving the petitioner for appearing in the admission test for no fault of his own.

10. Mr Tobarak Hossain has further argued that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in their reply (Annexure-E) dated 13-12-99, to the demand of justice notice, clearly stated that they followed their own policy in issuing the notice inviting application for admission in post graduate course and in the same breath they asserted that they are to abide by the government decision, and from the government notification dated 3-2-98 (Annexure-E) it is clear that the respondents have violated the said government notification because of the fact that the University has affiliated the course and the postgraduate degree would be conferred by the University and as such, the respondents are to follow the admission policy of the University and the respondents having not followed the government policy and the policy of the University, acted illegally in not allowing the petitioner to be admitted in the course of MS Urology.

11. In support of his contentions, Mr Tobarak Hossain has relied on a decision in the case reported in AIR 1996 Supreme Court, 1378 which we will consider at the appropriate place of the judgment.

12. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, in his private capacity, on the other hand, contended that the petitioner having had knowledge of the admission notice as published by the Dhaka Medical College applied for the admission test being aware of the age limit. The respondent No. 2 being Head of the Department and one of the members of the academic council has the authority to fix the age limit for his own department and as such, no illegality has been committed. It has been further contended that the memo dated 3-2-98 (Annexure- E) is the deputation policy issued by the Government and the same cannot be treated as a policy regarding admission and in that memo the age limit which has been mentioned is not for admission in any course. Further, the same is related to granting of deputation for higher studies and as such, the said memo dated 3-2-98 (Annexure-E) as claimed by the petitioner as a guideline for admission, cannot be accepted.

13. We have heard the learned lawyers of both sides at length. It appears that Dhaka Medical College is affiliated to Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University (Annexure-A) and the course of MS Urology is also affiliated to the said University (Annexure-B). The University issued a notification under memo dated 28-9-1999 vide Annexure-C inviting application from the candidates, including the candidates who are in Government service, fixing the age limit at 40 years, Subsequently, the University by amended notification dated 5-11-99 fixed the age at 45 years and as per the aforesaid notification the petitioner, in order to avail the last chance, obtained the admission form and submitted the same. But the petitioner was not allowed to sit for the admission test as no admit card was issued. The petitioner came to know that the respondent No. 2, Head of the Department of Urology, made an endorsement in admission form "over aged not eligible". The argument of Tobarrak Hossain is that as per amended notification dated 5-11-99 was to be followed by Dhaka Medical College since the petitioner on 31-12-99 was aged about 42 years 4 months 25 days, and as such, the petitioner was quite eligible for admission according to the said amended notification of the University. The Principal, Dhaka Medical College, also admitted that they published a notice on 7-10-99, on the basis of the notification dated 28-9-99 published by the University, and it was also admitted that the amended notice (Annexure-D) published by the University escaped the notice of the College authority, vide Annexure-3 of the affidavit-in- opposition.

14. It further appears that one Dr Amjad Ali, a candidate of the Department of Neuro Surgery, and Dr Gobinda Chanda Chandra Saha, a candidate of the department of paediatrics. who were aged more than 40 years of age were given the chance to appear at the admission test, but subsequently, the admission of Dr Amjad Ali was cancelled and on a representation to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Dhaka Medical College authority admitted said Dr Amjad Ali, vide annexure-M of the affidavit-in-reply. In view of the aforesaid aspect of the case we find substance in the argument of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

15. Admittedly the petitioner is a Government candidate being in Government service and we also find the argument of the respondent that the policy in Annexure-E is not applicable in case of the admission of the Government candidates cannot be accepted because of the fact that the Government made it clear that the said deputation policy is the admission policy also for the government candidates in Post Graduate Course, as is evident from .annexure-M to the affidavit-in-reply of she petitioner, wherein the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare made a clear reference about the guidelines and procedure for post graduate course of the doctors of BCS as contained in Annexure-E dated 3-2-98. The petitioner j, admittedly a member of BC (Health) Service and serving in the Dhaka Medical College, and, as such, he is a government candidate. We are of the view that the Annexure-E in its recent policy circulated by Medical Education Division of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, having fixed the age limit up to 45 years, was binding upon the respondent No. 2 and the petitioner was entitled to get admit card to sit for the admission test in the post graduate course (MS in Urology) and the respondent No.2 ought to have issued admit card in his favour. We, therefore, hold that the petitioner's right to pursue higher education is his fundamental right as guaranteed and has been infringed as well as he has been illegally discriminated.

<u>16. The argument of Mr Mahbubey Alam to the effect that the Post Graduate Cell of Acadamic Council of the Dhaka Medical College decided to fix age limit up to 40 years for the Government candidate is not tenable. Firstly because the Academic Council cannot have any authority to change the Government and University policy, secondly, the so-called Post Graduate Cell of the Academic Council had no legal enity, though the learned Counsel for the respondents produced one paper showing formation of the Academic Council which" was not annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition, and thirdly, the Academic Council has the power to make recommendations only and not to make any decision by itself.</u>

17. We, therefore, hold that fixation of age limit by the Dhaka Medical College is absolutely without any authority and contradictory in view of aforesaid annexure, particularly vide Annexure-E and Annexure-M as discussed herein above.

18. It further appears from Annexure-E, the letter of Ministry of Health, we have already found that though it is a deputation policy it is also the admission policy for the Government candidates in Post Graduate courses where there is scope of 5 seats in the 1st part Urology Course for the Government candidates in such Institution and it is evident from the Annexure-4 of the Government affidavit that only 3 seats in the said College have been filled up by the Government candidates and, thus there are 2 seats vacant still now.

19. The case as referred to by the learned Counsel for the petitioner in the case of Ritesh R Sha, petitioner vs Dr YL Yamul and others, respondent, reported in AIR 1996 Supreme Court 1378, the Supreme Court of India in the exercise of the writ jurisdiction directed to admit the petitioner in any of the colleges in MBBS Course in a vacant seat and even if there is no seat to create seat and also to condone any prohibition (like admission test in the present case) if there is any in the University regulation as an exceptional case. In the present case, the petitioner passed MBBS in 1983 and he has a brilliant academic carreer and he has been in active service in the government and now working in the Urology Department of Dhaka Medical College, and considering this aspect we find that petitioner is an experienced person and his case may be considered as an exceptional one. The facts of the above cited case, though are distinguishable from those of the present case, but the relief was granted to the petitioner by the Supreme Court considering his merit as an exceptional case.

20. Mr Mahbubey Alam has also relied on a decision in the case of Dr Vinay Rampal, petitioner vs State of Jammu and Kashmir and others, respondents reported in AIR 1983 Supreme Court. We have read the said decision. In the above cited case it was held that petitioner who was eligible for admission as per requirements set out in the advertisement could not be refused admission on the basis of Government order when other have been admitted on the basis of advertisement. In the present case we have already found that petitioner was eligible for sitting in the admission test as per advertisement by the Bangladesh Sheikh Mujib Medical University which increased the age limit of the government candidates from 40-45 for this year only vide Annexure-E.

21. In view of what has discussed above, we find substance in the Rule and we, therefore, hold that petitioner has been discriminated and he should be allowed to pursue his higher study in MS course Urology without admission test and by increasing one seat by the respondents.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.
