full_judgment:
Petitioner is the decree-holder who obtained this Rule against the order dated 11-6-2000 of the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 4. Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 31 of 1997 directing him to make over possession of schedule 'Kha' land to the third party opposite party.

2. This Rule arises out of the following facts: Petitioner instituted title Suit No. 180 of 1986 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against late Md Jalaluddin for Specific Performance of Contract for sale of schedule 'Ka' property. During pendency of the suit said Md Jalaluddin died and his heirs have been substituted in the suit and they were brought on record. Ultimately, the suit was decreed on the basis of solenama filed in the Court on 31-10-1996 between the plaintiff and the heirs of Md Jalaluddin, Pursuant thereto the decree was drawn up on 20-2-1997. Petitioner put the decree into execution in title execution case No. 31 of 1997 and got the sale deed registered through Court and got possession of schedule 'Ka' land' along with schedule 'Kha' land through Court. Subsequently, opposite party Haji Md Yusuf filed an application under Order 21 rule 101 read with section 151 CPC for restoration of possession of schedule 'kha' property on the ground that the decree-holder by practicing fraud upon the Court secured delivery of possession of his homestead which has been described in schedule 'kha' to the decree. Petitioner filed an application for rejection of the said petition filed by the 3rd party opposite party on the ground that he is a transferee from the judgment-debtor and therefore, he has no locus standi to maintain an application under Order 21 rule 101 CPC.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the application filed by the third party opposite party and rejected the application filed by the decree-holder petitioner and directed the decree-holder to hand over possession of the schedule 'Kha' property in favour of third party opposite party.

4. Being aggrieved by the said order, the decree-holder petitioner obtained this Rule.

5. Mr KS Salahuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law in entertaining the application filed by the third party opposite party who is a transferee from the judgment debtor and therefore, he is not legally entitled to maintain the application under Order 21 rule 101 CPC. Learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in disposing Of the application filed by the third party opposite party in a summary manner without making any inquiry as required by law and illegally directed the petitioner to hand over possession of the schedule 'kha' property and thereby he has committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

6. Mr M Enayetur Rahim, learned Advocate for the third party opposite party, submits that since the decree holder having practiced fraud and collusively obtained the homestead of the petitioner and since the learned Subordinate Judge having found such fraud on the face of the record, he has ample power to make an order for restoration of the property under section 151 CPC without making any inquiry under Order 21 rule 101 CPC.

7. Admittedly, schedule 'Kha' property is the homestead of the third party opposite party and the said property has been taken over possession by the decree holder petitioner through the process of the execution proceeding by evicting him therefrom. The learned Subordinate Judge in the impugned order for restoration of possession observed that the petitioner entered into an agreement on 6-1-1983 in respect of 0.33 acre of land of Dhakhin Khan mouza, that there has been disfiguration in clauses 'ga' and 'ja' of the solenama filed on 31-10-1996, which has been done for grabbing the property of Haji Md Yusuf and that by means of such disfiguring with corrections, 'Kha' schedule property has been included in the writ of delivery of possession.

8. Since there are allegations of interpolation of the solenama, I have called for the record and perused the same.

9. In the record I find a photo copy of the agreement dated 6-1-1983 executed between the petitioner and late Md Jalaluddin in respect of 0.33 acre of land of mouja Dhakhin Khan under Gulshan PS. There is a clause in the said agreement that in case the title of the vendor in respect of the land as described in the schedule to the agreement is found defective, the vendor shall be bound to execute a sale deed in respect of House No. 78, Sultanganj, Rayer Bazar. It further appears from the record that decree holder petitioner filed an application for amendment of the plaint on 15-11-1998 on the ground that the vendor has already transferred some land out of the suit land under the agreement for sale and therefore, as per terms of the agreement, the property of the vendor i.e. 78, Sultanganj, Mohammadpur Police Station be included as schedule 'Kha' to the plaint and that the decree holder petitioner may be allowed a decree for specific performance of contract in respect of the said house. The learned Subordinate Judge by order dated 24-5-1989 allowed the prayer for amendment of the plaint and schedule 'Kha' property has been included in the plaint.

10. In the solenama filed by the decree holder petitioner with the heirs of late Md Jalaluddin, I have noticed that in the solenama clauses 'ga' and 'ja' have been amended and schedule 'Kha' land has been written by hand and inserted in the solenama. This schedule 'Kha' property has been inserted in the plaint by way of amendment by order dated 24-5-1989. Pursuant to such decree, the decree holder petitioner got possession of the schedule 'ka' property along with schedule 'Kha' property. On the basis of the solenama the petitioner got 0.19 acre of land out of 0.33 acre in schedule 'Ka' land.

11. In the application filed by the 3rd party opposite party, he has stated that he purchased the schedule 'Kha' property by registered kabala dated 18-2-1990 and has been possessing the same and that the decree holder by practicing fraud upon the Court collusively obtained possession by evicting him from his homestead and that he had no knowledge about the said decree. The petitioner also filed an application on 18-1-2000 for rejecting the application filed by the third party on the ground that the 3rd party opposite party has purchased the schedule 'Kha' land from late Md Jalaluddin by kabala dated 18-2-1990 during the pendency of the suit and that since the third party being a transferee from the judgment debtor he has no Locus standi to make an application under Order 21 rule 101. The learned Subordinate Judge took up both the applications for hearing and by the impugned order rejected the application filed by the decree-holder petitioner and allowed the application of the 3rd party opposite party. The learned Subordinate Judge disposed of the application in a summary manner without examining the parties and also without starting a fresh Miscellaneous Case on the basis of the application filed by the 3rd party opposite party.

12. In the facts of the given case, let me examine whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in directing the decree holder-petitioner to make over possession without making any inquiry on the basis of the application filed by the 3rd party opposite party. In this connection Order 21 rules 100, 101 and 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure are relevant for the purpose of disposal of the matter, which are reproduced below:

"100. (1) Where any person other than the judgment-debtor is dispossessed of immovable property by the holder of a decree for the possession of such property or, where such property has been sold in execution of a decree, by the purchaser thereof, he may make an application to the Court complaining of such dispossession.

(2) The Court shall fix a day for investigating the matter and shall summon the party against whom the application is made to appear and answer the same.

101. Where the Court is satisfied that the applicant was in possession of the property on his own account or on account of some person other than the judgment-debtor it shall direct that the applicant be put into possession of the property.

103. Any party not being a judgment-debtor against whom an order is made under rule 98, rule 99 or rule 101 may institute a suit to establish the right which he claims to the present possession of the property; but, subject to the result of such suit (if any), the order shall be conclusive."

13. Rule 100 of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides the remedy for a person who is himself not a judgment debtor but who has been dispossessed on account of the execution of a decree against a 3rd party. He has to prove that he was in possession on the day of dispossession in execution of the decree. A plain reading of Rule 100 clearly provides that a person under the judgment debtor is not entitled to apply under this rule. The question as to the collusiveness of a decree or order are outside the scope of proceeding under rule 100 CPC. A Court dealing with an application under this rule is not concerned with the determination of the title of the property which is the subject matter of the application. It is only connected with the factum of possession at the time when the applicant is alleged to have been dispossessed by the decree-holder and the nature of such possession, whether it was on his own account or on account of a person other than the judgment-debtor. The proceedings following an objection under rule 100 of the Code are summary in character and the decision thereon is subject to a suit under rule 103 of Order 21 CPC, Since the determination of the Court is whether the applicant was in possession of the property on the day it was decreed and also whether he has been dispossessed not through the judgment debtor any order without oral evidence, relying upon the documents and the papers filed by the applicant is, in my view, not in accordance with law. Inquiry contemplated under rule 100 is restricted to the question of possession only and even though the applicant may not have good title to the property. if he can show that he was not in possession on behalf of the judgment debtor but on his own account, he must be put in possession under rule 101 CPC.

<u>14. In the instant case, I have noticed that the learned Subordinate Judge has not followed the above procedure and without making any sort of inquiry whatsoever, as contemplated under Order 21 rule 100 CPC and without recording a Miscellaneous Case pursuant to the application. disposed of the case in a summary manner on a superficial perusal of the record. He has not considered the objection filed by the petitioner that the third party-opposite party is claiming the schedule 'Kha' property on the basis of purchase from the judgment debtor during the pendency of the suit. He has not also considered as to whether schedule 'Kha' land was inserted in the solenama on the day of filing solenama or that it was in the plaint or not. If he finds that the third party-opposite party is a transferee from the judgment debtor, he is not entitled to maintain application under rule 100 and his remedies are by way of suit under rule 103 to establish his right. Though he has disposed of the case in a summary manner but he made observations of forgery and collusion against the decree-holder in securing decree which is not contemplated by rule 100 of Order 21 CPC.</u>

<u>15. Mr Rahim, submits that since there are apparent fraud practiced by the decree-holder for taking possession of the schedule 'Kha' property the Court can make an order without making any inquiry as contemplated under rule 100 of Order 21 of the Code in exercise of inherent powers under section 151 CPC. In support of his contention he has referred a decision in the case of Shahr Banoo Mohsin Asgar and another vs Lainun Nahar Ershad and others, 44 DLR 552. The decision referred by Mr Rahim has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case. Inherent powers of the Court exists only where there is no express provision of law applicable to the case. Section 151 cannot be invoked to defeat the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provision of the Code must be deemed to be exhaustive of all matters dealt with by it. A Court has no inherent power to do that which is prohibited by the Code. Inherent jurisdiction of the Court must be exercised subject to the rule that if the code does contain specific provisions which would meet the necessities of the case, such provisions should be followed and inherent jurisdiction should not be invoked. In other words, the Court cannot make use of the special provisions of section 151 where a party had his remedy provided elsewhere in the Code. The third party petitioners remedy lies under Order 21 rules 100 and 101 CPC and therefore, the Court cannot make an order in exercise of section 151. In this case question of exercise of section 151 does not arise as the opposite party made the application under rule 101 of Order 21. In the reported case referred by the learned Advocate, the question was whether an ex parte decree can be set aside under section 151 of the Code. In that case, the plaintiff after being unsuccessful upto the Appellate Division instituted another suit on the same subject matter and got a collusive ex parte decree. This Court found that there was wilful concealment of fact and fraudulent suppression of summons in obtaining the decree. In this case, the alleged forgery and collusion are yet to be established.</u>

<u>16. In this case since the decree holder petitioner asserted that the 3rd party petitioner is a transferee from the judgment debtor late Md Jalaluddin and since the 3rd party opposite party in his application did not make any statement as to how he got the schedule property, it was incumbent upon the learned Subordinate Judge to hold an inquiry as to whether the 3rd party opposite party can legally maintain an application or not under Order 21 rules 100 and 101 of the Code and that whether there was any fraud practiced by the decree-holder petitioner in taking possession of the property of the 3rd party opposite party.</u>

17. Considering all these aspects of the matter, I am of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in directing the decree holder petitioner to make over possession of the property without holding any inquiry as required by law. Accordingly, I find substance in this Rule.

18. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The order dated 11-6- 2000 of the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 31 of 1997 is set aside. The matter is remanded to the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka to decide the matter afresh in the light of the observation made above.

19. The learned Subordinate Judge is directed to dispose of the matter expeditiously preferably within 3 months from the date of receipt of the order.

Send down the lower Court records.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 4-2-93 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.497 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This appeal by leave by the defendant-appellants is from the judgment and order dated 4-2-93 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 497 of 1990 setting aside the concurrent decree of dismissal of Title Suit No. 106 of 1977 of the Court of Subordinate Judge. Kushtia by judgment and order dated 15-2-86. affirmed by the judgment and order dated 24-8-89 passed by the Additional District Judge, Kushtia in Title Appeal No. 58 of 1986.

2. Plaintiff-respondents filed the aforesaid suit for partition claiming 12 annas 10½ paisa share in the suit property stating, inter alia, that 15 acres of land with structures thereon in plot No.2379 of khatian No. 286 (old) khatian No. 409 (new). Mouza Kalishankarpur belonged to one Judhistir Chandra Nath who settled the same with Asia Khatun, the plaintiffs' mother, on 10th Aswin 1354 BS at a rent of Taka 5.00 per year. Possession thereof was delivered to the plaintiffs' mother who was the first wife of Md. Ibrahim. On 27-2-51 Judhistir transferred his malikana interest to Md. Ibrahim. The plaintiffs are the sons and daughters of Md. Ibrahim through his first wife Asia Khatun. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are Md. Ibrahim's son and daughter respectively through his second wife Lutfunnessa, defendant No.3 Asia Khatun used to live in a house on the suit land constructing a 6-room house in the southern side of the plot and letting out the rooms to different tenants. While in possession Asia Khatun died leaving behind her husband, two sons, plaintiff No.1 and Nurul Islam and four daughters. plaintiff-respondent Nos. 2-5. Nurul Islam died unmarried. Then died Ibrahim on 12-10-76 leaving behind two sons plaintiff No.1 and defendant No.1. second wife defendant No.3, and five daughters (plaintiff Nos.2-5 and defendant No.2). In this way the plaintiffs acquired 12 annas 10.50 paisa share in the suit property in respect of which they claimed partition.

3. The defendant-appellants in their written statement upon denying the allegations of the plaintiffs stated, inter alia, that Ibrahim was an inhabitant of Nabadwip, West Bengal. He exchanged his properties of Nabadwip with those of J udhistir at Kushtia. Ibrahim registered a deed in favour of Judhistir and in exchange Judistir executed a power of attorney in favour of his son Dhirendra for execution of necessary deeds at Kushtia. Ibrahim took loan from many people and to avoid the creditors Ibrahim got settlement of the suit land in the name of his first wife Asia Khatun. Thereafter Judhistir transferred malikana right to Ibrahim through Dhirendra on the basis of the power of attorney executed by him. Asia Khatun was a benamdar of Ibrahim. During the settlement operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Ibrahim. Thereafter Asia Khatun died and Ibrahim married defendant No.3 Lutfunnessa. On 3-11-75 Ibrahim made a registered deed of gift of 0.08 acres of land of with structures thereon in favour of defendant No.3 and delivered possession to her. She lives in this house and realises tents from the tenants. She also mutated her name and paid municipal taxes. Ibrahim died leaving only the northern half of the suit properties which was inherited by both the plaintiffs and the defendants.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff-respondents found that PW 1 Shamsuzzoha who is plaintiff No. 1 and his other witnesses failed to prove how and in what way Judhistir gave the bandabasta of his property to Asia Khatun, the first wife of Md. Ibrahim. Claiming as they do a share in the suit property through their mother Asia Khatun the plaintiffs have the onus to prove their prima facie title to the suit properly. The trial Court found that both from the evidence of the plaintiffs and the defendants the gift of 0.08 acres of land to defendant No. 3 has been proved. As such in a suit for simple partition the plaintiffs cannot succeed without a prayer for declaration of title in the suit property when the title of the plaintiffs to the suit property is not clear. The suit for simple partition is not maintainable.

5. The lower appellate Court concurred with the findings of the trial Court and additionally found that the partible property is admittedly a non-agricultural property within Kushtia Municipality. Under section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act such property can be transferred only by a bilateral registered deed and not by way of a settlement. Although it has been proved that plaintiff No.1 is in possession of a part of the suit property the basis of the title of the plaintiffs has not been proved and therefore the trial Court was right in holding that before partition the plaintiffs have to establish their right and title to the suit property.

6. In setting aside the concurrent judgment of the two courts below the learned Single Judge of the  High Court Division held that the appellate Court's finding that the defendants have been possessing  their share of the suit land is not very material  because in a suit for partition one co-sharer may hold  the land on behalf of all other co-sharers. The suit land has been recorded in the name of Ibrahim who is the predecessor of both the plaintiffs and the  defendants. As such the lower appellate Court erred in dismissing the suit for simple partition. The  finding as to the deed of gift made by Ibrahim in favour of defendant No 3. "docs not appear to be  based on sound reasoning". The High Court Division further held that the judgment of the lower appellate Court is based on "mis-appreciation of evidence" and as such the suit was sent back on remand to the court of appeal below for disposal in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made in the judgment.

7. Leave was granted to consider the defendant-appellants' submission that the High Court Division completely failed to see the point at issue namely, whether the plaintiffs proved their title to the partible property through Asia Khatun as claimed by them. The High Court Division also ignored the concurrent findings of the courts below, without any reason, that the plaintiffs could not prove their title to their share as alleged and for their title at least was not clear and as such they were not entitled to a decree in a simple suit for partition. The High Court Division's observations that the judgment of the lower appellate Court on the plaintiffs' title etc was based on "misappreciation of evidence was merely an opinion expressed without any basis or reason. Leave was also granted to consider the submission that the order of remand was unnecessary because if the courts below "committed a serious  error of law in dismissing the suit", as found, the High Court Division could itself pass a decree for partition as prayed for by the plaintiffs. In any case the concurrent findings of the courts below were not set aside at all.

8. Md. Aftab Hossain, learned Advocate-on-Record for the defendant-appellants submits that the two courts below, upon an exhaustive consideration of the evidence on record, found that the plaintiff-respondents were claiming right and title to the suit land through their mother Asia Khatun by way of settlement from Judhistir. The plaintiffs failed to prove this settlement and this was the concurrent finding of both the courts below. In passing the order of remand it was incumbent upon the High Court Division to give a finding that this concurrent finding of fact is bad either owing to misreading of evidence or omission to consider material evidence on record or for any other sufficient cause which has caused a miscarriage of justice. There is no such finding by the High Court Division. He further submits that both the courts below believed the appellants' story of gift of .08 acres of land by Ibrahim to his second wife defendant No. 3 by giving cogent reason and by analysing the oral and documentary evidence on record. The High Court Division dismissed this concurrent finding merely by saying that the judgment of the lower appellate Court suffers from "misapprcciation of evidence" on the score without pointing out in which way and in what manner the two courts below misappreciated the evidence. This observation was in the nature of a mere opinion without there being any hard facts or critical analysis backing the opinion. Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain then submits that the defendant appellants claim the southern portion of the suit land in their own right by virtue of the deed of gift made to defendant No. 3 and it is their case that only the northern portion of the plot is the joint property of the plaintiffs and the defendants. Both the courts below found the appellants' exclusive claim to the southern portion of the suit plot to be substantiated by evidence, but the plaintiffs claimed share of the entire plot. If the plaintiffs have no claim of title to the southern portion of the suit plot they cannot maintain their suit for portion without praying for declaration of title to the whole plot. In any view of the matter the order of remand has made.

9. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, learned Advocate- on-Record for respondent No. 1 submits that it is not necessary to pray for a declaration of title when admittedly the entire suit property stands in the name of Ibrahim, the common predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and the defendants. In any case without a formal declaration of title the lower appellate Court is in a position to decide how much land the plaintiffs can claim as partible properly and what share they have in the partible property. As such, he submits, the order of remand does not suffer from any illegality.

<u>10. It is difficult to follow the logic of the argument of the learned Advocate-on-Record for respondent No. 1. In a suit for partition the court will no doubt consider the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land in some details more than in a suit for  permanent injunction, but it cannot in either case convert itself into a court for determination of the respective titles of the parties if a serious dispute emerges from the pleadings as to the title of the plaintiffs to the partible property and if it is not possible to effect partition without formally determining the plaintiffs' title to the property claimed in the partition suit. Both the courts below concurrently held, without being reversed by the High Court Division, that the plaintiffs failed to prove settlement of the suit land with their mother Asia Khatun. If the plaintiffs are desirous of getting their full share as claimed in the present suit they must take the responsibility of proving their claim in a full-fledged suit for declaration of title. If the plaintiffs are driven to accept the deed of gift and the permanent alienation of the southern plot of the suit land to defendant No. 3, they must confine their claim for partition only in respect to the northern portion of the suit land in which the defendants admit the plaintiffs to be their co-sharers. The choice is with the plaintiffs but the way the suit was remanded leaves the appellate Court below with an impossible task. Its finding that the plaintiffs have not been able to prove settlement in favour of their mother remains unreversed. Its finding that the deed of gift was acted upon has been dismissed by the High Court Division by a slip-shod remark that it confusion worse confounded because the lower was based on "misappreciation of evidence". In other appellate Court will now have to re-write its own judgment, reverse its findings that (a) the plaintiffs failed to prove settlement in favour of their mother and that (b) the defendants' story of deed of gift is true and then give the plaintiffs full reliefs as asked for. That will be a judgment under duress without due reversal of the lower appellate Court's judgment by the High Court Division.</u>

11. As such we find that the interference of the High Court Division with the concurrent findings of fact of the two courts below was thoughtless, cryptic and devoid of any reason. It cannot be sustained.

The appeal is allowed with costs. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set aside.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 328 of 2001.
lawyer:
Mahamudul Islam with Abdul Quayam, Advocates ----- For the Appellants. 
Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Saroj Kanta Sarker being dead his heirs and legal representatives, Asit Sarker and others ------ Appellants
Vs
Seraj-ud-Dowla & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant No. 1 presented the above appeal against the decree dated 30-4-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Court No.3 at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 14 of 2001, which decreed the suit for specific performance of a contract dated 2-4-1985.

2. On 23-5-1991 respondent No. 1 Md Seraj-ud-Dowla instituted Title Suit No. 176 of 1991 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka, which was on transfer to the above court renumbered as Title Suit No. 14 of 2001. Plaintiff instituted the suit for specific performance of a contract and for a 'Kabala' in respect of 1.52 acre of land.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that defendant No 1 entered into a contract with the plaintiff for sale of 4.06 acres of land at a rate of 3,30,000 per pakhi (=26 decimals) as fully described in the schedule to the plaint at a consideration of Taka 51,53,073 and on 2-4-1985 on receipt of Taka 3,00,000 he executed an agreement 'Bainapatra' and agreed to execute and register necessary deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff or any person nominated by him.

4. Defendant No. 1 also entered into another contract with pro-forma defendant No.3 Md Nasir Uddin for sale of 1.083 acre of land at the same rate at a consideration of Taka 13,83,460 and on the same date on receipt of Taka 2,00,000 from said defendant executed another agreement agreeing to execute and register necessary deed of sale after receipt of the remainder of the consideration.

5. Further case of the plaintiff is that, although two agreements were executed, in fact, it was an agreement amongst the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and pro-forma defendant Nos. 3 and 4 that defendant No.1 would continue enjoying said 5.143 acres of land covered by two contracts and upon receipt of Taka 60,34,533 the remainder of the considerations from pro-forma defendant No.4 in cash or cheque would execute and register necessary deeds of sale in favour of the plaintiff and defendant No.3 or their nominated persons.

6. It was also agreed that the time limit mentioned in the contracts was cancelled by consent of the parties.

7. Pursuant to said understanding, on the date of the agreement and subsequently, by signing debit vouchers in cash or cheques up to 19-7-1988 defendant No. 1 received Taka 59,35,000 out of Taka 65,36,333 from pro-forma defendant No.4.

8. After receipt of said money of Taka, 59,35,000 defendant No. 1 on different dates executed and registered number of sale deeds in respect of 2.54 acres out of 4.06 acres and 0.086 acre out of 1.083 acre only up to 19-7-1988 in favour of the persons nominated by the plaintiff.

9. When the defendant No. 1 was demanding for more price of the land, on 15-8-1990 there was an agreement reached amongst the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 3 at 68 Motijheel Commercial Area in the office of proforma defendant No.4 in presence of Shahid Khan, Rafique Ahmed and Nasiruddin and others. The agreement was reached that if further Taka 20,00,000 was paid, defendant No. 1 would within one month execute and register sale deeds in respect of rest of 2.04 acres of land in favour of plaintiff or persons nominated by him and in respect of 0.223 acre of land in favour of defendant No.3 or persons nominated by him. Pursuant to the new contract, or understanding dated 15-8-1990, on 27-8-1990 and 2-9-1990 defendant No. 1 received Taka 20,00,000 and executed and registered two deeds dated 30-8-1990 and 9-9-1990 transferring 2 decimals of land only.

10. Defendant No.1 still did not transfer 1.52 acre of land to the plaintiff and 0.223 acre of land to defendant No.3 pursuant to the contract. Lastly, in April 1991 the defendant refused to transfer further land and the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit for specific performance of 1.52 acre of land only.

11. Defendant No. 1 opposed the plaintiff’s case by filing a written statement.

12. His case, in brief, is that, the suit was barred by limitation. The contract became unenforceable in law after 31-3-1986. The suit was also bad for mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties and causes of action. The suit was barred by principles of estoppel, acquiescence and waiver.

13. He denied specifically that two contracts were, in fact, one contract amongst the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and defendant No.3 to sell the entire land to defendant No.4 or that on 15-8-1990 they reached a new contract that he would execute and register sale deeds on receipt of Taka 20,00,000 in respect of rest of the land covered by two contracts.

14. His further case is that, he made two separate contracts on 2-4-1985 with the plaintiff and defendant No.3. It was stipulated in the contracts that the sale deeds had to be taken by 31-3-1986. Within the time limit, he executed and registered some deeds of sale transferring some land to the plaintiff pursuant to the contract. It was also stipulated that if the plaintiff failed to purchase the land within the time fixed then the entire earnest money would be forfeited and defendant No. 1 would be at liberty to transfer the land anywhere. As the plaintiff failed to take the sale deeds as per terms of the contract within the time the transaction under the contract could not be complete and the agreement expired.

15. Further case of defendant No. 1 was that pro-forma defendant No.3 never appeared before him nor got any deed executed and registered either in his own name or in the name of his legal representative. After the expiry of the contract, he executed and registered some other sale deeds transferring some more land on the basis of the deeds, but not the contract.

On the pleadings of the parties, the issues settled are

a.	 whether the suit as framed was maintainable;

b.	 was there any cause of action for the suit;

c.	 was the suit barred by limitation and

d.	 what relief the plaintiff was entitled to.

16.	 In support of his case, the plaintiff got 4 persons examined excluding him while defendant No. 1 examined 3 persons including him. Papers and documents produced by the plaintiff were marked exhibit 1 to 6 series while those of the defendant were marked as exhibit 'Ka', 'Kha' and 'Ga'.

17. On the evidence, oral and documentary, the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit as prayed for.

18. Mr Mahamudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate, took us through the record and submitted that it was clearly stipulated in Paragraph 7 of the agreement that purchase had to be completed by 31-3-1986 by the purchaser paying the balance of the price and the vendor would execute the sale deed, failing which the earnest money paid would stand forfeited and the vendor would be free to sell the land anywhere. In view of such stipulation, he submitted, the time was made an essence of the contract. The suit brought on 23-5-1991 for enforcement of the contract, the time for which already expired, was clearly barred under article 113 of the Limitation Act.

19. He submitted that being conscious of the time limit for performance of the contract, the plaintiff tried to extend the time for enforcement by introducing a story that on 15-8-1990 the plaintiff and defendant No, 1 agreed to extend the time limit, and defendant No. 1 would execute and register necessary deeds of sale in respect of balance of the land at increased rate of price. The plaintiff failed to prove such story by any evidence whatsoever.

20. He submitted that the plaintiff did not dare to tell lie on oath before the Court as he already performed Hajj. Plaintiff first tried to get him examined on commission but abandoned the idea thereafter. Evidence led to prove that the plaintiff was indisposed to come to court also could not be proved.

21. He submitted that the trial Court fell in error in relying upon the endorsement/acknowledgment alleged to have been made by defendant No. 1 on the back of the agreement receiving payments of money on different dates without noticing that there is no mention of such endorsement and/or acknowledgment in the plaint and without any proof thereof.

22. Next, he submitted that Mohammadi Housing Ltd was neither a necessary party nor a proper party to be added as defendant No.4 in the suit. It was now proved the Company was impleaded just for introducing its staff and employees as witnesses for bringing evidence as the plaintiff found no one to support his case.

23. He submitted that defendant No. 1 clearly denied to have received any payment by signing so-called debit vouchers issued from the company, and those vouchers were created for the suit. Learned Subordinate Judge fell in serious error in finding these vouchers genuine by comparison in the absence of any admitted or proved initial of the defendant on record.

24. Lastly, he 	pointed out certain circumstances and submitted that as the plaintiff did not come up with clean hands he would not be entitled to any decree whatsoever.

25. On the other hand, Mr Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, learned Senior Advocate, submitted that the acknowledgments on the back of the agreement as proved by PW 3 evidencing receipt of money on different dates clearly intended to extend the time for performance of contract under section 19 of the Limitation Act and, in fact, such acknowledgments extended the period of limitation for performance.

26. Secondly, he submitted that in the meeting held on 15-8-1990 defendant No. 1 agreed to execute and register necessary deeds of sale transferring the rest of the land at an increased price of Taka 20,00,000. Defendant No. 1 also in his written statement admitted in the agreement the time for performance was September 1990. PW 1 and PW 4 Sayeed Khan proved the holding of meeting and the decision taken therein. In view of such decision between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 on 15-8-1990 time for performance as intended in the agreement was clearly extended and institution of the suit on 23-5-1991 was clearly within time and as was correctly found by the Subordinate Judge.

27. Thirdly, he submitted that acting upon such decision the defendant No. 1 executed and registered two deeds of sale up to 6-9-1990. Therefore, the learned Subordinate Judge committed no error in decreeing the suit.

28. Lastly, he submitted that defendant No. 1 received in all 79,35,000 and transferred 2.54 acres of land out of the contract with the plaintiff and 0.86 acre of the contract with his brother Nasir Uddin, defendant No.3, Plaintiff proved the payment of said amount paid by debit vouchers exhibit 6 series as well as acknowledgments made by the defendant No. 1 on the back of the agreement on different dates.

29. Only issue facing us in this appeal is whether in the facts and circumstances of the case and on the evidence on record, learned Subordinate Judge was justified in decreeing the suit for specific performance of the contract.

30. More precisely, in view of the conflicting submissions of the learned Senior Advocates, the moot issue would be whether the contract of 2-4-1985 was still subsisting at the date of institution of the suit.

31. The suit is for specific performance of a contract for a sale deed in respect of 1.52 acre of land only. The contract ie the agreement, exhibit 2, was executed on 2-4-1985 between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 for sale of 4.06 acres of land fully described in schedule to agreement. The agreement is a bilateral one. Execution of the contract is not disputed.

32. Paragraph 2 of the agreement clearly stipulates that the price of said land was fixed at Taka 51,53,073 at the rate of Taka 3,30,000 per pakhi (=26 decimals). Taka 3,00,000 was paid to the vendor receipt of which he acknowledged as earnest money. The balance would be paid at the time of execution of the sale deed within one year of the date of execution.

33. Paragraph 7 stipulates that the purchase shall be completed on 31st day of March, 1986 by the purchaser paying the balance of the price and the vendor executing the sale deed.

34. Paragraph 9 further stipulates that if the purchaser fails to comply with the terms and conditions of the agreement on any ground whatsoever, his earnest money would be forfeited and the vendor would be at liberty to resell the land to anyone and, on the other hand, if the vendor fails to execute the sale deed on receipt of the balance of the price the purchaser would be entitled to get a sale deed executed through a proper Court of law.

35. A schedule appended at the end of the agreement fully describes the land measuring about 4.06 acres of plot Nos. 595, 592/740, 630, 628 and 661 appertaining to CS Khatian Nos. 404 and 92 corresponding to SA Khatian Nos. 217 and 55 respectively.

36. In order to understand the intention of the parties as to the time for performance, we have in detail placed paragraph 2, 7 and 9 of the agreement before us.

37. In paragraph 5 of the plaint, it is averred that even though tile agreements dated 2-4-1985 with the plaintiff and his brother pro-forma defendant No. 3 were separate but in fact, it was agreed between the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and proforma defendant No. 3 that defendant No. 1 would continue to enjoy possession of total 5.143 acres of land covered by two contracts and after receipt of Taka 60,36,533 from pro-forma defendant No. 4 Mohammadi Housing Ltd defendant No. 1 would execute and register sale deed in favour of the plaintiff and pro-forma defendant No. 3. It was also mentioned that the time limit for payment of the price fixed in the contracts was also rescinded with consent of the parties.

38. In paragraph 8, it is also averred that on 15-8-1990 at 68, Motijheel Commercial Area at the office of pro-forma defendant No.4 Mohammadi Housing Ltd it was agreed between the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and pro-forma defendant No.3 in presence of Shahid Khan, Rafique Ahmed, Nasir Uddin and others that defendant No.1 would execute within one month sale deed in respect of the balance of 2.04 acres of land in favour of the plaintiff or any person nominated by him and 0.223 acre of land in favour of pro-forma defendant No.3 if further Taka 20,00,000 was paid to the defendant No. 1.

39. In paragraphs 10 and 11 of the plaint, it was also claimed that on 15-8-1990 the parties reached a new contract.

40. The above averments were clearly made on clear understanding that the plaintiff with defendant No.1 intended to make the time as an essence of the contract.

41. Accordingly, he introduced the holding of a meeting on 18-5-1990 and taking of a decision to extend the time limit for performance, cancelling original time limit for performance ie 31-3-1986.

42. To prove the meeting and the decision. the plaintiff adduced oral evidence of PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain and documentary evidence of debit vouchers exhibit 6 series issued from the office of pro-forma defendant No.4 housing company and relied upon the endorsements or acknowledgments on different dates on the back of the agreement by defendant No. 1 receiving further payments under the contract.

43. When the defendant No. 1 did not dispute receipt of Taka 79,35,000 in total for sale of land by 9 deeds, then only purpose for the introduction of the debit vouchers would be to establish the case of the plaintiff that the defendant No. 1 agreed to the extension of the time limit by receipt of part of the consideration at various dates. Mr Alam also very much relied upon such vouchers to prove them as acknowledgments on the extension of the time for performance.

44. The debit vouchers are 27 in number dated from 25-4-1985 to 2-9-1990 showing payment by cheques of Taka 81,35,000 and Taka 2,10,000 in cash. The vouchers were proved by PW 2 Rafique Ahmed and PW 3 James Roger. PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain as an attorney of the plaintiff claimed that defendant No. 1 received by signing the vouchers in total Taka 59,35,000 and that he was present at the time of issue of each voucher. All of them were the employees of the company and were naturally interested witnesses.

45. Of the cheques two cheques each of Taka 2,00,000 were dishonoured. Consequently, total payment came down to Taka 79,35,000 which is not disputed. All the vouchers are printed as of Mohammadi Housing Ltd. Recipient's signing of the vouchers appear to be in initials. Defendant denied such initials as of his own hand. We failed to decipher such initials as to represent the name of Sharat Kanta Sarker. We could not find any initial of the defendant No.1 on the record for comparison. We fail to understand where learned Subordinate Judge got the admitted initials of defendant No. 1 from the record for comparison.

<u>46. We could not find any satisfactory explanation far less any evidence as to why the defendant No. 1 would receive any payment from the office of pro-forma defendant No.4 housing company. It is not disputed that the payments were made by cheques excepting partly amount paid in cash. In order to prove the dates of the cheques, the plaintiff could have easily called for the record of the bank. But the plaintiff preferred not to tread the path and thereby, withheld the best evidence from the Court.</u>

47. In paragraph No. 5 of the plaint it is averred that two agreements were, in fact, one agreement and that the defendant No. 1 would receive the balance of the consideration from said pro-forma defendant No.4 housing company. In paragraphs 8, 10 and 11 of the plaint, it is further averred that on 15-8-1990 the plaintiff reached a new contract with the defendant No.1. But in the trial, the plaintiff has given up that case altogether by seeking enforcement of the agreement dated 2-4-1985 only. Mr Rabiul Alam tried to explain that no new contract was entered into but the time for performance was extended.

48. It is true that the plaintiff was the managing director of the housing company. But the company did not enter into the contract with the defendant No. 1. There was no privity of contract in between the defendant No. 1 and the company. All the vouchers yet bear initials of the managing director. The vouchers do not evidence that the payments were made pursuant to the contract, exhibit 2. So, any payments, even if made on the vouchers of the company, cannot be accepted in law as part performance of the contract.

49. Secondly, the plaintiff relied heavily upon the endorsements on the back of the agreement. Mr Alam claimed them to be acknowledgments. Let it be so. We counted them to be 17 in number dated from 3-5-1986 to 19-7-1988 for a total amount of Taka 39,35,000 all by cheques excepting two. Debit vouchers were also used to show nearly same payments. There is no mention at all in the plaint of such receipt of the payments by defendant No. 1 by signing the acknowledgment/endorsements. No evidence was led to prove who wrote the acknowledgments. PW 3 James Roger deposed by a solitary statement that the defendant received money by signing at the back of the agreement.

50. It strikes the naked eye that 17 endorsements were written on 3/4 seatings. Name of defendant No. 1 on so-called acknowledgments as written on 1-1-1987; 31-1-1987; 18-2-1987 and 23-2-1987 appear to be of the same pen and ink; those on 13-6-1987 and 19-7-1988 appear to be of another pen and ink, those of 3-5-1986; 28-5-1986 and 16-7-1986 of different pen and ink and those of 13-7-1986; 19-7-1986 and 23-4-1987 were still of another pen and ink. We have examined the signatures on the acknowledgments with the admitted signature of defendant No. 1 on the agreement, exhibit 2, and we do not have any hesitation to say that the signatures on the acknowledgments do not tally with the admitted signature of defendant No.1.

<u>51. Section 19 of the Limitation Act provides that before the expiration of the period prescribed for a suit or application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of such property or right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed, or by some person through whom he derives title or liability, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgment was signed. The acknowledgment to take effect for fresh computation of the period of limitation must be proved to be of a time before the expiration of the period prescribed for an action and secondly, must be in writing and lastly, be signed by the person against whom the right is claimed.</u>

52. In the case at hand, the acknowledgments on the back of the agreement were not at all proved. Not even tendered for admission into evidence. Debit vouchers exhibit 6 series having no nexus with the contract were also not proved to have been signed by the defendant No.1.

53. Now, we shall discuss the oral evidence on extension of the time for performance.

54. PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain testified that on 15-8-1990 at 68, Motijheel Commercial Area in the office of pro-forma defendant No.4 Mohammadi Housing Ltd a meeting was held. It was decided that if Taka 20,00,000 was paid to the defendant No. 1 then defendant No. 1 would within one month of such receipt execute and register sale deed in favour of the plaintiff or the person nominated by him in respect of balance of the land of two contracts. In the meeting, besides the plaintiff, defendant No. 1 and pro-forma defendant No.3 were present Sahid Khan, Rafique Ahmed, Nasir Uddin and others. In paragraph 8 of the plaint, name of PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain was not mentioned. The plaintiff appointed Amjad Hossain by a power of attorney dated 16-10-2000, exhibit 1 as an attorney to depose on his behalf in the suit. PW 4 Sayeed Khan claimed that he was present. PW 2 Rafique Ahmed, cashier of the housing company, did not say a word about the meeting or decision. Defendant No. 1 categorically denied that there was any such meeting with him or any such new agreement was arrived at. Shortly, we find that the presence of PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain was not at all believable.

55. Mr Rabiul Alam took us through the written statement of the defendant No.1. Referring to the solitary sentence in paragraph 29 of written statement to the effect that after the expiration of the month of September 1990 there was no contract subsisting with the plaintiff for sale of land, he submitted that defendant No. 1 thereby admitted the extension of the time upto September 1990 and after such admission, no further evidence was necessary.

<u>56. We have perused the entire written statement. In last part of paragraph No. 13 defendant No. 1 has stated that the plaintiff committed breach of the contract and after the expiry of 31-3-1986 the contract dated 2-4-1985 expired. It became ineffectual, futile. More than at one place, defendant No. 1 has reiterated his case in the written statement. In the witness box, he as DW 1 testified consistently in line with such defence and cross-examination could not shift him an inch therefrom. He said that last deed he executed on 6-9-1990. That date was outside the contract. He could not say how many deeds he executed outside the contract. He further said that the time expired on 31-3-1986. The contract stood rescinded on 31-3-1986. He did not serve any notice in this regard. There was no talk of sale of land at the rate of Taka 5 or 10 lakh per pakhi. He denied that at first there was decision for sale at the rate of Taka 5 lac then of Taka 10 lac. He went to the office of the plaintiff at Motijheel 1/2 days. The above sentence of paragraph 29 of the written statement does not appear to have been drawn to the attention of the defendant No. 1 while he was in the dock. In the circumstances, that stray statement made without the context does not constitute any admission by defendant No. 1 on extension of the time for performance.</u>

57. If the meeting and the decision on 15-8-1990 could be proved then the contract dated 2-4-1985 must be held to have suffered novation by alteration and/or substitution of the consideration altogether, not only the time for performance. In paragraph 5 of the plaint, the plaintiff claimed that though two contracts were entered into by the parties but in fact it was agreed in between the plaintiff, defendant Nos. 1, and 3 that after receiving Taka 60,36,533 the balance of the consideration of the two contracts from defendant No.4 housing company, the defendant No. 1 would execute and register sale deed in favour of the plaintiff and, defendant No. 3 or persons nominated by them. Again, in paragraphs 8, 9 and 10 of plaint, the plaintiff claimed that on 15-8-1990 they reached a new contract. At the trial, though PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain deposed in line with those averments but none corroborated him at least in support of one contract. Besides, the suit as framed for enforcement of the contract dated 2-4-1985 belied exercise of the plaintiff.

58. On the above evidence, we hold that the parties clearly intended to make the time an essence of the contract dated 2-4-1985. The time for performance expired on 31-3-1986. The parties did not extend the time for performance of the contract.

59. It appears that the plaintiff got 9 sale deeds in all from the defendant No.1. The deeds are dated 21-12-1985; 13-3-1986; 20-4-1986, 3-5-1986, 19-7-1986, 25-2-1987, 27-6-1987, 30-8-1990 and 6-9-1990 and marked as exhibit 6 series. Of the deeds four were taken in the name of the plaintiff, two in the name of his wife and three in the names of two sons.

Of the deeds, two deeds dated 21-12-1985 and 13-3-1986 only were executed within the time fixed ie 31-3-1986. Deeds dated 13-3-1986; 20-4-1986; 3-5-1986; 19-7-1986 and 25-2-1987 include land of plot No.4, which was not the subject matter of the contract, exhibit 2. There is no recital in any of the sale deeds that transfer was effected pursuant to the agreement, exhibit 2. In each of the deeds, the price is quoted to be Taka 50,000 though the quantum of land sold was not the same.

<u>60. In an agreement for sale of land, the land, price and promisee are all integral parts of the contract besides the time. When the land sold and the price at which the land was sold as quoted in the sale deed do not represent the land and price as agreed in the agreement, such deeds cannot be accepted in law as executed as part performance of the contract. In the circumstances, only possible conclusion could be .arrived at that the parties made transactions, if any, independent of the contract on the basis of agreement, deed to deed. Therefore, both the parties must be held to have neglected the contract.</u>

61. In view of section 67 of the Contract Act and in such situation, any party would be justified in regarding himself as discharged from continuing liability under the contract.

62. Certain circumstances as pointed out by Mr Mahmudul Islam need to be considered to understand the conduct of the plaintiff, before we part with the case.

63. Nature of the agreement for sale of land is no doubt a personal one as entered into by two natural persons. No artificial person is involved in the contract. It was natural that the plaintiff would come and depose in the case.

64. But the plaintiff for no justifiable cause avoided coming before the Court to support his case. Mr Islam suggested the plaintiff performed Hajj and he could not be expected to tell a lie on oath, and so, he avoided facing the trial. His brother Nasir Uddin is also found missing during the entire proceeding. No explanation furnished.

65. The plaintiff however did not find any compunction in getting the sale deeds executed and registered at unconscionable price of Taka 50,000 each only to avoid the stamp duties and other costs.

66. All four witnesses examined by the plaintiff were the working staff and employees of pro-forma defendant No. 4 Housing Company. PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain was the manager, PW 2 Rafique Ahmed an Accountant, PW 3 James Roger, Sale Executive-cum-Accountant and PW 4 Sayeed Khan, Cashier of the company. PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain was appointed as an attorney by a power of attorney executed only on 16-10-2000 exhibit 1 to depose in the suit on behalf of the plaintiff. It was authenticated by a notary public. Before him one Abdul Hakim was similarly appointed an attorney to do the same job by a power of attorney dated 23-4-1991, which was revoked by a deed of revocation dated 5-10-2000, exhibit 3. In the circumstances, PW 1 Md Amjad Hossain could not be expected to be acquainted in any way with any transaction before 2000. Had it been not so, he as a manager would have witnessed the agreement instead of or in addition to PW 3 James Roger and be named to be present in the meeting on 15-8-1990 in the plaint. He was brought to say the case of the plaintiff in Court only.

<u>67. In a suit for specific performance of a contract, the parties to the contract are the only proper and necessary parties. In the suit at hand, pro-forma defendant No. 3 Nasir Uddin and 4 Housing Company were impleaded. They were neither necessary nor proper party to the suit. The only reason for their addition as borne out by the record is to supply witnesses and documents for the plaintiff.</u>

<u>Cheque No. 0220455 dated 19-7-1988 issued from the office of pro-forma defendant No. 4 is found to have been used in all three suits in between the parties showing payments in respect of three contracts.</u>

68. In the circumstances, Mr Mahmudul Islam submitted that the plaintiff would not be entitled to a decree of specific performance of a contract since he had not come to Court with dean hands. The principle is well-established principle of equity. But we are afraid the principle will not necessarily apply in a case when the contract is found to be not subsisting and/or barred by limitation.

69. In the facts and circumstances of the case and on the evidence, oral and documentary, on record, we find the suit was clearly barred under article 113 of the Limitation Act and the contract was not subsisting at the date of institution of the suit. Learned Subordinate Judge therefore, fell in serious error in decreeing the suit. The appeal accordingly, succeeds.

70. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby set aside. The suit is dismissed.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.
